source: IETF RFC 6357 — Design Considerations for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Overload Control
detail: [SOURCE STATUS] RFC 6357 is an Informational RFC describing SIP overload-control design considerations, not a normative mini-app scheduler. [SOURCE FACT] Its system model separates a control function that derives feedback/throttle from an actuator that enforces the throttle; the actuator can choose affected messages and reject or redirect them. It defines basic fairness as equal success chance for requests and customized fairness as priority/resource allocation such as an SLA. For rate-based control, each upstream neighbor can get a distinct cap, the sum should not substantially exceed actual capacity, and caps must be adjusted when neighbors join or leave; too-high caps can overload while too-low caps reject work that could have been processed. It lists goodput, delay, responsiveness, stability/no oscillation, fairness, self-limiting, changing neighbor sets, and computational overhead as evaluation dimensions. [MINI-APP STORE PROPOSAL] Treat app/publisher/tenant/operation as scheduler principals, allocate weighted or equal per-principal rate caps with explicit SLA/priority exceptions, recompute shares on active-principal changes, and choose reject/redirect/buffer only after checking alternate capacity and operation idempotency. Set the aggregate cap below measured safe capacity; publish default fairness versus exception rules; alert on cap oversubscription, underutilization, starvation, delay, and oscillation. [LIMITATION] RFC 6357 is a SIP design framework, not a normative mini-app scheduler; it does not define weights, admission tokens, tenant identity, cost accounting, or safe buffering/redirect semantics for web APIs.

source: IETF RFC 7339 — Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Overload Control
detail: [SOURCE STATUS] RFC 7339 is an Internet Standards Track specification for SIP overload control; its described SIP entities are assumed to support the specification unless stated otherwise. [SOURCE FACT] A SIP client MUST honor downstream overload values and MUST NOT forward more than allowed for that downstream server; control is hop-by-hop and scoped to a unique IP/port combination. Stored values expire and reset, and a server ends control by setting oc-validity=0 and incrementing oc-seq. Algorithm selection SHOULD remain unchanged for at least 3600 seconds so it can stabilize. After repeated timeouts or fatal transport errors, the client MUST stop sending, SHOULD probe conservatively such as with exponential backoff, and can resume after a normal response. A client may redirect only to a destination that is not overloaded and can take the extra load; otherwise it may buffer or reject with 503 without Retry-After. For a non-participating client, an overloaded server MUST reject some requests with 503 without Retry-After so nonparticipants do not gain an unfair advantage. [MINI-APP STORE PROPOSAL] Have the host negotiate and persist per-route runtime state: supported algorithm, current cap/reduction, validity, monotonic sequence, and effective principal/operation scope. Require SDKs to honor hard caps, expire stale state, fail closed after repeated gateway timeouts with bounded health probes, and use only health-checked alternate routes; apply the same rejection budget to legacy/non-participating mini-apps at the gateway. Keep scheduler mode stable for at least a configured soak period and expose state transitions and audit reasons. [LIMITATION] RFC 7339's hop-by-hop SIP/Via model is not an HTTP quota or billing model; it does not define per-user fairness weights, persistent queues, idempotency, or how to authenticate overload signals across a mini-app host boundary.

source: IETF RFC 7415 — Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Rate Control
detail: [SOURCE STATUS] RFC 7415 is an Internet Standards Track document and defines an optional rate-based SIP overload scheme under RFC 7339. [SOURCE FACT] It says a loss-based scheme cannot guarantee an upper bound and frequent updates may affect stability; the rate-based scheme guarantees an upper bound that is constant between server updates. The server MUST periodically evaluate overload and estimate a target rate and may allocate the same or different rate per client; the client algorithm must keep long-term rate below 1/T, with optional short bursts. With two thresholds TAU1<TAU2, all requests are admitted at or below TAU1, only higher-priority requests between the thresholds, and all requests are rejected at or above TAU2; this generalizes to n priorities. The RFC warns synchronized bucket occupancy can cause resonance, instability, poor delay, or loss and describes randomization to avoid it. [MINI-APP STORE PROPOSAL] Give each app/publisher/tenant/operation lane an explicit rate ceiling and token or leaky-bucket state over the whole request stream, not just low-priority calls; implement reserved high-priority lanes with bounded thresholds and a low-priority floor or aging rule to prevent starvation; add randomized refill or admission jitter for synchronized launches, while measuring long-term rate, burst size, queue age, and rejection by priority. Treat zero-rate state as an explicit stop condition and validity expiry as an explicit resume condition; only automatically retry operations that are idempotent or deduplicated. [LIMITATION] The RFC leaves target-rate allocation, threshold/tolerance values, communication between servers, and client priority policy out of scope; it is SIP-specific and does not itself define tenant fairness, costs, or safe retry semantics.

source: Privacy Community Group, Client-Side Storage Partitioning work item

[SOURCE FACT] It identifies user-agent state keyed only by one origin or site as a privacy/security problem; it describes adding the top-level site as an additional key and calls cross-site additional keying partitioning. It lists IndexedDB, Cache API, localStorage, sessionStorage, and persistent storage among the state affected by this work. [MINI-APP STORE DESIGN PROPOSAL] Give every mini-app a storage identity separate from the host's own origin. In embedded or multi-tenant contexts, account bytes by an explicit partition tuple such as (top_level_site, miniapp_origin, app_id, bucket_class), and default-deny sharing with other apps or the host. Show the effective partition in diagnostics and include it in quota, clear-data, and eviction records. [LIMITATION] The work item leaves per-standard changes and storage-access relaxations under discussion; it does not mandate one browser key or any quota amount, so a native host must specify and test its own partition contract.

detail: [SOURCE STATUS] The WHATWG Storage Standard is a Living Standard. [SOURCE FACT] A storage shed maps storage keys to shelves; the current storage key is a tuple containing an origin, and the document notes that this is expected to change with client-side partitioning. Local storage buckets have a `best-effort` or `persistent` mode and start as `best-effort`; storage usage is only a rough estimate and shelf quota is an implementation-defined conservative estimate, not a function of currently free device space. Persistence requires the `persistent-storage` permission; user agents should clear best-effort buckets first under storage pressure, must clear a bucket in its entirety when clearing it, and should offer users per-website storage clearing. [MINI-APP STORE DESIGN PROPOSAL] Treat `best-effort` as temporary/rebuildable cache durability and `persistent` as user-data durability, without claiming that either label is a universal byte guarantee. Assign every app an explicit host budget with separate byte ceilings for package/cache, rebuildable offline data, and user-created state; enforce both the per-app ceiling and a device-wide fair-share ceiling; disclose approximate usage, budget, mode, reclaim order, last eviction, and a user-triggered clear-app-data operation. detail: [SOURCE STATUS] This is the current WHATWG HTML Living Standard Web Storage section. The `setItem()` algorithm throws `QuotaExceededError` before changing the map when the new value cannot be stored; the specification gives disabled storage and an exceeded quota as examples. Make the store/runtime distinguish quota exhaustion from policy denial and storage corruption, and require the app to handle the error without assuming a write partially succeeded. [LIMITATION] Web Storage is synchronous string key/value storage, not a general offline-cache or per-app quota standard; it does not define host budgets, eviction order, or a universal byte accounting model.

source: W3C Indexed Database API 3.0 Editor's Draft
detail: [SOURCE STATUS] Indexed Database API 3.0 is a W3C Editor's Draft, intended to supersede the Indexed Database API 2.0 Recommendation. [SOURCE FACT] The specification uses `QuotaExceededError` when an operation fails because remaining storage is insufficient, the quota was reached, or the user declined more space. IndexedDB transactions must write changes atomically; if a commit error such as a disk-write failure occurs, none of the changes are written and the transaction abort steps run. Aborting reverts all changes made by that transaction. [MINI-APP STORE DESIGN PROPOSAL] Use a transaction as the commit boundary for offline app state: write package metadata, cache index, generation pointer, and user-state journal together; only mark a new app release active after commit; on quota failure retain the last-known-good generation and surface a recoverable state. Put rebuildable blobs and user-created records in separate stores/buckets so cache eviction cannot silently invalidate the durable-state index. [LIMITATION] These guarantees are for IndexedDB transactions; a host's native cache/filesystem must implement equivalent staging, rollback, and error mapping rather than claiming IndexedDB semantics automatically.

source: Chrome for Developers, Not all storage is created equal: introducing Storage Buckets
detail: [SOURCE STATUS] This is official Chrome web-platform guidance/blog material, not a cross-browser normative standard; the article says the Storage Buckets API is available as of Chromium 122. [SOURCE FACT] Chrome describes one all-or-nothing `persist()` decision for a single bucket, while Storage Buckets allow multiple buckets that the browser may delete independently and for which developers can specify eviction prioritization. The documented `persisted` option controls persistence, and `durability` is a hint: `strict` aims to reduce power-loss data loss at possible performance/battery/device-lifetime cost, while `relaxed` may forget writes from the last few seconds after power loss. Chrome's guidance also says buckets can be inspected in the DevTools Application > Storage tree. [MINI-APP STORE DESIGN PROPOSAL] Make the mini-app manifest declare bucket names, max bytes, reconstructible versus user-only data, eviction priority, persistence class, and power-loss durability; display those fields with current approximate usage and an app-scoped delete control. Map cache/package buckets to best-effort and low-priority eviction, while protecting only explicitly justified user state; never present `persistent` or `strict` as an absolute backup or availability guarantee. [LIMITATION] These bucket APIs, hints, and Chromium availability are implementation-specific; the store needs a fallback contract for hosts without buckets and must test actual eviction and power-loss behavior.

Its policy engine makes and logs an approved or denied decision. [MINI-APP DESIGN PROPOSAL] Maintain a versioned operation-risk registry for flows such as discovery, account mutation, scarce inventory/reservation, rewards/referrals, outbound notifications, purchases, and provider-backed AI or storage work. Evaluate context at the operation boundary and map the result to a friction ladder—allow, slow or queue, re-authenticate/step up, human review, or deny—without making one IP, device score, or behavioral signal decisive. title: MiniApp Manifest defines the store and runtime contract for identity, routes, permissions, icons, and window/theme configuration
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Manifest — Conformance; pages, req_permissions, color_scheme, widgets, and window member-processing sections
detail: The manifest is a JSON document that extends/profiles the Web App Manifest and Web App Manifest - Application Information. Its root MUST contain app_id, icons, name, pages, platform_version, and version; every icon resource MUST include src. The pages list contains relative page routes and its first item is the homepage/entry point. Optional req_permissions entries declare concrete system features such as location, contacts, sensors, or camera and may include a reason; the specification says user agents ask for consent and app stores/hosts may filter MiniApps using this data, privacy policy, user preferences, or device capabilities. Optional widgets use name/path entries. The optional window object covers navigation/title/background styles, fullscreen, pull-to-refresh, and orientation. color_scheme MUST be auto, light, or dark and overrides related window colors; theme_color, scope, and shortcuts are not currently supported by MiniApp user agents.
superapp_applicability: Make manifest validation a submission gate: require stable app_id/version, verify every route and icon, derive the default launch page from pages[0], expose declared permissions and reasons in review and consent UX, filter eligibility by device/capability, and map window/orientation/color-scheme settings to host UI policy. Treat unsupported Web Manifest members as non-portable rather than silently assuming PWA behavior.

title: MiniApp Packaging standardizes the ZIP artifact, reserved file layout, integrity hooks, and runtime processing while leaving split-package signing open
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Packaging — Package Conformance; Directory and File System Structure; MiniApp ZIP Container; package processing and signature sections
detail: A conformant package MUST use a root directory plus pages directory and MUST contain root manifest.json, app.js, app.css, with the whole package wrapped as a ZIP file. Page resources are matched by basename (HTML structure, CSS style, JavaScript logic) and routes are listed in the manifest; common and i18n directories are optional, with i18n filenames using BCP 47 language tags. ZIP containers MUST use UTF-8 filenames, CRC32 per-file integrity, and MUST NOT use ZIP encryption, split/spanned archives, or patented features; an optional signing block sits immediately before the central directory. Retrieval accepts the MIME type application/miniapp-pkg+zip, then the user agent retrieves, verifies, unzips, parses manifest.json, prepares the runtime, and selects the start page. The security guidance calls for a sandbox that blocks powerful features by default, CSP/resource restrictions, and discarding undeclared package resources. Package confidentiality encryption is not recommended by this specification. The RPK example defines a signing-block header with uint64/uint32 length fields, ID-value pairs, the magic string RPK Sig Block 42, and digest/certificate/signature sections. The document notes that distribution platforms may split a package into sub-packages, but additional signatures for each sub-package and the whole package are further study; the White Paper describes on-demand main/subpackage loading separately, not as core ZIP conformance.
superapp_applicability: Treat the ZIP as the store supply-chain artifact: unpack and validate structure, MIME, routes, declared resources, and malware/CSP policy before publication; retain author and distributor signatures where supported; serve immutable package versions and verify integrity on download/cache; design subpackage manifests, per-subpackage digests/signatures, cache eviction, and progressive loading as explicit platform extensions because the base specification does not finish that contract.

title: MiniApp Addressing defines deep-link syntax and host/provider resolution from OS dispatch to an in-package resource
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Addressing — URI syntax, URI components, dereferencing, HTTPS package retrieval, and conformance sections
detail: The ABNF is miniappuri = uri-prefix uri-infix "/" identify path-abempty ["?" query] ["#" fragment], with uri-prefix either a custom-scheme followed by :// or an HTTPS host path, uri-infix fixed to miniapp, and identify formed from mandatory id plus optional ;version=. The task shorthand miniapp:// is not the literal grammar: examples use forms such as platform://miniapp/foo/pages/index and https://platform.org/miniapp/foo/pages/index. id identifies a MiniApp under a package provider; id plus version selects a package, while an omitted version lets the user agent/provider choose a current/default/mapped version. The host is a logical namespace and is explicitly not the download location. OS dispatches by URI prefix, the user agent parses id/version/path/query/fragment, prefers a local package path before a remote package server, resolves the resource using path/query/fragment and Manifest rules, and MUST handle dereferencing failures. The HTTPS example requires HTTPS, returns errors for failed authentication/unsupported methods/not found, and recommends an integrity identifier plus package format from MiniApp Packaging; security guidance recommends anti-replay and package-integrity checks.
superapp_applicability: Use one canonical deep-link resolver for QR codes, search results, catalog cards, push notifications, and cross-MiniApp navigation. Maintain an explicit provider/host-to-package-registry mapping, resolve id/version before path, keep path/query/fragment separate for routing and privacy, support offline local-cache precedence, and return actionable errors for missing/unauthorized/version-incompatible packages. Do not assume the host string is the CDN URL or collapse the custom-scheme and HTTPS forms into one unvalidated parser.

title: MiniApp Lifecycle supplies global and page state machines with host callbacks for foregrounding, suspension, errors, rendering readiness, and unload
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Lifecycle — Global Application Lifecycle and Page Lifecycle events, states, IDL interfaces, and security/privacy considerations
detail: The global application states are launched, shown, hidden, error, and unloaded, exposed through GlobalState and ongloballaunched, onglobalshown, onglobalhidden, onglobalerror, and onglobalunloaded handlers. Closing or backgrounding does not immediately destroy the MiniApp; the user agent can later unload it after resource/time criteria. Page states are loaded, ready, shown, hidden, and unloaded, exposed through PageState and onpageloaded, onpageready, onpageshown, onpagehidden, and onpageunloaded handlers. The first-render sequence initializes View and Logic layers, establishes their communication channel, sends initial data from Logic to View, and marks page ready after the UI update. PageInputObject.pageInputQuery carries query parameters supplied by navigation/redirect APIs, and global input exposes page path/referrer information. The specification cautions against locally storing these values and says privacy-sensitive query data must not be cleartext.
superapp_applicability: Implement lifecycle callbacks in the host container and use them for deterministic resource suspension/resumption, page-level analytics, crash/error reporting, cache cleanup, and sensitive-data redaction. Keep global and page state distinct, preserve state while hidden when policy allows, unload under resource pressure, and test that query/referrer data is not leaked into logs, analytics, or persistent storage.

title: MiniApp White Paper positions a super app as a host platform using hybrid rendering, a JavaScript-worker logic layer, and controlled native bridges
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Standardization White Paper version 2 — What is MiniApp; MiniApp/PWA comparison; separate view/logic layers; security and privacy considerations
detail: The White Paper defines a super app as a software platform that hosts and supports other applications, and contrasts MiniApps with PWAs: MiniApps are bound to a specific platform/super app and are packed/self-contained, while PWA resources are distributed across the Web. Its architecture separates a View layer (Web and native components, hybrid rendering) from a Logic layer implemented with JavaScript Workers for events, API calls, and lifecycle; a JavaScript Bridge mediates access to host/OS capabilities such as payment, scanning, files, and calls. Rendering can be stateless while state lives in the worker, enabling parallel rendering and native page-stack management. The document describes widgets as URI-addressed host content with isolated data between host/widgets and between widgets, and notes that MiniApps in one host environment are independent. Its platform-security model includes capability authentication, user authorization, pre-publication audit, configured HTTPS/domain allowlists, and multiple permission levels. This is an architectural/industry reference rather than a standalone conformance specification; the normative package guidance is in MiniApp Packaging.
superapp_applicability: Use the architecture as a store reference model: catalog/review services manage manifests, packages, permissions, domains, signatures, and versions; the host runtime owns isolated rendering/worker contexts and a narrowly allowlisted native bridge; lifecycle and addressing provide the control-plane events and entry points. Separate store trust/review from runtime enforcement, and require consent/audit evidence for high-risk capabilities instead of treating WebView isolation alone as a security boundary.

topic: TUF multi-role trust model for mini-app package metadata
title: Separate Root, Targets, Snapshot, and Timestamp trust with threshold signatures
standard_reference: TUF Specification 1.x, §§1.5, 2.1 (Root, Targets, Snapshot, Timestamp), and 5.4–5.7
detail: [NORMATIVE] TUF defines four fundamental top-level roles: Root, Targets, Snapshot, and Timestamp. Root delegates trust to keys for the other roles; Targets signs metadata describing trusted target files and may delegate full or partial trust; Snapshot records the latest versions of top-level and delegated targets metadata and prevents mix-and-match; Timestamp periodically signs a statement containing the Snapshot hash to prevent replay of out-of-date signed metadata. Every role may use multiple keys and a signature threshold, and clients ship trusted root keys for each configured repository. [SUPER-APP DESIGN] Treat each mini-app package and its release metadata as TUF targets, pin the catalog Root trust anchor in the host/store verifier, and use separate delegated Targets roles for publisher, tenant, or app namespaces with an explicit threshold (for example, a reviewed multi-party release policy). Verify the complete Timestamp→Snapshot→Targets chain before install or update and then verify the package digest and length. A compromised CDN edge can serve bytes but cannot authorize an arbitrary package unless the trusted signing threshold or client Root trust is also compromised; TLS/CDN provenance is transport evidence, not the package trust anchor.
superapp_applicability: Use TUF at the client package-fetch boundary and at the catalog service. Keep Root keys offline and outside mini-app JavaScript; scope delegated roles so one publisher or tenant cannot sign another tenant’s namespace; make install, update, rollback, and quarantine decisions only after host-side threshold and digest verification.

topic: SLSA v1.0 mini-app developer submission provenance
title: Require digest-bound provenance for every submitted mini-app artifact
standard_reference: SLSA v1.0 Build track, Producing artifacts requirements and Provenance predicate
detail: [NORMATIVE] SLSA v1.0 requires a producer to choose a build platform capable of the desired level, follow a consistent build process, and distribute provenance to consumers. The build platform must generate provenance that unambiguously identifies the output package by cryptographic digest and describes how it was produced. The recommended predicate records the builder.id, buildType, externalParameters (untrusted inputs that must be included and verified downstream), resolvedDependencies when known, and subject artifacts. Build L1 provides provenance but may be incomplete or unsigned and is trivial to forge; L2 adds hosted-platform provenance with authenticity validation, while L3 adds strong anti-forgery controls. [SUPER-APP DESIGN] At submission, require an attestation for the exact mini-app archive/digest, source repository and commit, build template/version, manifest and lockfile inputs, builder identity, and relevant dependency resolutions. The store should compare those values with the registered publisher and release policy, reject a missing or digest-mismatched attestation, and retain provenance beside the package and TUF target metadata. Do not describe SLSA L1 as non-falsifiable; use L2 or L3 controls when the store needs provenance authenticity and resistance to tenant forgery.
superapp_applicability: Creates an auditable link from a developer submission to source, builder, inputs, and package bytes. The store can require provenance before review/publication and can bind the provenance subject digest to the TUF Targets entry, preventing a valid attestation for one archive from being reused for another.

topic: SLSA v1.0 hosted and isolated store builds
title: Use hosted, isolated, control-plane-generated provenance for multi-tenant store builds
standard_reference: SLSA v1.0 Build L2 and Build L3; Producing artifacts requirements for authentic and unforgeable provenance
detail: [NORMATIVE] SLSA Build L2 means builds run on a hosted platform that generates and signs provenance, with downstream validation of provenance authenticity. Build L3 requires strong controls to prevent one run from influencing another, including runs within the same project, and to prevent provenance-signing secret material from being accessible to user-defined build steps. The v1.0 requirements further place provenance generation in the trusted control plane and require controls against tenant tampering; all required provenance fields must be generated or verified by that control plane. [SUPER-APP DESIGN] Build store releases in a dedicated hosted service with per-run isolation, immutable inputs, a control-plane signer, and no publisher-supplied signing key in the build container. Verify the provenance before publication, require builder/workflow identity and expected parameters, and bind the resulting subject digest to the TUF Targets record. Quarantine when a co-tenant, compromised upload credential, build cache, or user step could alter the attestation. SLSA describes strong resistance and verification guarantees, not an absolute claim that an artifact is safe or mathematically impossible to forge.
superapp_applicability: Directly addresses malicious or compromised mini-app submissions in a shared store build farm. L2 is a practical minimum for signed hosted provenance; L3 is the target for sensitive capabilities or high-risk packages because it limits cross-tenant build influence and keeps attestation keys outside developer-controlled steps.

topic: Sigstore keyless signing Fulcio OIDC and Rekor transparency
title: Bind publisher identity and build attestations to package digests with Sigstore
standard_reference: Sigstore keyless signing architecture; Fulcio Certificate Authority; Rekor transparency log; Cosign verification
detail: [INDUSTRY STANDARD] Sigstore documents keyless signing as associating an identity rather than a long-lived key with an artifact signature: Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate binding an ephemeral key to an OpenID Connect identity, and the signing event is recorded in Rekor. Fulcio’s official documentation describes short-lived X.509 certificates based on an OIDC identity (10-minute validity in the documented public service), while Rekor provides an immutable, tamper-resistant ledger with querying, inclusion-proof, and log-integrity verification capabilities. Sigstore’s security model uses OIDC authentication to prove account ownership and relies on transparency monitoring to make unauthorized certificates detectable. [SUPER-APP DESIGN] Have publisher CI sign both the mini-app artifact and its SLSA provenance, then require the store verifier to check the signature, Fulcio chain and issuer, registered publisher/repository/workflow identity claims, artifact digest, and Rekor inclusion before accepting the release. Monitor transparency entries for unexpected identities or duplicate/conflicting attestations. Keyless signing reduces long-lived developer-key distribution but does not establish build correctness, TUF freshness, or package safety; protect the OIDC account and CI workflow and combine Sigstore identity evidence with SLSA provenance and TUF metadata.
superapp_applicability: Provides scalable publisher identity and public audit evidence for a multi-tenant store without distributing persistent private signing keys to every developer. Use it for package/provenance attestations, while TUF remains the client update/freshness layer and SLSA remains the build-integrity layer.

title: Use Permissions Policy as the host capability envelope before user consent
standard_reference: W3C Permissions Policy §§4.1, 4.3–4.5, 6.1–6.2, 9.4–9.10; W3C Permissions §5.1 and §6.3.4
detail: [NORMATIVE FACT] Permissions Policy controls policy-controlled features independently of end-user permission: the HTTP Permissions-Policy header sets the document/descendant envelope, while an iframe allow attribute delegates only to a selected container. Allowlists support *, (), self, src, and explicit origins; parent policy and container policy are both evaluated, so an iframe cannot grant a feature that the parent header withheld. The current Permissions API specification describes this as permission delegation: most powerful features grant the top-level origin and delegate to the requesting document through Permissions Policy. When a policy-controlled feature is not allowed, the Permissions API permission state is denied and the user should not be prompted. PermissionStatus exposes granted/denied/prompt and asynchronously fires change/onchange when the state changes. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat the header/iframe policy as a hard pre-consent gate: generate a per-mini-app allowlist from the registered capability manifest, default sensitive features to (), never use * for privileged device access, and query state before showing host UX. Bind the policy to the exact HTTPS origin/package release and tear down delegated frames on navigation or quarantine; browser permission consent must not substitute for host package identity or bridge authorization.
superapp_applicability: For each mini-app, maintain separate declared, effective, and runtime capability sets. Emit a host-owned Permissions-Policy header and exact iframe allow directives from the effective set; require explicit review for camera, microphone, geolocation, bluetooth, sensors, and screen-wake-lock. Use navigator.permissions.query() plus PermissionStatus.onchange where supported to reconcile browser state with host state, and fail closed when policy, origin, or package identity does not match.

title: Make location access visible, foreground-bound, and precision-limited
standard_reference: W3C Geolocation §§2.7, 3.1–3.4, 6.5–6.7, 7.1, 9.1; Permissions Policy geolocation default allowlist
detail: [NORMATIVE FACT] Geolocation is a secure-context powerful feature named geolocation. Its default allowlist is self, so cross-origin frames need explicit delegation; getCurrentPosition() and watchPosition() require express permission unless the existing state is already granted/denied. The request algorithm waits for a hidden document to become visible, and watch updates are delivered only to fully active, visible documents; user agents may rate-limit significant position changes. clearWatch() removes a watch. enableHighAccuracy is a request that the user agent may ignore, maximumAge permits a cached position, and the returned coordinates include an accuracy value; the API does not guarantee that the underlying source is the device's actual location. The specification recommends short permission lifetimes, commonly a session, and advises recipients to minimize use, retention, retransmission, and unauthorized access. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Do not treat enableHighAccuracy as an entitlement or browser permission as background access. The host should show an app-specific consent sheet, allow location only while the mini-app is foreground/visible unless a separately reviewed native background capability exists, clear watches on pause/navigation/revocation, cap update frequency and retention, and return coarse or fuzzed coordinates through the host adapter when exact coordinates are unnecessary. Precision reduction/fuzzing is an additional host policy, not a promise made by the Geolocation API.
superapp_applicability: Expose location as separate coarse-location, precise-location, and background-location capabilities with distinct review and consent. Record purpose, precision, update cadence, retention, and recipient scope per grant; deny undeclared precision escalation and invalidate cached location handles when the mini-app loses foreground status or the host revokes access.

title: Gate camera and microphone per mini-app and make capture revocable
standard_reference: Media Capture and Streams: ConstrainablePattern/MediaStreamTrack lifecycle; Permissions Integration; Permissions Policy Integration; Privacy Indicator Requirements
detail: [NORMATIVE FACT] Media Capture defines camera and microphone as powerful features and policy-controlled features with default allowlist self. If either policy feature is disabled in a document, content in that document cannot use getUserMedia() for the device, and enumerateDevices() exposes only devices the document is allowed to use. getUserMedia() requires a secure context and user permission; constraints select a source and operating range, can be changed later, and may fail with an overconstrained or not-allowed error. When a source is stopped, the user agent updates its live/access state; camera/microphone tracks can be muted by privacy controls or ended when the user rescinds permission. The specification requires user-visible indication when aggregate accessible/live capture state changes and encourages ongoing and hardware-light indicators. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Keep camera and microphone grants separate, per app and per session/use case. Show a host-owned recording indicator that cannot be hidden by mini-app UI, stop tracks and invalidate capture handles on host revoke, navigation, background/quarantine, or renderer failure, and require the mini-app to reacquire permission. Treat constraints as resource limits rather than authorization: cap resolution/frame rate/channel count in the host policy, avoid exposing raw frames beyond the approved consumer, and log only capability events rather than media contents.
superapp_applicability: A capability manifest should declare camera versus microphone, front/rear or device class, maximum resolution/frame rate, expected duration, and whether simultaneous capture is allowed. The host must require an exact origin/package match before iframe delegation, maintain an always-visible active-capture indicator, and propagate native permission revocation as track end/mute plus a typed bridge error.

title: Constrain Web Bluetooth to user-selected devices and declared GATT services
standard_reference: MDN Web Bluetooth API security considerations; Bluetooth.requestDevice() filters, optionalServices, and Permissions Policy integration
detail: [PLATFORM/WEB API FACT] Web Bluetooth is limited to secure contexts and is controlled by the bluetooth Permissions Policy directive, whose default allowlist is self; cross-origin use requires both an allowed origin in the Permissions-Policy header and a matching iframe allow directive. A new device request requires explicit user permission and transient activation; navigator.permissions.query({name: "bluetooth"}) can report the permission state. requestDevice() supports filters over GATT services, names/prefixes, manufacturer data, service data, and exclusion filters. After pairing, a page may access only GATT service UUIDs listed in filters.services or optionalServices; acceptAllDevices requires optionalServices to make later service access possible. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat Bluetooth as a high-risk, per-device capability rather than a generic radio switch: require a host confirmation naming the device and services, reject acceptAllDevices by default, intersect requested services with an app manifest allowlist, require foreground/transient activation, and avoid sharing prior device handles across package identities. On host revoke, disconnect/close the GATT session, clear the bridge capability, and force a fresh user gesture and grant; user permission is not proof that the peripheral or its data is trustworthy.
superapp_applicability: Register each allowed BLE service UUID, characteristic operation (read/write/notify), device-selection rule, and session lifetime per mini-app release. The host should expose only the approved service facade, deny undeclared optionalServices, partition grants by exact origin and package identity, and treat all characteristic values and advertisement data as untrusted input.

title: Keep Web NFC visible, NDEF-only, and read-before-write
standard_reference: Web NFC Community Group draft: Scope; NDEFReader; Obtaining permission; Handling visibility change; Releasing NFC; Writing content; NDEFWriteOptions
detail: [SPEC/DRAFT FACT] The Web NFC draft limits the API to NDEF use cases; low-level I/O such as ISO-DEP/NFC-A/B/NFC-F and host-based card emulation are outside its scope. NDEFReader is secure-context-only. The nfc powerful feature is permission-gated, and scan()/write() can trigger permission handling; the draft's visibility algorithm suspends NFC when the document is hidden, presents no received content while suspended, and attempts to abort pending writes. Unloading releases NFC resources. A write supports overwrite and AbortSignal controls, and the draft recommends the read-then-write flow so the app can inspect the tag before changing it. NDEF readings can include a tag serial number, which may be stable or randomized by the tag. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Do not assume that an iframe allow="nfc" is a portable standard boundary: the current draft defines the nfc powerful feature and visibility/resource lifecycle but does not define a Permissions Policy integration section. The super-app must therefore enforce its own exact-origin/package embedder allowlist and native bridge gate. Require an explicit host confirmation immediately before write or makeReadOnly, read and validate the existing NDEF message first, cap record count/size/types, treat URLs/MIME/text/payloads as untrusted, avoid retaining serial numbers without purpose, abort pending operations on background/navigation/revoke, and never offer background NFC to an embedded mini-app.
superapp_applicability: Model NFC read, write, and make-read-only as separate capabilities. Bind each to a visible user action and short-lived session, require schema validation and an app-specific tag namespace, keep the raw NDEF payload out of general telemetry, and invalidate the reader plus all pending promises when the mini-app leaves the foreground or the host closes the capability.

title: Throttle and foreground-bind motion sensors; do not promise a universal sensor rate
detail: [NORMATIVE FACT] Generic Sensor requires secure context, Permissions Policy permission for the sensor type, the Permissions API, a visible document, and a successful focus-and-origin check before readings are exposed. The requested SensorOptions.frequency is bounded by implementation- and device-defined minimum/maximum sampling frequencies; reporting frequency cannot exceed platform acquisition frequency or the device maximum, and the actual calculation is implementation-defined. Sensor types can define permission names, policy feature names, bounds, threshold checks, and reading quantization. The privacy section identifies location inference, eavesdropping, keystroke monitoring, fingerprinting, and cross-sensor correlation as threats, and lists maximum-frequency limits, stopping the sensor, limiting delivered readings, and reducing/quantizing accuracy as mitigations. Permission revocation deactivates live sensors and queues a NotAllowedError. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer as separate high-risk capabilities; do not promise a fixed Hz value across devices. Set host-side ceilings for frequency, readings per session, timestamp precision, and retention; quantize or aggregate data where possible; stop or suspend sensors on background/hidden/inactive state; and deny combinations that create a tracking or keystroke-inference channel. The host should expose only the minimum sensor axes and derived events required by the mini-app.
superapp_applicability: Require a declared purpose and sensor set in the mini-app manifest, with a foreground-only default. Enforce the effective cap in the native/host adapter rather than trusting the requested frequency, propagate revocation as a typed error, and keep raw motion streams out of persistent logs unless a reviewed diagnostic purpose exists.

title: Treat screen wake lock as a visible, revocable, budgeted capability
standard_reference: Screen Wake Lock API: Policy control; Permissions and user prompts; WakeLock.request(); WakeLockSentinel.release()/onrelease; automatic wake-lock management
detail: [NORMATIVE FACT] Screen Wake Lock is secure-context-only and a policy-controlled feature named screen-wake-lock with default allowlist self; third-party frames need explicit allow delegation, and a header can disable it with screen-wake-lock=(). request() rejects when the document is not fully active, not policy-allowed, denied by the user agent, or hidden. Acquisition is advisory: low battery, power-saving mode, OS policy, or other implementation conditions may prevent or later release the underlying lock. A sentinel represents the active handle, release() is idempotent, onrelease reports user-agent release, and wake locks are released when the document loses full activity or visibility. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Keep wake lock foreground-only by default, enforce a maximum duration and battery/power budget in the host, release it on mini-app pause/background/navigation/revoke, and show host-owned UI identifying the app that is keeping the screen awake. Never treat a resolved request() promise as proof that the OS will keep the screen on; the mini-app must handle onrelease and be prepared to fall back.
superapp_applicability: Declare wake-lock purpose (navigation, scan, presentation, or accessibility), expected duration, and whether the app may reacquire after release. Require an exact origin/package match before iframe delegation, rate-limit reacquisition, deny hidden/background requests, and record only grant/release/reason events rather than continuous device state.

title: Bind the private file-system root and handles to the mini-app origin
standard_reference: WHATWG File System Standard §3 (Accessing the Bucket File System) and §2.2 (FileSystemHandle serialization/deserialization)
detail: [SPEC FACT] The standard exposes navigator.storage.getDirectory() as the root of a bucket file system; its algorithm obtains a local storage bottle map for the current environment and the fileSystem endpoint, while FileSystemHandle serialization records the relevant origin and rejects deserialization when it is not same-origin. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat each registered mini-app/package origin as a distinct storage principal: allocate a separate bucket or namespace, bind every handle and path operation to app ID plus origin plus runtime instance, reject foreign handles and traversal outside that root, and invalidate handles on origin change, uninstall, quarantine, or package replacement.
superapp_applicability: Required for any shared container that runs multiple mini-apps or tenants; origin/app identity must be part of the filesystem authorization decision, not inferred from an untrusted path.

title: Use OPFS-like storage for fast private app data without weakening isolation
standard_reference: MDN File System API: Origin private file system; WHATWG File System Standard §3
detail: [SPEC FACT] MDN describes OPFS as private to the page origin, not visible like the regular file system, optimized for performance with in-place writes, and accessible through navigator.storage.getDirectory(); synchronous access is available in workers, while storage remains subject to browser quota and clearing site storage deletes OPFS. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Give each mini-app its own OPFS-equivalent bucket for databases and caches, enforce per-app and global quotas with backpressure, keep sensitive values encrypted with app-scoped keys, prohibit raw host-filesystem exposure, and delete or rotate the bucket on uninstall or tenant reset.
superapp_applicability: Useful for high-performance offline data in a WebView or browser-like runtime; the host must preserve origin partitioning and lifecycle controls even when the storage API is permissionless and fast.

title: Partition local files by user and mini-app appId
standard_reference: Weixin Mini Program File System: Local files; wx.getFileSystemManager(); local user files
detail: [SPEC FACT] Weixin documents a globally unique wx.getFileSystemManager() for Mini Program filesystem operations and says local files are a separate storage area partitioned by user: different WeChat users cannot access one another's files, and different appId values for the same user cannot access one another's files; the local user directory is exposed through wx.env.USER_DATA_PATH. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Make appId/package identity a mandatory storage partition key in the host, not merely a user key; derive the current app identity from the trusted runtime, canonicalize all paths beneath that app root, deny foreign wxfile-style URIs and appId switching, and run cross-app read/write/delete/rename tests against the FileSystemManager facade.
superapp_applicability: Directly applicable to a super-app filesystem service: the host must reproduce WeChat's user-plus-app partition boundary before exposing any manager method to mini-app code.

title: Separate immutable package files, ephemeral temp files, and persistent user files
standard_reference: Weixin Mini Program File System: Code package file, Local temporary files, Local cache files, Local user files, Read and write permissions, Cleanup Strategy
detail: [SPEC FACT] Weixin classifies code-package files and local files separately: package files cannot be dynamically modified or deleted after launch; temporary files are only guaranteed for the current lifecycle and may be cleaned after exit; local cache plus local user files have a documented 200 MB total limit, and local user files permit custom paths under wx.env.USER_DATA_PATH with read/write access. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Model an immutable package store, a `temp/` class with lifecycle and pressure eviction, and a per-app persistent `usr/`-equivalent class with explicit quota; never silently promote temp data to persistent storage, enforce read-only package mounts, and apply cleanup, backup, export, and deletion decisions within the owning app partition.
superapp_applicability: Required when the container offers bundle assets, downloaded resources, or user-created data; tier and lifecycle must be explicit so one app's eviction or persistence cannot affect another app.

title: Protect sensitive data at rest independently of storage location and tenant
standard_reference: OWASP MASVS-STORAGE-1; related MASWE-0001 through MASWE-0004
detail: [SPEC FACT] OWASP MASVS-STORAGE-1 states that an app securely stores sensitive data and explains that data may come from the user, backend, system services, or other apps; storage may be private or public, so intentionally stored sensitive data must be properly protected regardless of target location. Its related weaknesses include unencrypted private storage, unencrypted storage outside private storage, keys outside a platform keystore, and sensitive data hardcoded in the app package. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Classify mini-app data, encrypt sensitive values at rest with keys scoped to the owning app and tenant, keep keys in host-controlled keystore services, exclude secrets from package, temp, logs, and backups, erase app data on uninstall or tenant reset, and add negative tests proving no mini-app can read another app's persistent, temporary, or package-derived private data.
superapp_applicability: This is the cross-tenant acceptance criterion for a shared container: private storage is necessary but not sufficient; encryption, key separation, lifecycle deletion, and isolation tests must cover every storage tier.

title: Enforce a default-deny CSP and explicit connect-src egress allowlist for every mini-app
standard_reference: W3C Content Security Policy Level 3, Section 6.1.2 (connect-src), Section 6.1.3 (default-src), and Section 8.6 (Exfiltration)
detail: [SPEC FACT] CSP Level 3 says connect-src restricts URLs loaded by script interfaces, including fetch, XMLHttpRequest, EventSource, Beacon, ping, and WebSocket connections, and can ensure those connections open only to trusted origins. It also says default-src 'none' improves robustness against exfiltration because requests such as prefetch may not be addressed by a more-specific directive. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The host MUST inject an enforced response-header policy per mini-app release with default-src 'none' and explicit connect-src origins for approved backend endpoints; mediate native HTTP, WebSocket, upload, and download paths separately and fail closed on undeclared destinations. Treat wildcard hosts and arbitrary URL construction as review failures, and log only non-sensitive blocked-destination metadata.
superapp_applicability: Applies to every WebView or JavaScript runtime that can issue outbound requests. The manifest and host broker should define the allowed scheme, hostname, port, and capability before the bundle is executed; CSP is a browser-layer control and does not by itself govern native sockets.

title: Restrict executable sources and disable plugin content to suppress rogue bundle code
standard_reference: W3C Content Security Policy Level 3, Section 1.1.1 (Control Execution), Section 6.1.9 (object-src), Section 6.1.10 (script-src), and Section 8.5 (Strict CSP)
detail: [SPEC FACT] CSP Level 3 defines script-src as restricting locations from which scripts may be executed, including inline script blocks; object-src restricts plugin content, and object-src 'none' blocks plugin content even without a URL. The specification's example pairs script-src with a trusted CDN and object-src 'none', while its Strict CSP guidance recommends nonce or hash script sources with 'strict-dynamic'. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The host SHOULD use a per-release nonce or hash, or a small approved script-origin set, set object-src 'none', and reject packages that require broad script or plugin allowances. This reduces a compromised bundle's ability to execute code that reaches egress mediators; it does not replace host-side API authorization.
superapp_applicability: Applies to mini-app entry documents, injected bootstrap code, dynamically added scripts, and any legacy plugin-like content. The store should lint the declared CSP and test that disallowed script, eval-like execution, object, and embed paths are blocked before publication.

title: Prevent hostile embedding of mini-app documents with frame-ancestors
standard_reference: W3C Content Security Policy Level 3, Section 6.4.2 (frame-ancestors) and Section 6.4.2.2 (Relation to X-Frame-Options)
detail: [SPEC FACT] CSP Level 3 says frame-ancestors restricts URLs that can embed a resource through frame, iframe, object, or embed; 'none' is roughly equivalent to X-Frame-Options DENY and 'self' to SAMEORIGIN. It says frame-ancestors does not fall back to default-src and must be enforced as a response policy because a meta-delivered frame-ancestors directive is ignored. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Serve mini-app entry documents with frame-ancestors 'none' by default, or with exact host-owned parent origins for an approved embedding flow; reject or rewrite navigation when the parent origin is outside the manifest and host policy. Pair this with bridge origin and frame checks, and do not treat it as a substitute for network egress mediation.
superapp_applicability: Applies when mini-app pages can be opened inside nested WebViews, provider shells, partner pages, or host-owned frames. It protects the app surface and its user-mediated flows from hostile embedding while the separate egress broker controls outbound data paths.

title: Require pre-registered, exact-domain HTTPS and WSS endpoints for mini-app traffic
standard_reference: Weixin Mini Program Network, Server Domain Name Configuration and HTTPS certificate requirements
detail: [SPEC FACT] WeChat's official network guide says a mini program must configure a communication domain in advance and can communicate only with specified domains for wx.request, wx.uploadFile, wx.downloadFile, and wx.connectSocket. It restricts those APIs to HTTPS or WSS, disallows IP addresses and localhost, requires configured HTTPS ports to match the requested URL, and says certificates are verified, the certificate hostname must match, the trust chain must be complete, and TLS must support version 1.2 and above. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mirror this model in the super-app manifest and host network broker: pre-register exact scheme, host, and port tuples per capability; reject IP literals, localhost, undeclared redirects, and protocol downgrades; enforce hostname and certificate validation with TLS 1.2 or stronger; and keep developer skip-domain-verification modes disabled outside isolated test builds.
superapp_applicability: Applies to all third-party mini-app network APIs and to host-mediated resource loads such as images, audio, and video. A release is not eligible until every declared endpoint is registered, certificate-checked, reachable through the broker, and covered by audit and revocation procedures.

title: Make host-side secure transport and egress mediation mandatory for WebView and third-party bundles
standard_reference: OWASP MASVS-NETWORK-1; OWASP MASTG-KNOW-0015 Certificate Pinning; OWASP Mobile Top 10 2023 M5: Insecure Communication
detail: [SPEC FACT] MASVS-NETWORK-1 requires all network traffic to follow current best practices and explains that privacy and integrity are typically provided by encryption and remote-endpoint authentication, while low-level APIs and third-party libraries can bypass platform secure defaults. OWASP's MASTG says certificate pinning can limit communication to endpoints with specific identities; on Android it can cover WebView traffic when platform Network Security Configuration governs it, while other network stacks need separate mechanisms. Mobile Top 10 2023 M5 calls out deprecated protocols, bad or wrong-host certificates, TLS inconsistency, and recommends TLS, trusted certificates, certificate pinning, chain verification, and endpoint identity verification. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Put all mini-app WebView fetch, XHR, WebSocket, upload, download, and native network calls behind a host broker with an exact manifest egress allowlist, TLS and hostname validation, and per-app pinning where operationally supportable; instrument and block raw sockets, third-party stacks, cleartext, certificate bypass, and undeclared destinations. Treat pinning as defense-in-depth, not as a replacement for egress policy or package integrity.
superapp_applicability: Applies to the container's network stack and every mini-app execution path, including WebView resources and SDKs bundled by third parties. The host should prove enforcement with dynamic traffic tests, negative tests for rogue hosts and invalid certificates, and telemetry that records policy decisions without collecting payloads or credentials.

title: Make outbound sharing an explicit, host-mediated user action
standard_reference: W3C Web Share API: Navigator.share() algorithm; validate share data; share targets; privacy and Permissions Policy integration
detail: [SPEC FACT] navigator.share() requires a fully active document, an allowed web-share policy, and transient activation; it consumes the user activation, validates title/text/url/files, rejects invalid or local URL schemes and potentially hostile files, and presents a user choice of target with an abort path as a security confirmation. The API does not reveal available or chosen targets, and a resolved promise means the payload was handed to the target or OS, not that the target accepted it. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Permit sharing only from a foreground, user-initiated host action; enforce an exact mini-app capability/origin policy, declared field allowlist, URL-scheme checks, file count/size/MIME limits, redaction of tokens and private identifiers, and a host-owned preview/confirmation. Treat resolution as handoff-only telemetry, not delivery or recipient approval.
superapp_applicability: Use this contract for share buttons and any native share bridge. The host should reject background or timer-triggered calls, keep target choice in the OS/UA chooser, and expose only sanitized data approved for the specific mini-app release and user action.

title: Require a trustworthy, in-scope manifest target and bounded incoming-share handler
standard_reference: W3C Web Share Target: share_target manifest processing; ShareTarget action/method/enctype/params; obtaining ShareData; launching a web share target; security and privacy considerations
detail: [SPEC FACT] A share_target manifest member declares the action URL and parameter names; manifest processing rejects missing or malformed members, an action outside manifest scope, or a non-potentially-trustworthy origin. The target supports GET or POST, with POST limited to application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data; the user agent maps incoming host data to ShareData and serializes configured title/text/url values, with GET suited to drafting and POST intended for an immediate side effect. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Verify the exact registered package, origin, scope, release, and handler before accepting a share; parse query/body fields as untrusted input, cap lengths and request rate, validate URL schemes and content types, add replay/CSRF protection at the host boundary, and require an explicit user confirmation before any side effect. Do not let a web target's display name or icon substitute for origin and package identity.
superapp_applicability: Treat share_target as a declarative ingress route, not a trusted internal call. Route incoming shares through a host-owned broker that authenticates the target, enforces schema and quotas, records minimal provenance, and keeps draft creation separate from send/publish actions.

title: Treat inbound files as an explicit extension, not an implicit Web Share Target guarantee
standard_reference: W3C Web Share Target: ShareTargetParams; obtaining a ShareData; launching a web share target; multipart/form-data encoding; security and privacy considerations
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Web Share Target draft's defined ShareTargetParams and launch algorithm enumerate only title, text, and url; although POST multipart/form-data is allowed, the draft does not define a files manifest parameter or a standardized file-object mapping. Incoming data may arrive in an unspecified host format and may be heuristically mapped to ShareData, so a mini-app cannot assume that the standard delivers file bytes. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Reject unexpected file parts by default. If the host offers an inbound-file extension, require an explicit manifest capability with MIME, count, size, quota, and retention limits; quarantine and scan content before use, never execute or auto-fetch untrusted bytes, keep files separate from text/URL fields, and delete temporary copies after the approved handoff.
superapp_applicability: Make file receipt a separately reviewed capability rather than silently inferring it from share_target. This preserves portability across user agents and gives the super-app a clear malware, storage, privacy, and lifecycle boundary for shared files.

title: Keep badges host-aggregated, actionable, permission-aware, and rate-limited
standard_reference: W3C Badging API: responsible badge usage; badge model and lifecycle; displaying badges; platform limitations; setAppBadge()/clearAppBadge(); privacy and security considerations
detail: [SPEC FACT] An installed web application's badge starts as nothing; the OS stores and manages the value while the user agent mediates changes. setAppBadge() represents a flag or positive number, clearAppBadge() and setAppBadge(0) clear it, and the latest set/clear can remain visible after the app closes. The OS or user agent may require notification-linked permission, reset or degrade values, localize numbers, honor user preferences, and rate-limit updates; the API is write-only to avoid storage/fingerprinting. The specification says badges should be reserved for states that merit attention or action, not marketing or rapidly changing engagement signals. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Maintain per-mini-app badge state in the host and compute a deterministic aggregate for the single super-app icon (for example, a capped sum or actionable flag); never allow one mini-app to overwrite the global badge, and recompute/clear on launch, sign-out, revoke, uninstall, and stale-event expiry. Require a declared purpose, host-side debounce/rate limits and caps, user opt-out propagation, accessible in-app equivalents, and audit alerts for badge or notification spam.
superapp_applicability: Expose badge writes through a host broker rather than direct global OS access. Keep aggregation rules versioned and explainable, preserve semantic intent when the platform only supports a flag or 99+ style, and treat a successful API call as a requested state change subject to OS and user settings.

title: Keep address-book access picker-mediated, top-level, secure, and one-off
standard_reference: W3C Contact Picker API Working Draft: privacy/security constraints; ContactsManager.select(); Contact Picker UI requirements; contact-property selection
detail: [SPEC FACT] Contact Picker provides one-off access to contact information with user control over shared data. select() requires transient activation, a top-level traversable, and a secure context; the user agent must show UI identifying the origin, requested properties, and information to be shared, allow individual selection and cancellation, and return only requested fields for selected contacts. The model permits user-selected multiple contacts but does not provide silent background address-book access. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Invoke it only from a foreground user gesture, require per-use host confirmation, intersect requested properties with a mini-app allowlist, cap the number of selected contacts, redact unnecessary fields, rate-limit repeated prompts, and prohibit background or iframe harvesting. Do not cache the address book or build a persistent contact graph; retain only the minimum selected fields for the declared action and delete transient results on completion, cancellation, revoke, or timeout.
superapp_applicability: Implement contact selection as a host-mediated, one-shot capability. The host should surface the mini-app origin and purpose, make support/denial explicit, and use a separate reviewed bridge for any native contact workflow rather than treating browser permission as a reusable address-book grant.

title: Make WebCrypto keys non-extractable and capability-scoped, without treating WebCrypto as hardware-backed storage
standard_reference: W3C Web Cryptography API §§13.3-13.4, 14.3.10-14.3.11, and 6.2
detail: [SPEC FACT] CryptoKey is an opaque user-agent-managed reference with an extractable flag and an explicit usages set. The exportKey operation must fail when extractable is false, and wrapKey must also fail because wrapping effectively exports the key. The specification does not require any particular underlying storage or hardware protection and warns that key material may still be persisted to disk; same-origin or explicitly shared CryptoKey objects retain access across that boundary. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The host should generate sensitive mini-app keys with extractable=false and only the minimum usages, keep each key in an app-and-tenant origin namespace, reject CryptoKey transfer between mini-app principals, and expose operation-scoped host capabilities rather than raw key material. For payment, signing, credential, or long-lived encryption keys, route the operation through Android Keystore or Apple Secure Enclave; never claim hardware backing solely because a WebCrypto key is non-extractable.
superapp_applicability: Required for WebView or browser-like mini-app runtimes: use WebCrypto for constrained in-context operations, but make the trusted host the policy boundary and native keystore broker for high-value keys.

title: Prefer Android StrongBox for high-value mini-app keys and attest the resulting security level
standard_reference: Android Keystore system and StrongBox KeyMint documentation; KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder; Android hardware key attestation guidance
detail: [SPEC FACT] Android documents that Keystore key material is non-exportable, does not enter the application process, and can be bound to secure hardware such as a TEE or Secure Element. KeyInfo security levels identify TRUSTED_ENVIRONMENT or STRONGBOX; StrongBox KeyMint is an Android 9+ option with stronger isolation and tamper resistance than the TEE, but fewer algorithms and lower performance. The host can request StrongBox with KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder.setIsStrongBoxBacked(true), must detect availability and handle StrongBoxUnavailableException, and can set immutable purposes, digests, modes, user-authentication requirements, unlocked-device requirements, and an attestation challenge. Android says attestation validation belongs on a separate trusted server: verify the Google root, chain signatures, revocation, and the expected TEE or StrongBox security level. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Generate keys only in a trusted native host alias namespace such as superapp/<tenant>/<app>/<purpose>/<version>; prefer StrongBox for release signing, payments, credentials, and other high-impact operations, with an explicit policy for TEE fallback. Verify KeyInfo and attestation server-side, bind the approved key identity to the mini-app and tenant, require user authentication for sensitive use, and expose only sign/decrypt/unwrap operations through a capability API; never return key bytes or allow a mini-app to select another app's alias.
superapp_applicability: Use as the Android host baseline for high-value mini-app capabilities; treat StrongBox as an availability-checked security tier, not a universal requirement, and fail closed when the requested assurance cannot be met.

title: Broker Secure Enclave P-256 operations through Keychain access controls
standard_reference: Apple Security framework: Protecting keys with the Secure Enclave; kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave; kSecAttrAccessControl and SecAccessControlCreateFlags
detail: [SPEC FACT] Apple describes the Secure Enclave as a hardware-based key manager isolated from the main processor: the app receives operation outputs, while the plaintext private key is not handled by the app. Secure Enclave keys must be generated in the enclave, cannot import preexisting key material, and are limited to NIST P-256 operations. The documented attributes use kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave and a Keychain access-control object; kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly restricts access to the creating device while unlocked, privateKeyUsage enables signing, and biometryAny can require Touch ID or Face ID (with the system's fallback behavior). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Implement a native host key broker that creates one Secure Enclave key per app/tenant/purpose, applies kSecAttrAccessControl and the strictest compatible unlock/biometric policy, and returns only an operation result or signature. Do not expose SecKey references, Keychain queries, or private-key data to mini-app JavaScript; reject non-P-256 requests, generate rather than import sensitive keys, and delete or revoke the host binding on app uninstall, tenant reset, or account offboarding.
superapp_applicability: Required on Apple hosts for mini-app signing, payment approval, and device-bound credentials; the host must mediate every Secure Enclave operation and surface capability denial when hardware or policy prerequisites are unavailable.

title: Enforce current strong cryptography and platform-backed generation at mini-app review and runtime
standard_reference: OWASP MASVS-CRYPTO-1; related MASWE-0007 through MASWE-0012 and MASWE-0047
detail: [SPEC FACT] MASVS-CRYPTO-1 requires the app to employ current strong cryptography according to industry best practices and notes that physical access to mobile devices is a likely threat. Its related weaknesses cover improper encryption, hashing, MACs, signature generation and verification, random-number generation, and use of non-standard APIs for security-critical functionality; the control itself does not prescribe one fixed algorithm list. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Publish a versioned host cryptography profile that names approved algorithms, parameters, modes, signature encodings, random-source APIs, and deprecation dates; require each mini-app manifest and release to declare its cryptographic use, reject custom or weak primitives and non-CSPRNG key generation, and route security-critical operations to reviewed platform APIs. Add static and runtime conformance tests for algorithm negotiation, nonce/IV handling, signature verification, and failure behavior, with an exception process owned by the store rather than by mini-app code.
superapp_applicability: Use as the store-wide cryptography acceptance gate for every mini-app, especially apps handling payment, identity, health, financial, or cross-tenant data; keep the approved profile centrally updateable so a platform or standard change does not require trusting publisher code.

title: Make key lifecycle, keystore use, access gating, rotation, and invalidation mini-app conformance requirements
standard_reference: OWASP MASVS-CRYPTO-2; related MASWE-0001, MASWE-0003, MASWE-0013 through MASWE-0017, MASWE-0020, MASWE-0022, and MASWE-0046
detail: [SPEC FACT] MASVS-CRYPTO-2 covers cryptographic-key management across generation, storage, and protection. Its related weaknesses explicitly include sensitive data stored unencrypted, keys stored outside the platform keystore, improper key generation or derivation, missing rotation, unrestricted key access, failure to enforce a secure device lock, bypassable local authentication, and failure to invalidate keys after biometric enrollment. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The host should own a per-app and per-tenant key lifecycle: generate inside Android Keystore or Secure Enclave when feasible, record the verified hardware/security tier, keep aliases and policy metadata out of mini-app control, require user or biometric authentication for high-impact use, rotate and revoke by version, and invalidate bindings on uninstall, tenant reset, credential recovery, or relevant authenticator changes. Store no raw key material in package files, JavaScript, logs, analytics, backups, or cross-app storage; provide negative tests proving that a mini-app cannot request another principal's key or continue using a retired key.
superapp_applicability: This is the cross-platform acceptance criterion for a shared mini-app store: hardware-backed storage is a preferred tier, while lifecycle ownership, least-privilege access, revocation, and evidence of key isolation are mandatory on every supported host.

title: Treat PaymentRequest as user-agent mediation, not authorization
detail:
[SPEC FACT] Payment Request API places the user agent between the payee, payer, and payment method. show() starts user interaction, returns a promise resolved when the user accepts, processes method data, selects applicable registered handlers, and rejects with NotSupportedError when no handler can make the payment. The API is exposed only in a secure context (HTTPS in practice). canMakePayment() reports support for a desired method; true does not prove that a provisioned instrument is ready. After acceptance, PaymentResponse is returned: complete() closes the interaction, retry() lets the user correct errors and requires the merchant to revalidate the response, and retry() cannot switch to a different payment handler. abort() is only valid while the request is interactive and may fail when responsibility has been delegated to another app.
[SUPER-APP CONTROL] The mini-app host checkout broker should create the request only from a server-issued order snapshot containing the currency, amount, items, expiry, and a transaction nonce. Keep the page on HTTPS and treat show() and canMakePayment() as mediation/UX signals, never as authorization. Authorize and commit with the backend or PSP before calling response.complete("success"); use response.retry(...) only for server-identified recoverable fields and revalidate the full response; call request.abort() when the order expires or inventory changes. Record distinct outcomes for user abort, unsupported handler, validation retry, and PSP failure.
superapp_applicability: Make the super-app host a server-backed checkout broker: mini-apps submit an order intent, the broker constructs PaymentRequest, and only the broker receives and validates PaymentResponse before fulfillment.

title: Gate cross-origin mini-app payment frames with the payment Permissions Policy
standard_reference: W3C Payment Request API §§2.10, 16, 19.2-19.3
detail:
[SPEC FACT] Payment Request defines payment as a policy-controlled feature whose default allowlist is self. The specification gives the cross-origin iframe form allow="payment"; if a frame can navigate across multiple supported origins, allow="payment *" is possible. A document whose policy disables payment cannot construct PaymentRequest, and the payment handler can see both the origin hosting the iframe and the origin of the iframe that initiated the request. The API is exposed only in secure contexts, and the privacy/security guidance ties show() to a visible document and user activation protections.
[SUPER-APP CONTROL] The super-app shell should grant payment per checkout frame and per approved origin, not globally to every mini-app. For a partner frame at an approved HTTPS origin, use an origin-scoped parent Permissions Policy plus iframe allow="payment"; do not use allow="payment *" unless every possible navigation target is trusted. Reject or recreate frames after navigation to an unapproved origin, require the checkout to begin from a visible user action, and keep payment-capable frames isolated from untrusted mini-app content.
superapp_applicability: Implement payment as a capability of the host shell: maintain an allowlist of named mini-app/PSP origins, grant payment only to the active checkout iframe, and deny the feature by default to catalog, analytics, and advertising frames.

title: Use SPC to bind user verification to the order and payee
standard_reference: W3C Secure Payment Confirmation §§4.2-4.11, 7.1, 8-9, 11.1, 12.1
detail:
[SPEC FACT] Secure Payment Confirmation defines the standardized payment method identifier secure-payment-confirmation. Its request carries a server-generated random challenge, rpId, credential IDs, and a PaymentCredentialInstrument whose display name/icon/details are shown and signed with transaction data; payeeName or payeeOrigin is also required. The user agent MUST present a transaction confirmation UX communicating the payee, origin when supplied, total currency/value, instrument details, and payment-entity logos, and collect consent. The authentication path uses payment.get and user verification; the relying party verification procedure checks the expected credential, challenge, caller origin, rpId, top-level origin, payee data, and other signed payment fields. securePaymentConfirmationAvailability() indicates API/permission/authenticator availability, not that a particular credential exists. For privacy, unavailable credentials and a user declining SPC use the same NotAllowedError outcome.
[SUPER-APP CONTROL] The host must not invent or locally validate SPC success. The issuer/bank or payment relying party should create the challenge and credential binding through an authenticated backend channel; the host backend must verify the returned assertion against the live order, expected payment.get type, challenge/expiry, credential ID, rpId, top-level origin, merchant payee origin/name, exact currency and amount, and order state before capture or fulfillment. Keep payment credentials and login credentials in separate relying-party scope/storage where possible, expose SPC only through the payment Permissions Policy, reject arbitrary third-party WebAuthn extensions in cross-origin calls, and fall back to the PSP's approved 3DS/WebAuthn flow when feature detection is unavailable. Treat platform user verification as an authenticator signal; do not assume it is necessarily biometric.
superapp_applicability: Run SPC in a host-controlled payment broker or issuer-approved checkout origin, with issuer challenge/verification on the server; mini-apps receive only a final backend decision and never receive reusable credential material.

topic: Payment Method Manifest discovery and origin control
title: Use Payment Method Manifests as an explicit allowlist for wallet/payment apps
standard_reference: W3C Payment Method Manifest §§1.2-1.3, 2, 3.2-3.5, 4
detail:
[SPEC FACT] A URL-based payment method identifier points to its machine-readable manifest through an HTTP Link header with rel="payment-method-manifest"; the identifier URL itself need not contain the manifest. A valid manifest has at most default_applications and supported_origins. Default application URLs must be HTTPS. supported_origins is either the wildcard string or a non-empty list of HTTPS origins with no userinfo, path, query, or fragment. The processing model fetches URL-based identifiers with a HEAD request and credentials omitted, follows the manifest link, validates/parses the JSON, can install default web payment apps, and associates supported origins with the method. The security section warns that manifest ingestion can disclose user activity/IP information to a payment service and suggests limiting fetches to installed or explicitly requested apps.
[SUPER-APP CONTROL] The super-app operator should publish any proprietary payment method manifest from a stable HTTPS origin it controls, return an explicit Link header to a versioned manifest path, list only host-controlled or issuer-approved default applications, and use an exact allowlist of approved payment-app/PSP origins. Never publish supported_origins="*" for a mini-app ecosystem.
