Validate the JSON and canonical origins in CI, review manifest and Link-header changes as payment security changes, and treat manifest discovery as eligibility/distribution only: independently authenticate the merchant session and verify PSP/issuer authorization before fulfillment.
superapp_applicability: Make the host payment registry the sole publisher of the method identifier and manifest; allow a mini-app to request enrollment, but admit its origin only after review, HTTPS validation, and explicit addition to supported_origins.

title: Paint Timing gives the host FP/FCP launch milestones with explicit missing-data semantics
standard_reference: W3C Paint Timing §4 PerformancePaintTiming; §5.3 reporting paint timing; §1.2 PerformanceObserver usage
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C Paint Timing defines PerformancePaintTiming entries with entryType "paint", startTime, duration 0, and the names "first-paint" and "first-contentful-paint". Its usage example observes the "paint" entry type with PerformanceObserver. First paint is optional; the document notes that a blank or non-contentful document may never produce first-paint or first-contentful-paint, while implementations should at least mark first contentful paint. Paint timestamps are best-effort rendering milestones, and the presentation timestamp is coarsened when the context is not cross-origin isolated. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat FP/FCP as host-observed launch evidence, not as a guaranteed value: emit a per-page record with app_id, release_digest, page_route, navigation_id, metric_name, timestamp, support flag, and missing_reason; never encode an absent metric as zero. Use FCP-to-ready as a release/cohort SLI, keep FP as a diagnostic milestone, and aggregate route/query data only after redaction. If the embedded WebView lacks paint timing, require the native host to emit an equivalent measured milestone with an explicit implementation label.
superapp_applicability: Inject a host-owned PerformanceObserver at every MiniApp page launch, record FP/FCP once per navigation, and feed FCP coverage plus latency into rollout gates while preserving an unsupported/missing state for pages that cannot produce the entry.

title: LCP candidate tracking exposes visual readiness but must be scoped to MiniApp route navigations
standard_reference: W3C Largest Contentful Paint §3.1; §4.2–4.4 candidate processing and entry creation
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Largest Contentful Paint algorithm tracks content seen so far and creates a new entry whenever a larger candidate is found; removed content remains considered, and the algorithm terminates after scroll or input events. LargestContentfulPaint exposes loadTime, renderTime, size, id, url, and element, with startTime defined from renderTime; eligible content does not need an author annotation. The specification describes the API as heuristic and warns that early input can yield no or meaningless results; it is not reset for back-forward-cache restoration or same-document history navigation. A removed candidate's element getter can later return null. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The host must define the measurement window instead of treating one page lifetime as one MiniApp session: assign a navigation_id for every launch and SPA route transition, record the latest candidate before the first trusted input/scroll, and tag termination_cause, bfcache_restore, and same_document_navigation. Store renderTime/loadTime/size plus a coarse content class, not raw DOM identifiers or URL query strings; use release/device/network cohorts to compare visual readiness and do not turn a missing or input-terminated LCP into a passing value.
superapp_applicability: For each MiniApp launch and host-recognized route change, collect the last LCP candidate before interaction, redact url/id/element attribution, and make LCP coverage and cohort percentiles part of visual-readiness review rather than a universal hard-coded threshold.

title: Event Timing supplies interaction-latency primitives for host-defined INP governance
standard_reference: W3C Event Timing §1.2–1.6; §2.1 PerformanceEventTiming; §3.3, §3.6, and §3.9
detail: [SPEC FACT] Event Timing exposes PerformanceEventTiming for selected trusted input events and excludes continuous events such as mousemove, pointermove, wheel, and drag. Each entry provides startTime, processingStart, processingEnd, duration, target/targetSelector, and interactionId; duration measures from the event timestamp to the next rendering update and is rounded to 8 ms or less. The default buffered cutoff is 104 ms, while a PerformanceObserver may request a different future-entry threshold with a minimum of 16 ms. interactionId groups related events, and the specification identifies that grouping as a basis for Interaction to Next Paint (INP); the first-input entry is separately exposed even below the normal threshold. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Have the host observe event and first-input entries in every MiniApp view, compute input delay (processingStart−startTime), handler duration (processingEnd−processingStart), and the maximum duration per interactionId, then aggregate by route and coarse action class. Do not ship raw targetSelector, text, account identifiers, or DOM ids to governance telemetry; allowlist a stable action label and redact at the boundary. Treat W3C instrumentation as the primitive, not a prescribed SLO: define device/network cohorts, minimum sample rules, and p75/p95 or tail guardrails in the store policy, and distinguish page work from native bridge work.
superapp_applicability: The host SDK should install a 16 ms-capable Event Timing observer, group entries by interactionId, emit one redacted worst-event record per interaction, and block or pause a release only when the approved cohort guardrail is breached with adequate coverage.

title: Reporting API enables secure out-of-band diagnostic collection but cannot be a reliable control channel
standard_reference: W3C Reporting §2.1–2.4; §3.2–3.5 endpoint configuration/delivery; §4 ReportingObserver
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Reporting API defines named endpoints through the Reporting-Endpoints response header; endpoint values must be valid URI references and potentially trustworthy. A Report has a type, url, body, user agent, destination, timestamp, and attempts, while ReportBody is the abstract body type for feature-specific reports; serialized submissions use application/reports+json. The user agent delivers reports out of band, but delivery is best effort rather than guaranteed: it may delay, reject, withhold, or discard reports, and it may prioritize user traffic over reporting. ReportingObserver can observe report types visible to JavaScript and can request buffered reports from the same environment, but it is not a substitute for a collector. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Configure a host-controlled HTTPS endpoint on the MiniApp shell/worker response, keep endpoint names and accepted report types on an allowlist, and make the collector accept only application/reports+json with schema validation, rate limits, deduplication, and tenant isolation. Strip query strings and sensitive fields before collection; treat reports as diagnostics rather than authorization, payment, rollback, or incident-acknowledgement signals. Keep a local observer for immediate developer diagnostics, but assume the out-of-band path can be absent and expose collector coverage separately.
superapp_applicability: The Super App gateway should attach a Reporting-Endpoints policy to governed MiniApp responses, route reports to an independently operated telemetry collector, and use the data for detection and triage only—not as the sole evidence for a release or safety decision.

title: NEL supplies client-observed DNS/TLS/HTTP failure telemetry with sampling and privacy boundaries
standard_reference: W3C Network Error Logging §3.3–3.6; §4.1 NEL response header; §5.4 network error report generation
detail: [SPEC FACT] Network Error Logging opts an origin into client-side network telemetry through the HTTP NEL response header; the policy requires report_to and max_age, and a meta element is ignored. It classifies failures in DNS resolution, secure connection establishment, and request/response transmission, including HTTP error responses, and can sample successful requests with success_fraction so failure rates have a denominator. success_fraction and failure_fraction are numbers from 0.0 to 1.0; if failure_fraction is absent all failed requests are collected, while an absent success_fraction collects no successful requests. Reports use the Reporting API type network-error, are not visible to ReportingObserver, and may contain sampling_fraction, elapsed_time, phase, type, and conditionally server/protocol/status/header data. Policies are cached by network partition key and origin and become stale after 48 hours. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Enable NEL only on the governed MiniApp host origin and configure the Reporting endpoint group on infrastructure independent of the app origin; set success_fraction and failure_fraction explicitly, start with a small success sample and full failure sample, and do not request request_headers or response_headers unless a reviewed incident use case permits named non-sensitive headers. Aggregate phase/type/elapsed_time by app release, region, device, and network class; include_subdomains only when every covered subdomain is governed; retire a policy with max_age 0; and treat missing reports as unknown because NEL delivery is not guaranteed. Verify the target WebView's support and its endpoint-header compatibility before making NEL a conformance gate.
superapp_applicability: At the Super App edge, emit explicit NEL policy headers for MiniApp origins, send reports to a separate telemetry service, and use DNS/connection/application failure rates plus elapsed time for regional routing, incident detection, and release rollback—not for user-visible denial by themselves.

title: Web Locks scope follows the storage bucket and must never cross origins
standard_reference: W3C Web Locks API, §§2.1-2.2 and 6.1-6.3; §3.1 SecureContext exposure
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Web Locks draft defines resource names as global across agents sharing a storage bucket, and gives each storage bucket one lock manager. Pages and workers sharing that bucket in the same user agent share the manager even when they are in unrelated browsing contexts. The lock-scope security rules require locking to track storage partitioning and require implementations to ensure locks do not span origins; the API is exposed only in secure contexts on Window and Worker. The document is a Working Draft, so a runtime should pin the supported revision and test it as a draft dependency. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Define and enforce a host-owned lock namespace for every MiniApp resource, for example app identity plus release identity plus logical resource, and map that namespace to the runtime's actual storage partition. Document whether sibling frames, workers, and separate MiniApp instances share a manager; never assume a lock coordinates contexts in a different partition or origin. Treat Web Locks as cooperative coordination, not an authorization boundary: enforce app isolation and privileged-resource authorization in the host broker, and reject or normalize reserved resource names beginning with a hyphen before invoking the API.
superapp_applicability: Use for per-MiniApp state stores, primary-tab/service-worker election, cache migration, and single-writer synchronization. It is directly relevant to cross-context arbitration, but host capability checks remain necessary because the API only coordinates cooperating scripts within its defined scope.

title: Web Locks provide exclusive/shared arbitration with callback-bounded ownership
standard_reference: W3C Web Locks API, §§2.3-2.5 and 3.2.1; §4.4
detail: [SPEC FACT] A lock mode is either exclusive or shared. An exclusive lock prevents any other lock with the same name; shared locks may coexist with other shared locks but block an exclusive lock, and exclusive is the default. The request callback receives the lock when granted, and the lock is held until the callback's promise settles; the returned request promise resolves with the callback result after release, while callback return or throw releases the lock. The queue algorithm permits only the first request for a resource to be grantable, so normal processing preserves request order for that resource, subject to options such as steal. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Require every MiniApp read-modify-write, migration, entitlement-cache update, and network-sync critical section to run inside a named lock callback; use shared mode only for genuinely read-only operations and exclusive mode for mutations. Set a maximum callback budget and use the AbortSignal path for requests that may wait, avoid holding a lock across user interaction or unbounded network work, and define a deterministic global lock ordering when a workflow needs multiple resources. Record lock name, mode, owner context, wait duration, callback duration, release outcome, and contention metrics without exposing cross-app data.
superapp_applicability: Use as the runtime's cooperative transaction primitive for same-partition windows, workers, and MiniApp instances. It can serialize state transitions and elect a primary synchronizer, but it does not make an untrusted MiniApp's code correct or prevent host-level privilege violations.

title: Web Locks define explicit non-waiting, cancellation, recovery, and diagnostic semantics
standard_reference: W3C Web Locks API, §§3.2.1-3.2.2 and 4.1-4.5
detail: [SPEC FACT] With ifAvailable true, a request does not wait for an unavailable lock and invokes the callback with null. An AbortSignal can cancel a request before grant, causing the returned promise to reject with the signal's abort reason, including AbortError in the documented timeout example; after grant, the signal is ignored. steal releases held locks for the name, rejects their released promises with AbortError, prepends the request, and is restricted by the algorithm to exclusive mode without ifAvailable or signal. query() returns held and pending lock information, but the result is only a snapshot: lock state may change before delivery, pending order is guaranteed only per resource, and held-state order is not guaranteed. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Make waiting policy explicit in the host runtime: use ifAvailable for opportunistic work, AbortSignal timeouts for bounded acquisition, and normal queued requests for required transactions. Reserve steal for a host-controlled recovery path with an incident reason, fencing or generation token, and reconciliation before writes; never expose routine steal to arbitrary MiniApp code. Treat query() as telemetry/debug evidence only, never as a pre-check for correctness or authorization, and surface cancellation, timeout, recovery, and stale-snapshot events to the runtime audit stream.
superapp_applicability: Supports resilient synchronization under tab suspension, worker loss, crashes, and contention. The host should own recovery and fencing because a stolen lock does not guarantee that previously executing code has stopped or that other contexts no longer act on stale state.

title: Window postMessage delivery is origin-targeted and requires origin and schema validation
standard_reference: HTML Standard, §§9.3.2-9.3.3 Cross-document messaging
detail: [SPEC FACT] HTML's window postMessage algorithm structured-serializes the message and queues delivery only when the target document's origin matches targetOrigin, unless targetOrigin is the literal wildcard. The options form defaults targetOrigin to a solidus, which is converted to the incumbent origin; an invalid target origin throws SyntaxError, cloning or transfer failure throws DataCloneError, and a mismatch discards the message. The security guidance tells authors to check event.origin, validate the expected data format, avoid wildcard targetOrigin for confidential information, and consider rate limiting when accepting arbitrary origins. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Route all cross-frame MiniApp messages through a host broker or a declared peer allowlist. Require exact HTTPS target origins (never wildcard for tokens, user data, or capability grants), verify the received origin and an application/session identity bound to the frame, validate a versioned message schema before dispatch, reject oversized or replayed requests, and apply per-app rate and work quotas. Use an explicit ready handshake after navigation before sending stateful messages, and bind every privileged request to an auditable request ID and capability decision.
superapp_applicability: Use for host-to-MiniApp, MiniApp-to-MiniApp, iframe, and worker bootstrap messages. Origin matching provides delivery filtering, not application authorization; the broker must still authenticate the MiniApp session and authorize each operation.

title: MessageChannel and MessagePort create transferable channels with explicit start and close lifecycle
standard_reference: HTML Standard, §§9.4.2-9.4.4 Channel messaging and §9.4.6 garbage collection
detail: [SPEC FACT] MessageChannel constructs two MessagePorts and entangles them as a two-way channel; data posted through one port is structured-serialized and delivered as a message event at the other. MessagePort is transferable: transfer marks the port as shipped, moves its queued tasks to the receiving port, and re-entangles the remote port with the received port. A port message queue starts disabled; start() enables it, while assigning onmessage implicitly starts it. close() detaches and disentangles the port, and the specification strongly encourages explicit close to release resources. Unlike the Window postMessage delivery algorithm, the MessagePort delivery steps carry data and transferred ports rather than an origin-bound target check, so the trust decision must be made when the port is handed off. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat a transferred MessagePort as a scoped capability, not as a generic bus: create one channel per MiniApp session or narrowly defined service, deliver it only through an authenticated exact-origin bootstrap, bind it to app ID, release, session, and allowed operations, and validate every port message against a schema and sequence/request budget. Require handlers to call start or use onmessage deliberately, close ports on app suspension, navigation, revocation, and error, and log channel creation, transfer, close, and messageerror events. Never infer authorization merely from possession of a port, and do not expose a host-wide unrestricted port to third-party MiniApps.
superapp_applicability: Provides low-overhead isolation between frames, workers, and host services while preserving a stable RPC-like interface. The host can use port transfer to grant least-privilege service capabilities, but must supply authentication, revocation, quotas, and lifecycle cleanup outside the channel primitive.

title: Gate one-shot Background Sync registrations per MiniApp and keep tags host-namespaced
standard_reference: WICG Web Background Synchronization Community Group Draft, §§1-4 and 6.1-6.2; the document states that it is not a W3C Standard or on the W3C Standards Track.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The API is service-worker based and available only in a secure context. Each service-worker registration has sync registrations with a DOMString tag and a lifecycle state; tags MUST be unique within that registration. register(tag) MUST reject when there is no active worker, when the user has disabled background sync, or when no top-level or auxiliary client exists for the origin; otherwise it creates or reactivates a pending registration and can fire immediately if the user agent is online. The user agent may use a stricter definition of online. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Expose a host capability instead of a raw SyncManager. Bind every request to app_id, publisher, user/tenant, service-worker registration, and a host-generated tag namespace; reject caller-supplied collisions, undeclared scopes, inactive workers, and background-origin registrations. Enforce host permission/allowlist and secure-context checks, persist registration state, and return an explicit queued or denied result rather than promising execution time.
superapp_applicability: Use for small, idempotent MiniApp outbox operations such as message or event upload and reconciliation after connectivity returns; do not use it for exact-time jobs or as a substitute for a host scheduler.

title: Model one-shot Sync as eventual, retryable, online-gated delivery
standard_reference: WICG Web Background Synchronization Community Group Draft, §§2, 5.2-5.3, and 6.3 The sync event; the document states that it is not a W3C Standard or on the W3C Standards Track.
detail: [SPEC FACT] If the registering page or worker is running, the user agent should fire the sync event as soon as network connectivity is available; otherwise it should run it at the soonest convenience. When the user agent changes to online it SHOULD fire each pending registration, in any order. A successful waitUntil() normally removes the registration; rejection or service-worker termination can move it to a waiting state for a user-agent-defined retry when lastChance is false, while lastChance true means no further attempt will be made. Re-registering while firing returns the registration to pending. The user agent MAY impose stricter lifetime and execution limits, and retries follow user-agent-defined heuristics. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Require a durable outbox, idempotency keys, bounded work chunks, and server-side deduplication. Track attempts separately from task completion; use lastChance for host dead-letter, user notification, or compensating action; apply host-owned backoff, retry budgets, and connectivity policy; do not depend on event ordering or interpret online as proof of delivery.
superapp_applicability: Use for offline actions that must eventually reconcile, including queued writes and acknowledgements; provide a foreground or host-scheduler fallback for expired, denied, or last-chance work.

title: Treat Periodic Background Sync as permissioned best-effort refresh with a lower-bound interval
standard_reference: WICG Web Periodic Background Synchronization Community Group Draft, §§4.1-4.3, 5.1, 7.2, and 8.3; the document states that it is not a W3C Standard or on the W3C Standards Track.
detail: [SPEC FACT] register(tag, options) MUST reject without an active worker, without PermissionState granted for periodic-background-sync, or when no top-level or auxiliary client exists. Permission revocation MUST remove affected active registrations, and disabled permission MUST prevent periodicsync dispatch. minInterval is an [EnforceRange] unsigned long long and is a suggestion to the user agent, but the actual interval MUST be greater than or equal to it. The scheduler adds a user-agent-defined amount to the effective interval; that amount may depend on origin engagement and may change between evaluations. Recommended per-origin and cross-origin frequency caps default to twelve hours when undefined. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Require explicit host/user opt-in per MiniApp, maintain an allowlist and engagement tier, and expose minInterval only as a lower bound. Apply host floors, quotas, permission-revocation cleanup, and an observable last-attempt state; never promise a wall-clock schedule or treat periodic sync as a transactional trigger.
superapp_applicability: Use for low-volume stale-while-revalidate work such as catalog hints, non-critical inbox refresh, or content metadata; keep payment, entitlement, security, and deadline-sensitive work on explicit host-controlled flows.

title: Budget periodic wakeups for battery, network state, and data consumption
standard_reference: WICG Web Periodic Background Synchronization Community Group Draft, §§4.2-4.3, 5.2-5.3, 6 (non-normative resource guidance), 7.1, and 8.4.1; Background Fetch is the referenced large-resource mechanism.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The scheduler waits for the cross-origin minimum interval, may add a user-agent-defined delay to group registrations into one device wake-up, waits until online, then fires only pending registrations whose per-origin and anchor-time minimums have elapsed. The draft's non-normative resource guidance notes that launching the user agent and keeping it awake can drain battery, recommends capping event duration and frequency, and says engagement and Data Saving Mode may adjust frequency; its privacy guidance also allows firing only on the network where registration was made. Large resources should be downloaded with Background Fetch. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Aggregate MiniApp schedules in the host, enforce per-app and global wakeup/CPU/network/data budgets, and suppress or defer refresh under low battery, metered connection, or Data Saver unless the user explicitly opts in. Surface best-effort timing and the reason for deferral, and route large asset transfers to the host's Background Fetch policy instead of periodic events.
superapp_applicability: Use periodic sync only for bounded refreshes whose staleness is acceptable; it is unsuitable for guaranteed cron semantics, battery-intensive polling, or large asset delivery.

title: Use Background Fetch for user-visible large transfers, with stricter upload replay controls
standard_reference: WICG Background Fetch Community Group Draft, §§1, 3.2.1, 4.1-4.3, 6.3.1, 6.4-6.7, and 8; the document states that it is not a W3C Standard or on the W3C Standards Track.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Background Fetch is designed to continue a multi-request large upload or download even after all windows and workers for the origin close, while exposing progress and user pause/abort UI. fetch() rejects when background-fetch permission is denied, the active worker is absent, a request is no-cors, the id is duplicated, or storage quota is exceeded. The displayed UI MUST show the service-worker registration's origin, remain non-dismissable while active unless the operation is aborted, and provide an abort path; it may pause on a permission prompt, metered connection, or background start. For temporarily unavailable resources, the algorithm can wait and retry GET requests and uses byte ranges for partial responses; it does not automatically replay non-GET requests because replay may have side effects. Progress, success, failure, abort, and click events integrate with the service worker, and clearing a service-worker registration clears its associated fetches. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Let the host create opaque job IDs, bind them to MiniApp ownership and declared URLs/methods, and enforce storage, size, network, and concurrency budgets. Preserve origin/app title, determinate progress, pause, and abort semantics in host UI. For uploads require an idempotent or resumable server protocol and treat non-GET failure as uncertain; do not promise arbitrary upload resumption. On uninstall or revocation, abort jobs and clear the app's service-worker registration, and expose only status/results to MiniApp code.
superapp_applicability: Use for offline asset packs, media, maps, updates, and explicitly user-approved large uploads/downloads; keep credentials and transfer policy host-owned and do not use it as an invisible background channel.

title: Expose one active media session with metadata, state, and lockscreen control mapping
standard_reference: W3C Media Session Working Draft (5 June 2026), §§2.1–2.2, 4.1–4.4, 5–6, 9–11; the publication identifies itself as work in progress
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Media Session Working Draft lets a page publish media metadata to platform UI and receive media-key/lockscreen-style controls. The user agent MUST select at most one MediaSession as the active media session; it MUST run the metadata update algorithm when the active session or its metadata changes, and MUST run the media-session-actions update algorithm when actual playback state changes. setActionHandler registers or removes supported handlers, whose action vocabulary includes play, pause, seekbackward, seekforward, previoustrack, nexttrack, stop, and seekto. playbackState is a declared hint used with guessed state to determine actual play/pause behavior. The privacy guidance calls for care with metadata in incognito mode and origin visibility to reduce spoofing. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Make media controls a declared host capability with one arbitration slot per user/device audio focus group. Bind title, artist, album, artwork, and position state to the authenticated mini-app package; sanitize fields, clear them on stop/navigation/revoke, and redact private or tenant-sensitive metadata from lockscreen surfaces. Route only the active authorized app's OS actions to its bridge, require explicit play/pause/seek/next/previous/stop handlers, validate position-state ranges, and expose a fallback when the host cannot provide platform controls rather than claiming portability.
superapp_applicability: Use this as the cross-host media contract: a MiniApp manifest declares metadata and supported actions, while the super-app owns arbitration, origin/app attribution, privacy redaction, lifecycle cleanup, and fallback behavior.

title: Require a reviewed background-audio entitlement and make playback lifecycle explicit
standard_reference: Weixin Mini Program wx.getBackgroundAudioManager documentation: global BackgroundAudioManager, background continuation, requiredBackgroundModes, and client-version/review behavior
detail: [SPEC FACT] WeChat documents wx.getBackgroundAudioManager() as returning a globally unique background-audio manager. If a Mini Program enters the background while audio is playing, playback can continue, but the background state cannot manipulate audio playback state through the API. Starting with WeChat client 6.7.2, continued background audio requires requiredBackgroundModes in app.json; development and experience builds can take effect directly, while a production build additionally requires review. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat background audio as a separately reviewed capability, not an automatic consequence of media playback. At install and launch, compare the package manifest, app.json declaration, host policy, and review grant; deny undeclared or unreviewed background continuation. Require a foreground user-intent transition before starting, stop or suspend audio on host revoke/quarantine/logout, bound duration and concurrent tracks, and reconcile play/pause/seek/track state after every lifecycle transition. Do not promise W3C lockscreen metadata or action parity on WeChat unless the adapter has tested that client/version; report unsupported controls explicitly.
superapp_applicability: The host should expose background-audio as an auditable entitlement with per-package review, lifecycle hooks, usage limits, and an adapter boundary that prevents a MiniApp from treating WeChat background continuation as universal OS media control.

title: Treat screen wake lock as a visible, revocable, advisory lease
standard_reference: W3C Screen Wake Lock API Working Draft (29 September 2026), §§2–4, 8.1, 9, 11.1–11.5, 12–13
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Screen Wake Lock draft defines a SecureContext screen wake lock that only visible documents can acquire. request() rejects with NotAllowedError when the document is not fully active, policy-disallowed, denied by the user agent, or hidden. WakeLockSentinel exposes released, type, release(), and onrelease; acquisition is advisory because the user agent does not check the operating-system acquisition result. The user agent must release locks on loss of full activity or visibility and may release them for low battery, power-saving mode, abnormal operation, or OS screen policy. The screen lock is not applicable after the user manually switches the screen off until it is switched on again; the draft also recommends user-visible indication and permits ignoring low-battery/power-saving requests. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Represent each request as a host lease with an app-declared purpose, maximum duration, and battery budget. Grant only while the MiniApp is foreground/visible, release on pause/background/navigation/revoke/renderer failure, propagate an onrelease-equivalent event, and rate-limit reacquisition. Show a host-owned indicator naming the app, deny or shorten leases in low-power policy, and never treat a resolved request as proof that the OS will keep the screen on.
superapp_applicability: Implement wake lock as a brokered, revocable resource for scanning, navigation, presentation, or accessibility—not as a background keep-alive. The host owns duration, power policy, user disclosure, and fallback when the platform releases or ignores the lock.

title: Broker WeChat screen-on and battery signals through a host power governor
standard_reference: Weixin Mini Program wx.setKeepScreenOn and wx.getBatteryInfo documentation: current-Mini-Program screen scope, battery/charging/low-power fields, and platform/version limits
detail: [SPEC FACT] WeChat wx.setKeepScreenOn({keepScreenOn}) controls whether the screen stays on and is scoped only to the current Mini Program; the setting becomes ineffective after leaving it. WeChat wx.getBatteryInfo returns level as a number in the range 1–100, isCharging, and isLowPowerModeEnabled (documented from base-library 3.5.0); the synchronous API is unavailable on iOS. These are host APIs with platform/version mediation, not a guarantee of full W3C WakeLock or Battery Status semantics. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Map any web-style wake request to a host lease around wx.setKeepScreenOn, grant it only while the MiniApp is active, and call the false path on background, route change, release, timeout, or revoke. Use battery and low-power signals inside a host governor to throttle high-drain video decoding, polling, uploads, prefetch, and refresh work; shorten or deny screen-on leases under low-power policy unless the user explicitly overrides. Return coarse, purpose-limited battery bands and charging/low-power state instead of a raw cross-app telemetry stream, handle unsupported/iOS/error results as unknown, and record no precise battery history by default.
superapp_applicability: The adapter must normalize WeChat's callback/Promise APIs and version differences into a capability result with grant, denial, release, unsupported, and unknown states. Power governance remains host-owned even when a MiniApp requests screen-on or battery-aware behavior.

title: Expose coarse battery governance signals; do not export a raw fingerprinting surface
standard_reference: W3C Battery Status API Working Draft (24 October 2024), §§3, 5.2, 6.1–6.6; the draft states that it is work in progress
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Battery Status draft makes getBattery() SecureContext-only and rejects it when the battery policy-controlled feature is disallowed. BatteryManager exposes readonly charging, chargingTime, dischargingTime, and level attributes plus chargingchange, chargingtimechange, dischargingtimechange, and levelchange handlers. The user agent SHOULD avoid high-precision readouts because they create a fingerprinting vector, MAY require access or private-mode permission, SHOULD inform the user, and MAY obfuscate values. When status cannot be reported, default values emulate a full/plugged battery to reduce fingerprinting and prevent forced performance degradation; event frequency is implementation-defined. The introduction advises deferring or scaling work when not charging or low on battery and warns that naïve use can itself harm battery life. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Keep battery data behind a per-MiniApp, purpose-bound host capability. Expose coarse bands and charging/low-power categories, rate-limit change delivery, suppress charging/discharging time and other high-precision fields unless essential, and never allow apps to correlate raw battery history across tenants, devices, or sessions. Treat unavailable/default values as unknown or safe-governance input rather than evidence that the device is healthy; use the signal to reduce high-drain work, not to deny core access, and provide host disclosure/revocation plus deletion/retention limits for any telemetry.
superapp_applicability: The super-app should mediate battery access at the bridge and apply the same privacy budget across web MiniApps and native WeChat adapters. A package may request low-power-aware scheduling, but only the host can decide throttling, screen-lock eligibility, disclosure, and retention.

title: The host owns compliance and safety controls for non-embedded mini-app software
standard_reference: Apple App Store Review Guidelines §4.7 and §4.7.1
detail: [SPEC FACT] Apple permits HTML5/JavaScript mini apps and mini games, streaming games, chatbots, plug-ins, and downloadable emulator games that are not embedded in the binary, but makes the host responsible for all such software; noncompliant software can cause the host app to be rejected. Section 4.7.1 requires privacy compliance (including Guideline 5.1 and sensitive kids data), objectionable-material filtering, content reporting with timely responses, abusive-user blocking, and Guideline 3.1 compliance for digital goods or services. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat every mini-app as a governed tenant: require intake and an allowlisted manifest, content review, report/block workflows with response SLAs, audit/takedown and appeal records, a data inventory, and controlled IAP handling; block publication or disable a mini-app when any required control is missing.
superapp_applicability: Applies to any super app that downloads, renders, streams, or otherwise offers software after the host binary is shipped; the host platform needs a single compliance and abuse-control plane across all mini-apps.

title: Native API exposure and host permission reuse are prohibited without Apple permission or per-instance consent
standard_reference: Apple App Store Review Guidelines §4.7.2 and §4.7.3
detail: [SPEC FACT] Section 4.7.2 says the app may not extend or expose native platform APIs or technologies to offered software without prior permission from Apple. Section 4.7.3 says the app may not share data or privacy permissions with any individual software offered in the app without explicit user consent in each instance. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Put each mini-app behind a deny-by-default capability broker: use per-mini-app scoped tokens and storage/network/data namespaces, require a fresh consent decision for each permissioned mini-app instance, log the decision and purpose, and prevent ambient host permissions or unrestricted native-bridge passthrough.
superapp_applicability: Applies whenever mini-app code can call host bridges, access host data, or rely on permissions granted to the container; permission isolation must be enforced at runtime rather than only documented in developer policy.

title: Every offered mini-app must be indexed with metadata and a working universal link
standard_reference: Apple App Store Review Guidelines §4.7.4
detail: [SPEC FACT] Section 4.7.4 requires an index of the software and metadata available in the app, and requires universal links leading to all software offered in the app. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Maintain a signed, versioned catalog or manifest as the publication source of truth; require stable per-mini-app metadata, owner/status/version and safety labels, and run link-resolution tests before release. Reject publication when an offered route, package, or software item is absent from the index or its universal link does not resolve to the intended item.
superapp_applicability: Applies to the catalog, search, recommendations, deep links, and any alternate entry point that can expose mini-app software; discovery inventory must cover the complete offer set, not only featured items.

title: The host must surface over-rating mini-apps and enforce age restrictions, with parental gates for Kids Category flows
standard_reference: Apple App Store Review Guidelines §4.7.5 and §1.3
detail: [SPEC FACT] Section 4.7.5 requires a way for users to identify software that exceeds the host app's age rating and an age-restriction mechanism based on verified or declared age to limit underage access. Section 1.3 says Kids Category apps must keep links out, purchasing opportunities, and other distractions behind a designated parental gate, and the requirement continues in later updates even if the category is deselected. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Compute and store a rating for every mini-app, show an over-rating marker in catalog and launch UI, enforce the host rating ceiling plus verified/declared-age policy before content, purchase, or outbound-link access, and require a separate adult interaction for parental-gated areas.
superapp_applicability: Applies to catalog metadata, search/recommendations, launch routing, purchases, external links, and updates; an app-wide rating is not a substitute for per-mini-app identification and access enforcement.

title: Child-directed or minor-data mini-apps need statutory privacy controls and a default ban on third-party analytics and advertising
standard_reference: Apple App Store Review Guidelines §1.3 and §5.1.4(a)-(b)
detail: [SPEC FACT] Section 5.1.4 directs developers to review COPPA, GDPR, and other applicable children’s-privacy laws; permits birthdate and parental contact collection only for statutory compliance; says primarily child-directed apps should not include third-party analytics or third-party advertising; and requires a privacy policy plus compliance with children’s privacy statutes when a Kids Category app, or an app that collects, transmits, or can share personal information from a minor, handles data such as names, contact details, location, photos, drawings, chat, other personal data, or relevant persistent identifiers. Section 1.3 separately bars Kids Category apps from sending personally identifiable or device information to third parties, with only limited documented exceptions for qualifying analytics or contextual advertising. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Tag child-directed and minor-accessible mini-apps, disable behavioral or personalized advertising and third-party analytics by default, isolate identifiers and device data, limit age or parental-data collection to the stated statutory purpose, and require child-specific privacy notices, consent/retention/deletion controls, and vendor review before publication.
superapp_applicability: Applies even when the host is not itself in the Kids Category if a mini-app is child-directed or can collect, transmit, or share a minor’s personal information; the host must audit child-data flows across the mini-app boundary and third parties.

title: Make child-first DPIA, age application, and transparency host release gates
standard_reference: DPA 2018 s123; ICO Children’s Code standards 1–4: best interests, DPIA, age appropriate application, transparency
detail: [SPEC FACT] DPA 2018 s123 requires the Commissioner to prepare guidance on age-appropriate design for relevant information-society services likely to be accessed by children, having regard to children’s different needs at different ages and the UNCRC. ICO standards 1–4 make the child’s best interests a primary consideration; require a DPIA before launch and before significant processing changes with attention to age, capacity, development, and child-specific harm; require risk-based age recognition or application of the standards to all users; and require concise, prominent, age-suitable information with bite-sized explanations at the point a data use is activated. The ICO DPIA standard specifically calls out parental controls, age establishment, profiling, geolocation, and nudge techniques as processing to document. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat the container as the enforcement boundary: require every mini-app manifest to declare audience and age bands, data purposes, capabilities, parental controls, profiling, geolocation, nudges, sharing, SDKs, and a child-impact DPIA attestation before install or release. If age confidence is below the risk of the processing, apply the high-privacy child policy to all users. Render host-owned age-appropriate just-in-time notices before bridge calls or optional processing, and block release when publisher policies lack a testable enforcement plan.
superapp_applicability: Applies to any mini-app likely to be accessed by children or not reliably age-excluded. A central host can enforce age mode, DPIA metadata, capability declarations, and notices consistently across publishers while leaving jurisdiction-specific age thresholds configurable.

title: Ship high-privacy, minimal-data, no-sharing mini-app defaults
standard_reference: ICO Children’s Code standards 5–9: detrimental use, policies and community standards, default settings, data minimisation, data sharing
detail: [SPEC FACT] Standards 5–9 prohibit using children’s data in ways shown to harm wellbeing; require published privacy, age, behaviour, and content policies to be upheld; require high-privacy defaults unless a compelling child-interest reason supports another default; require only the minimum data needed for an element in which a child is actively and knowingly engaged, with separate choices for optional elements; and prohibit disclosure unless there is a compelling reason. The detailed standards warn against data-driven engagement features, bundling optional processing with the core service, general or unlimited sharing, commercial resale, and third-party uses with foreseeable harm. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Define a host-owned child/unknown-age policy: deny optional analytics and ad SDKs, personalised recommendations, discoverability, contact sync, cross-mini-app data, and third-party sharing until separately activated for a named purpose. Enforce per-capability collection and retention limits, per-app storage namespaces, egress recipient allowlists, and policy/moderation release tests. Make publisher promises executable: quarantine or reject a mini-app when runtime evidence contradicts its declared privacy, age, behaviour, or content policy; require a documented compelling-reason decision and recipient due diligence for any sharing exception.
superapp_applicability: High for every mini-app because the host controls storage, bridge egress, SDK permissions, defaults, and publication. The same envelope protects children when age is unknown and prevents one mini-app from reusing another app’s data by default.

title: Make location session-bound and parental monitoring visible
standard_reference: ICO Children’s Code standards 10–11: geolocation and parental controls
detail: [SPEC FACT] Standard 10 requires geolocation off by default unless a compelling reason, an obvious sign while location tracking is active, and automatic return to off at the end of each session for options that make a child’s location visible to others. ICO guidance distinguishes core location processing from optional enhancements, requires no more granularity than necessary, and says tracking should stop when the map is closed or the destination is reached. Standard 11 requires age-appropriate information about parental controls and an obvious sign when a parent or carer monitors activity or tracks location; the guidance recognises that persistent monitoring also affects the child’s privacy and agency. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Make the host geolocation bridge deny-by-default and grant it per mini-app, purpose, and foreground session, with precision tiers and a host-owned indicator that cannot be hidden by mini-app UI. Stop watches and revoke handles on session end, navigation, pause, quarantine, or user revocation; reset outward location sharing to off. Expose parental-control state and active monitoring or tracking to the child in the same interface, and require distinct, age-appropriate authorization paths for time limits, purchases, activity monitoring, and location tracking rather than allowing silent parent surveillance.
superapp_applicability: Directly applies when a mini-app requests location or host parental controls. If a mini-app declares no location or monitoring need, the container should block undeclared bridge calls; if it does need them, the host is the practical place to enforce indicators, session reset, and child disclosure.

title: Disable child profiling for ads and block privacy-weakening nudges
standard_reference: ICO Children’s Code standards 12–13: profiling and nudge techniques
detail: [SPEC FACT] Standard 12 requires profiling options off by default unless a compelling reason and appropriate safeguards protect the child from harmful effects. ICO guidance says profiling purposes must be separated rather than bundled, behavioural advertising should have its own privacy setting off by default in the usual case, activation needs age-appropriate explanation, and recommendation systems must guard against detrimental content. Standard 13 prohibits nudges toward unnecessary personal data or weaker privacy; the detailed guidance identifies unequal-click paths, preselected older ages, pressure to lie about age, automatic engagement extension, and data-driven autoplay as problematic, while supporting pro-privacy and wellbeing nudges. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] In child or unknown-age mode, disable behavioural advertising, cross-app identity graphs, interest-based ranking, profiling-derived targeting, and personalised commercial rewards by default. Permit only narrowly justified core, safety, or age-assurance processing under a documented DPIA, separate purpose controls, and content safeguards; do not repurpose age-assurance signals for advertising. Review host and publisher UI for equal prominence and effort, no prechecked low-privacy choices or older ages, no countdown or loss-pressure tactics, and no data-driven autoplay; require pause, stop, and easy high-privacy recovery controls. Treat host personalization as profiling too, not only publisher code.
superapp_applicability: Critical for a multi-mini-app host because the container can create cross-app profiles even when individual publishers cannot. The host should provide a single deny-by-default profiling policy, prevent publisher access to shared identity or behavioural segments, and require separate review for any safety or age-assurance exception.

title: Add device kill switches and prominent child rights/reporting tools
standard_reference: ICO Children’s Code standards 14–15: connected toys and devices and online tools
detail: [SPEC FACT] Standard 14 requires effective tools for connected toys or devices to conform to the code. ICO guidance covers internet-connected toys, bands, speakers, cameras, and microphones; expects safe defaults for multiple users of different ages, clear purchase and setup information, active indicators for recording or listening, and an easy connection-off or non-connected mode. Standard 15 requires prominent, accessible, age-appropriate tools for data rights and concerns, including access/download, deletion, stopping or restricting use, correction, progress tracking, and urgent safeguarding escalation. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] If a mini-app can reach host-connected sensors or toys, require a device and capability manifest, per-profile isolation, host-owned capture and location indicators, a physical or host kill switch, and no passive collection; unknown household users must receive child-safe defaults, and publishers must not bypass the container through a native bridge. Add a prominent child-facing privacy/help/report control and self-service export, delete, stop-sharing, and correction paths; show request status and route urgent safety reports to escalation with auditable host-level handling times.
superapp_applicability: Conditional for connected-device mini-apps and universal for the host’s rights/reporting layer. The container can centralize indicators, revocation, profile separation, rights workflows, and safeguarding escalation even when device or mini-app interfaces are inconsistent.

title: Single questionnaire, regional algorithmic ratings, and local storefront display
standard_reference: International Age Rating Coalition (IARC) Global Rating System — About IARC, How IARC Works, and FAQ
detail: [SPEC FACT] IARC describes a storefront-integrated SaaS solution: a developer completes one questionnaire through a participating storefront, and IARC immediately assigns age ratings for each participating authority using algorithms based on distinct regional standards plus a generic rating for the rest of the world. The storefront ingests the result and displays the regionally appropriate rating; IARC says it does not host a centralized public ratings site. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Ingest the questionnaire result and certificate metadata during mini-app onboarding, keep the IARC regional outputs separate from any generic fallback, select the output from a jurisdiction policy table, and make parental controls key off the viewer's applicable local rating rather than a single global age value.
superapp_applicability: Use IARC as the catalog's external age-rating federation layer: map account/device jurisdiction to the correct regional rating, preserve raw IARC metadata for audit, and quarantine an app when the region or rating payload is missing instead of silently treating the generic rating as universally authoritative.

title: Canonical participating-authority map covers the requested regional systems
standard_reference: IARC Participating Rating Authorities and IARC Milestones
detail: [SPEC FACT] IARC's participant page lists Australian Classification Board (Australia), Classificação Indicativa (Brazil), Digital Game Self-regulation Committee/DGSC (Taiwan), Entertainment Software Rating Board/ESRB (US & Canada), General Authority for Media Regulation/Gmedia (Kingdom of Saudi Arabia), Game Rating and Administration Committee/GRAC (Republic of Korea), Indonesia Game Rating System/IGRS (Indonesia), Pan European Game Information/PEGI (UK & Europe), and Unterhaltungssoftware Selbstkontrolle/USK (Germany). The milestones page records the initial 2013 group (ClassInd, ESRB, PEGI, USK) and later additions including ACB, GRAC, DGSC, IGRS, and Gmedia. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Store both IARC's canonical authority name and its region scope; use a versioned region-to-authority policy table and preserve the raw label so aliases such as TESRI or GAMR are not substituted without separate verification.
superapp_applicability: Render the locally applicable authority's mark/name and age band, while retaining the other regional outputs for cross-border catalog operations, parental-policy testing, compliance review, and later re-rating.

title: Interactive disclosures cover purchases, user interaction, location sharing, and Internet access
standard_reference: IARC Interactive Elements and Content Descriptors
detail: [SPEC FACT] IARC says the questionnaire result includes Content Descriptors and Interactive Elements. The official description gives upfront notice for in-game purchases, including randomized purchases, interaction with other users, sharing users' location, and Internet access; the About page likewise identifies in-app/game purchases (including randomized ones), location collection/sharing with other users, and unrestricted Internet. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Persist these as machine-readable catalog capabilities (purchase, randomized digital-item/loot-box purchase, user interaction, location sharing, unrestricted web access) in addition to the age rating; expose them before install and bind purchase, communication, location, and embedded-browser permissions to the parent's local policy. Do not infer chat, voice, or fine/coarse location scope unless the questionnaire metadata explicitly supplies it.
superapp_applicability: Use the flags as pre-install risk signals and parental-gating inputs for mini-apps: require explicit consent or stronger age gates for randomized purchases, user-to-user features, location sharing, and unrestricted web access, with an audit record of the metadata version shown to the user.

title: Authority monitoring, API corrections, and rating-check disputes are part of the digital workflow
standard_reference: IARC Post-release Monitoring, Corrections, and Rating Checks
detail: [SPEC FACT] IARC explains that its automated process issues ratings instantly without authority review before release, so some assignments may require post-release modification. Its How IARC Works page says rating authorities monitor assigned ratings and that corrections are promptly implemented through APIs with storefronts. Developers may request a rating check, explain why a rating should differ, and provide evidence such as video clips or a build for evaluation by the relevant authority or authorities. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat a rating as mutable catalog metadata: retain payload versions and timestamps, poll or receive API updates, invalidate cached regional gates when a correction arrives, and preserve the developer's dispute request, evidence references, authority response, and resulting decision in an audit trail.
superapp_applicability: A super-app catalog should support post-publication re-rating without republishing the whole mini-app, including notification/re-consent when an age band or interactive element becomes stricter and an escalation path for developer rating-check requests.

title: Certificate ID enables reuse across participating storefronts, including named major stores
standard_reference: IARC Rating Certificate ID/Certification Code Portability
detail: [SPEC FACT] IARC says a developer completes the questionnaire once and can use the IARC rating certificate ID on other IARC storefronts so those storefronts can access all rating information. The FAQ qualifies this as reuse in most cases of the certification code on another participating storefront, eliminating a repeat rating process; only licensed storefronts can display IARC ratings because IARC may need to modify them through APIs. IARC's milestones identify deployments on Nintendo eShop (2015), Google Play (2015), Microsoft Store for Windows and Xbox (2016), and the Oculus Store, identified as Meta Quest (2017). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Preserve the immutable certificate ID/code alongside the mini-app's package identity and questionnaire metadata, submit it during federation onboarding, verify the returned ratings belong to the same app, and consume correction updates; do not display an IARC rating on a non-licensed path or assume portability outside participating IARC storefronts.
superapp_applicability: Implement certificate-aware onboarding so a mini-app can be rated once and reused across catalog surfaces, while retaining per-surface licensing status, regional display mappings, update timestamps, and a fail-closed path when certificate lookup or authority correction cannot be verified.

title: Enforce Trusted Types at every mini-app DOM XSS sink
standard_reference: W3C Trusted Types §4.2.1 require-trusted-types-for directive; §2.1.1 DOM XSS injection sinks; §3.5 Get Trusted Type compliant string
detail: [SPEC FACT] The specification groups the DOM XSS sinks under the 'script' sink group, including script URL/text setters, eval-like code execution, javascript: navigation, HTML parsing setters such as Element.innerHTML, ShadowRoot.innerHTML, Element.outerHTML, Document.write, and parseFromString. The require-trusted-types-for directive configures whether that group requires matching Trusted Types; when enforcement is active, compliant-input processing accepts the matching Trusted Type, otherwise invokes an allowed default policy or blocks the string with a TypeError. MDN documents the deployed header form as Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script'. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Make the mini-app document and worker realms enforcement boundaries: require the header (or an equivalent host-enforced policy) for every registered package, fail closed on raw-string sink violations, and include host-created templates and bridge-generated DOM in the same boundary. Capture sink name, package identifier, version, realm, and code location in a privacy-minimized violation event; do not treat a report-only deployment as protection.
superapp_applicability: container: provision Trusted Types CSP and isolate each mini-app realm; store: require this control in the package security profile and reject runtimes that cannot enforce it; runtime: block raw strings at DOM/script sinks and emit actionable, non-sensitive violation telemetry.

title: Allowlist and review Trusted Type policy factories
standard_reference: W3C Trusted Types §2.3 Policies; §2.4.1 Content Security Policy; §4.2.2 trusted-types directive; §4.2.5 Should Trusted Type policy creation be blocked by Content Security Policy; §5.4 Best practices for policy design
detail: [SPEC FACT] TrustedHTML, TrustedScript, and TrustedScriptURL objects are created through application-defined policies; the specification treats policy creation as security-critical and says insecure policies can still expose sinks to attacker-controlled data. The trusted-types directive controls policy creation: an enforced allowlist blocks a policy name not listed, while the default policy routes strings passed to enforced sinks through its callbacks. The specification advises secure-for-all-input policies or tightly limited access to policies and self-contained, reviewed policy code. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Require a finite policy-name allowlist in each mini-app manifest and deploy production CSP with only approved names; prohibit wildcard and duplicate-name allowances, and permit a default policy only as a time-bounded migration profile. Review every createHTML/createScript/createScriptURL callback as privileged code, pin its sanitizer configuration and dependency versions, and make TrustedScriptURL policies allow only registered HTTPS origins and paths (or disable dynamic script URLs). Quarantine packages that create unregistered policies or mutate policy decisions from unreviewed global state.
superapp_applicability: container: enforce the policy-name allowlist and restrict policy creation per realm; store: record policy names, callback purpose, sanitizer dependency, and approved resource origins during review; runtime: expose only approved policy capabilities and block or quarantine policy-creation violations.

title: Pin executable and stylesheet bytes with SRI before mini-app execution
standard_reference: W3C Subresource Integrity §3.1 Integrity metadata; §3.2 Cryptographic hash functions; §3.3.3 Get the strongest metadata from set; §3.3.4 Do bytes match metadataList?; §3.7 Handling integrity violations
detail: [SPEC FACT] SRI requires integrity metadata containing a hash function and digest to validate a response; conformant user agents must support SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512. When multiple algorithms are present, the user agent selects the strongest supported metadata, compares the computed digest to the expected value, and refuses to render or execute a response that fails the check, returning a network error. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The store should bind every executable script and security-relevant stylesheet in a mini-app package manifest to an exact URL or package path, approved version, and SRI digest; generate a new approval record whenever bytes change. The container must not execute a resource with a missing, malformed, or mismatched digest, must quarantine the package and surface a safe update or rollback path, and should retain a failure event linking package/version/resource without logging sensitive payloads. Pair SRI with source review and signer or provenance controls: a matching hash proves byte identity, not that the approved bytes are benign.
superapp_applicability: container: verify integrity metadata before applying styles or executing code; store: calculate, review, and persist hashes for package and permitted remote resources; runtime: fail closed on mismatch, quarantine the mini-app, and support a trusted fallback or rollback.

title: Require CORS and integrity metadata for cross-origin mini-app resources
standard_reference: W3C Subresource Integrity §3.3.4 Do bytes match metadataList? (CORS requirement); §3.4 Verification of HTML document subresources; §3.8 Integrity-Policy; §3.8.2 Should request be blocked by Integrity Policy
detail: [SPEC FACT] The SRI specification states that integrity-protected cross-origin requests require CORS and that using SRI without CORS is a logical error. Its Integrity-Policy and Integrity-Policy-Report-Only headers govern integrity metadata for script and style destinations: an enforcing policy blocks requests lacking integrity metadata or using no-CORS mode, while report-only mode allows them and reports violations. MDN likewise requires a CORS-enabled response and the crossorigin attribute for cross-origin SRI. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The mini-app loader should classify every cross-origin script and stylesheet request, require an explicit CORS response and crossorigin=anonymous, and deny no-CORS external code or styles. Deploy Integrity-Policy-Report-Only in staging and on existing packages to inventory legacy loads, then enforce the script/style destinations with a reporting endpoint after the store's manifest corpus is clean. Treat a CORS failure, missing integrity metadata, or integrity-policy block as a package-load failure rather than falling back to an unverified URL.
superapp_applicability: container: own the URL loader, CORS mode, crossorigin attribute, and Integrity-Policy headers; store: reject manifests that reference cross-origin code without CORS and SRI metadata; runtime: report-only during migration, then block nonconforming script/style loads and expose a safe recovery state.

title: Default-deny dangerous DOM sinks and use text or DOM construction for untrusted mini-app data
standard_reference: OWASP DOM Based XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet RULE #6 Populate the DOM using safe JavaScript functions or properties; RULE #7 Fixing DOM Cross-site Scripting Vulnerabilities; GUIDELINE #1; GUIDELINE #3; GUIDELINE #4; GUIDELINE #5
detail: [SPEC FACT] OWASP recommends textContent for untrusted display data, says innerText or textContent should replace innerHTML for ordinary text updates, and identifies createElement, setAttribute (only for limited non-executable attributes), and appendChild as safer construction primitives. It says to avoid innerHTML, outerHTML, document.write/writeln, and implicit eval paths, and warns that event-handler attributes such as onclick are command-execution contexts. W3C Trusted Types independently identifies these classes as DOM XSS injection sinks. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Make the host SDK's default rendering helpers use textContent or vetted DOM-node builders for catalog metadata, reviews, permissions, and error text; allow URL-valued attributes only after scheme, origin, and path validation. Reject or gate innerHTML/outerHTML/document.write, eval, Function, string setTimeout/setInterval, javascript: URLs, and event-handler attributes in static analysis and runtime wrappers. Permit an HTML sink only through a reviewed TrustedHTML policy with a pinned sanitizer, and test every package against a DOM-XSS payload corpus in the same sandbox used in production.
superapp_applicability: container: expose safe DOM APIs and enforce sink telemetry or blocking; store: lint and review package code for dangerous sinks and context-specific encoding mistakes; runtime: render untrusted values as text, restrict executable attributes and dynamic code, and use Trusted Types as a fail-closed backstop.

title: Make Wasm imports the only host capability and keep linear memory app-scoped
standard_reference: WebAssembly Core Specification §1.1.1 (Design Goals), §1.1.3 (Security Considerations), and §4.2.6 (Module Instances); WebAssembly Web API 2 §6 (Security and Privacy Considerations)
detail: [SPEC FACT] Core says validated code executes in a memory-safe, sandboxed environment; a module has no ambient access, and I/O, resources, or operating-system calls can only occur through functions provided by the embedder and imported into the module; the embedder controls or limits those capabilities. The module-instance model collects imported, defined, and exported entities. The JavaScript Memory API permits memory to be imported/exported, while shared memory is an explicit constructor mode. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Start each mini-app in an app- and tenant-bound Wasm instance with an empty default import set; expose only host-broker functions named in a signed manifest, validate import module/name/signature, and never hand out raw OS handles, host pointers, or a Memory object shared with another app. Use fresh unshared linear memory by default; make shared Memory an explicit capability with owner, scope, lifecycle, and revocation checks; put high-risk packages in a separate process or equivalent OS/hardware boundary because the Core security section leaves embedder isolation and side-channel mitigations to the host.
superapp_applicability: container: isolate each mini-app runtime and capability namespace; store: require manifest-declared imports and app/tenant ownership for any persisted or shared memory; runtime: deny undeclared imports, raw host handles, cross-app Memory sharing, and side-channel-sensitive execution without an additional OS boundary.

title: Fail closed on out-of-range, empty, or type-mismatched indirect calls
standard_reference: WebAssembly Core Specification 1 §2.3.6 (Table Types), §3.3.5.11 (Validation of call_indirect), and §4.4.5.11 (Execution of call_indirect)
detail: [SPEC FACT] Core 1 defines a table as an array of opaque values whose funcref entries may have heterogeneous function types and constrains its minimum and optional maximum number of entries. The call_indirect validation rule requires a table and funcref element type. At execution, an index not smaller than the table length traps, an uninitialized entry traps, and a callee whose actual function type differs from the instruction's expected type traps before invocation. MDN also documents that a WebAssembly.Table is accessible and mutable from both JavaScript and Wasm and exposes get, set, and grow operations. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Allocate a table per mini-app, require an explicit initial/max-entry declaration, and never import a host table containing another app's or the container's callable references. Bind table imports/exports to the owning package and runtime instance, wrap JavaScript get/set/grow paths with ownership and bounds checks, reject unauthorized table mutation, and test all three trap cases plus cross-app function-reference attempts. Treat a table entry as a code capability, not as inert data.
superapp_applicability: container: prevent cross-runtime table and function-reference sharing; store: lint and sign table initial/max-entry and import declarations; runtime: preserve Wasm bounds, initialization, and signature checks and surface traps as contained app faults rather than host crashes.

title: Gate instantiateStreaming on exact media type, CORS status, and package identity
standard_reference: WebAssembly Web API 1 §1 (Streaming Module Compilation and Instantiation); current WebAssembly Web API 2 §2 (Streaming Module Compilation and Instantiation)
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WebAssembly Web API algorithm for instantiateStreaming compiles a potential WebAssembly Response and then instantiates the resulting module with the import object. It rejects with TypeError when the response is not CORS-same-origin, does not have an ok status, or does not have the exact application/wasm MIME type; extra parameters such as an empty application/wasm; are not allowed. Compilation is asynchronous and may be performed in a streaming manner, while compilation or instantiation failures reject with a CompileError or another relevant error. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Make the package gateway serve only the registered artifact with Content-Type application/wasm, an approved origin/CORS policy, and an ok response; bind the response URL and digest/signature to the store manifest before allowing compilation, because MIME, CORS, and status checks do not authenticate package identity. Fail closed on redirects or response identities outside the manifest, validate the import object against the capability policy, and cache compiled modules only under artifact digest plus runtime-policy version. Do not treat streaming or browser MIME checks as a substitute for signature verification or host sandboxing.
superapp_applicability: container: mediate fetch/Response creation and reject untrusted origins or response metadata; store: publish exact Wasm media type and immutable digest/signature metadata; runtime: enforce import policy, contained compile/link/runtime errors, and cache isolation per package and policy version.

title: Allow Wasm compilation narrowly without granting JavaScript eval
standard_reference: W3C Content Security Policy Level 3 §2.3.1 (Source Lists), §4.5.1 (EnsureCSPDoesNotBlockWasmByteCompilation), and §6.1.10 (script-src)
detail: [SPEC FACT] CSP3 lists new WebAssembly.Module(), compile(), compileStreaming(), instantiate(), and instantiateStreaming() as WebAssembly execution sinks gated by the wasm-unsafe-eval or unsafe-eval source expressions. It defines wasm-unsafe-eval as the more specific keyword: it permits WebAssembly compilation/instantiation without permitting JavaScript eval, whereas unsafe-eval permits both. MDN likewise states that without wasm-unsafe-eval WebAssembly is blocked and that unsafe-eval is broader. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Default a mini-app policy to omit both keywords so Wasm compilation is blocked; where Wasm is an approved capability, grant only script-src 'wasm-unsafe-eval' to the vetted package and keep unsafe-eval prohibited. Store-lint response and manifest CSP, reject broad wildcard/unsafe-eval policies, test compile and instantiate paths under enforcement and report-only modes, and keep native API/import mediation separate because CSP is a browser execution policy rather than an OS or host-bridge boundary. Treat CSP3's working-draft status as a compatibility input and verify target WebView behavior before release.
superapp_applicability: container: inject and enforce a per-app CSP on the entry document/WebView; store: require a reviewed CSP declaration and reject unsafe-eval for untrusted packages; runtime: apply the policy to all Wasm compile/instantiate entry points and separately deny undeclared native or broker capabilities.

title: Convert Wasm page limits into enforced per-app and aggregate host memory budgets
standard_reference: WebAssembly Core Specification §1.1.2 (Scope), §2.3.12 (Limits), §2.3.15 (Memory Types), §2.4.5 (Memory Instructions), §2.5.5 (Memories), and §4.2.9 (Memory Instances); Core 1 §2.3.4–§2.3.5 and §2.4.4
detail: [SPEC FACT] Core 2 makes the memory minimum the initial size and an optional maximum the size ceiling to which the memory can grow; limits are in page units, a page is 65,536 bytes, and the memory-instance invariant says the byte length never exceeds the declared maximum. memory.grow returns the previous size or -1 when enough memory cannot be allocated. If no maximum is present, the specification permits growth to any valid size, and the core specification leaves environment-specific resource policy outside its scope. MDN describes Memory.grow in 64 KiB pages and shows separate initial and maximum values. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Require every submitted memory and imported Memory object to declare a finite maximum; reject missing or excessive maxima before instantiation, charge initial pages and every growth request against an app, publisher/tenant, and global budget, and make the engine/host adapter deny growth before the aggregate budget is crossed. Account Wasm linear memory separately from JavaScript heap, tables, compiled-code cache, and process RSS; use a process/cgroup/microVM ceiling for high-risk apps, rate-limit repeated growth failures, emit non-secret quota telemetry, and terminate or quarantine an app that exceeds policy. A Wasm per-memory maximum is necessary but is not a whole-container physical-memory limit.
superapp_applicability: container: enforce runtime and process-level memory ceilings per mini-app and aggregate tenant; store: lint finite initial/max page declarations and bind them to the artifact digest; runtime: meter instantiation and memory.grow, deny over-budget growth, isolate JS/compiled-cache overhead, and preserve the -1/error path without allowing host exhaustion.

title: COOP same-origin plus COEP require-corp or credentialless is the cross-origin-isolation header gate
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Standard §7.1.3 Cross-origin opener policies (same-origin-plus-COEP and §7.1.3.1 The headers); §7.1.4 Cross-origin embedder policies (compatible with cross-origin isolation) and §7.1.4.1 The headers
detail: [SPEC FACT] WHATWG defines same-origin-plus-COEP as the cross-origin-isolation mode produced by Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin together with a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy value compatible with isolation; require-corp and credentialless are the compatible COEP values. MDN further states that Permissions-Policy: cross-origin-isolated must not block the feature. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat the tuple COOP: same-origin + COEP: require-corp (strict resource opt-in) or credentialless (no-CORS credentials stripped) as an explicit runtime capability profile, not as independent optional headers. The container must emit and preserve both headers on the mini-app top-level response, keep the policy through redirects and worker/iframe initialization, and report an isolation failure instead of exposing privileged APIs when the tuple or permission gate is absent.
superapp_applicability: Container: owns the top-level response headers, secure-context requirement, redirects, iframe/worker policy propagation, and Permissions Policy. Store: declare whether an app requires the isolated profile and test its dependency graph against that profile. Runtime: expose isolated-only APIs only after the effective context reports the capability.

title: COEP require-corp makes CORP or CORS an explicit opt-in for cross-origin no-CORS resources
standard_reference: MDN Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy, Directives (require-corp and credentialless) and Description; MDN Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy, Syntax/Directives; WHATWG HTML Standard §7.1.4 Cross-origin embedder policies and §7.1.4.2 Embedder policy checks
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under COEP: require-corp, a no-CORS cross-origin resource is admitted only when it is same-origin or its response explicitly permits embedding with Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy; a CORS-mode request is governed by CORS instead. CORP: same-origin, same-site, and cross-origin respectively restrict or permit which origins/sites may load a resource. COEP: credentialless permits no-CORS cross-origin loads by omitting credentials, while other credentialed cases still need CORS or CORP. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Require every mini-app script, stylesheet, image, worker script, iframe, and other dependency to declare its intended CORS/CORP mode in a resource manifest; fail closed or use an explicitly approved credentialless profile when a dependency lacks the required opt-in. Test nested frames and worker initialization, and surface the blocked URL and policy disposition to publishers rather than silently weakening COEP.
superapp_applicability: Container: enforces subresource admission and nested-frame/worker inheritance. Store: scans declared and discovered cross-origin dependencies and records CORP/CORS evidence per release.
