Runtime: blocks non-opted-in resources under require-corp and prevents an app from bypassing the platform's isolation policy by loading opaque third-party assets.

title: crossOriginIsolated is the effective Window/Worker status bit for isolated execution
standard_reference: HTML Standard API definition #dom-crossoriginisolated-dev; MDN Window: crossOriginIsolated property, Cross-origin isolating a document and Checking if the document is cross-origin isolated
detail: [SPEC FACT] Window.crossOriginIsolated returns a boolean indicating whether the document is cross-origin isolated; the corresponding WorkerGlobalScope property can be checked in workers. The effective status requires COOP: same-origin, COEP: require-corp or credentialless, and permission for the cross-origin-isolated feature; otherwise the property is false and the reduced restrictions do not apply. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Make this status the runtime source of truth for each mini-app window and worker. Do not infer capability from a stored app declaration or from seeing headers in a manifest: redirects, embedding, a failed subresource check, a worker policy mismatch, or host Permissions Policy can make the effective status false. Gate SAB, high-resolution timing, and other isolation-dependent APIs on the live status and provide a deterministic non-isolated fallback/error state.
superapp_applicability: Container: exposes/records Window and Worker isolation status and controls Permissions Policy. Store: validates an app's declared isolation requirement but does not treat declaration as proof. Runtime: checks the boolean before privileged API use and records the status with diagnostics for support and audit.

title: SharedArrayBuffer creation and message-based shared memory require the isolated app/worker boundary
standard_reference: MDN Window: crossOriginIsolated property, Cross-origin isolated documents operate with fewer restrictions; WHATWG HTML Standard §7.1.4.2 Embedder policy checks (worker initialization); MDN COEP, Features that depend on cross-origin isolation
detail: [SPEC FACT] MDN identifies SharedArrayBuffer as an API with reduced restrictions in a cross-origin-isolated document: it can be created and sent through Window.postMessage() or MessagePort.postMessage(), while the non-isolated example uses ArrayBuffer. WHATWG's embedder-policy check applies the owner's policy to dedicated-worker initialization, so an isolated page cannot assume that an unapproved worker script belongs to the same isolated execution boundary. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Permit SAB allocation and sharing only inside a mini-app's verified isolated scope; require all dedicated-worker scripts and nested frames participating in that scope to pass the same embedder-policy checks. Never pass a SAB to an untrusted cross-app/plugin boundary; use ArrayBuffer copying or a serialized protocol when isolation is false or cannot be proven, and surface the exact fallback rather than silently downgrading shared-memory semantics.
superapp_applicability: Container: isolates app/worker agent boundaries and controls postMessage/MessagePort exposure between apps. Store: scans worker and iframe dependencies and marks shared-memory capability as an explicit permission requiring isolation evidence. Runtime: gates SAB construction and cross-context sharing, with ArrayBuffer/serialization fallback for ordinary mini-apps.

title: performance.now() is coarsened for timing-attack resistance and gains finer resolution only with isolation
standard_reference: High Resolution Time Level 3 §4 Time Origin (coarsen time algorithm), §7.1 now() method, and §9.1 Clock resolution
detail: [SPEC FACT] High Resolution Time Level 3 defines coarsen time with a default resolution of 100 microseconds or a higher implementation-defined value; when the cross-origin-isolated capability is true, the resolution is 5 microseconds or a higher implementation-defined value, and the user agent may coarsen and potentially jitter timestamps. The security considerations identify cache, statistical-fingerprinting, and micro-architectural timing attacks and list resolution reduction and jitter as mitigations. performance.now() remains a monotonic elapsed-time API, not a promise of an exact 5-microsecond clock. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Treat timer precision as an effective runtime property, never as a fixed entitlement: record whether the mini-app was isolated, avoid using timer deltas as authorization/fraud/security proofs, and prevent cross-app timing correlation in telemetry. Performance tests should tolerate implementation-defined coarsening, background throttling, and jitter; publish separate isolated and non-isolated benchmark classes.
superapp_applicability: Container: selects the isolation profile and must not expose a synthetic higher-resolution timer that defeats browser coarsening. Store: labels benchmark requirements and rejects apps that require an exact timer precision as a security primitive. Runtime: returns platform-controlled performance.now() values, records isolation context for diagnostics, and keeps timing data scoped to the app/worker rather than correlating unrelated apps.

title: RFC 8030 defines HTTP/2 push delivery with TTL, Urgency headers and Topic message replacement
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8030 §5 Delivering Push Messages, §5.2 TTL Header Field, §5.3 Urgency Header Field, §5.4 Topic Header Field
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 8030 establishes the protocol for delivering push messages from an application server to a push service. An application server requests message delivery by sending an HTTP POST request to the push endpoint URL. The request includes the TTL (Time-To-Live) header field specifying the duration in seconds for which the push service should retain the message if the user agent is offline. The Urgency header field specifies delivery priority with four discrete values: 'very-low' (device power saving, background sync), 'low' (low priority, non-urgent updates), 'normal' (standard message arrival), and 'high' (real-time communication, alerting). The Topic header field provides a receipt-replacement mechanism where a new push message containing the same topic token overwrites any pending undelivered message with that topic, preventing stale notification pileup. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app platforms operating an internal push gateway must enforce strict protocol mapping for mini-apps: (1) map mini-app push requests through an authenticated host gateway rather than exposing raw device registration tokens directly to third parties; (2) validate and clamp mini-app TTL values to prevent zombie message retention (e.g. maximum 72 hours for transactional, 4 hours for promotional); (3) police the Urgency header, reserving 'high' urgency for critical user-initiated flows (security verification, active orders) while downgrading unverified notifications to 'low' or 'very-low' to preserve client battery; (4) require mini-apps to supply Topic headers for stateful updates (e.g. order tracking status) so obsolete messages are superseded automatically at the gateway before hitting client radios.
superapp_applicability: Container: receives wake-up push intents and routes them to the appropriate isolated mini-app runtime worker. Store: defines push capability tiers in the developer console and audits mini-app message quotas. Runtime: exposes PushManager endpoint interfaces while ensuring push payload delivery activates only the target mini-app without leaking cross-app messaging events.

title: RFC 8291 mandates aes128gcm single-record payload encryption using ECDH P-256 and HKDF-SHA-256
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8291 §2 Push Message Encryption Overview, §3 Push Message Encryption, §3.2 Push Message Authentication, §4 Restrictions on Use of 'aes128gcm'
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 8291 specifies an end-to-end message encryption scheme ensuring confidentiality and integrity for push messages transmitted across untrusted push services. When creating a subscription, the user agent generates an Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key pair on the NIST P-256 curve (secp256r1) and a cryptographically strong 16-octet authentication secret (auth). When encrypting a push message, the application server creates an ephemeral P-256 ECDH key pair and a 16-octet random salt. A shared secret is computed via ECDH and combined with the auth secret using HKDF-SHA-256 to produce Input Keying Material (IKM). Following RFC 8188 ('aes128gcm' content coding), a Content Encryption Key (CEK, 16 octets) and nonce (12 octets) are derived. An application server MUST encrypt the message with a single record (rs parameter greater than plaintext length + padding delimiter + auth tag of 16 octets). The uncompressed 65-octet public key is placed in the 'keyid' header parameter. Maximum plaintext payload is 3993 octets (derived from the 4096-octet push service body limit minus 86 octets header, minimum 1 octet padding delimiter 0x02, and 16 octets AEAD tag). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The super-app host container must handle push decryption in a trusted security zone: (1) generated ECDH keys and 16-octet auth secrets must be cryptographically isolated per mini-app tenant; (2) push services (whether FCM, APNs, or a custom host carrier gateway) only route opaque ciphertexts and cannot inspect push payload content; (3) decrypting runtime must verify the 0x02 padding delimiter, rejecting malformed or multi-record payloads to defend against compression-leak and padding-oracle attacks; (4) payload size is strictly capped at 3993 bytes at submission time to guarantee reliable delivery across constrained radio networks.
superapp_applicability: Container: hosts the cryptographic key storage and executes hardware-backed or WebCrypto-compliant ECDH decryption. Store: verifies that developer backend push integrations comply with RFC 8291 single-record aes128gcm encoding without relying on plaintext push tunnels. Runtime: delivers decrypted plaintext buffers to the mini-app Service Worker or background event handler within an isolated memory sandbox.

title: RFC 8292 specifies Voluntary Application Server Identification (VAPID) using ECDSA P-256 signed JWT tokens
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8292 §2 Voluntary Identification, §2.1 VAPID Authentication Scheme, §2.2 Application Server Contact Information ('sub' claim)
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 8292 defines the VAPID authentication scheme, enabling an application server to voluntarily identify itself to a push service without requiring proprietary developer account registration with every intermediate delivery provider. The application server signs a JSON Web Token (JWT) using ECDSA with SHA-256 (ES256) on the NIST P-256 curve. The JWT payload MUST include: 'aud' (the push service origin URI), 'exp' (expiration time, recommended not exceeding 24 hours), and 'sub' (subject contact URI, either a 'mailto:' address or an 'https:' URL allowing the push service operator to contact the application administrator in cases of abuse or high error rates). The request carries the 'Authorization: vapid t=<jwt>, k=<raw_uncompressed_public_key>' header (or RFC 8292 legacy Authorization/Crypto-Key header pairs). The push service uses the uncompressed public key (k) to verify the token signature (t) and attributes all push requests to that application identity, allowing rate-limiting and quota management per application server. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app platforms must adopt VAPID principles for mini-app publisher attribution: (1) generate or require a dedicated VAPID P-256 key pair during mini-app developer registration, binding the public key directly to the mini-app AppID; (2) require all push requests directed to the host push gateway to present an ES256 VAPID token signed by the registered mini-app private key; (3) validate the 'sub' claim against the publisher's verified technical contact email on file; (4) enforce token expiration (exp) windows <= 12 hours to prevent replay of captured VAPID authorizations; (5) isolate push quotas and abuse throttling per VAPID public key so malicious or malfunctioning mini-apps cannot compromise the host app's push reputation or exhaust device delivery budgets.
superapp_applicability: Container: validates incoming push messages against the subscribed mini-app's registered VAPID public key. Store: issues and registers publisher VAPID public keys and maintains contact identity bindings. Runtime: ensures subscribe() calls pass the canonical applicationServerKey matching the mini-app's verified store credentials.

title: W3C Push API establishes PushManager subscription lifecycle, userVisibleOnly constraints and secure endpoint scoping
standard_reference: W3C Push API Candidate Recommendation §6 PushManager interface, §7 PushSubscription interface, §8 PushEvent and pushsubscriptionchange
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Push API defines the web platform interfaces connecting client workers to remote push services. The PushManager interface exposes subscribe(options) and getSubscription(). The PushSubscriptionOptions dictionary requires: 'userVisibleOnly' (a boolean indicating that every received push message will result in a user-visible notification; browsers reject subscribe() requests where userVisibleOnly is false to prevent silent background tracking) and 'applicationServerKey' (an ArrayBuffer/BufferSource containing the P-256 public key identifying the application server, matching RFC 8292 VAPID). A successful subscription returns a PushSubscription object containing: 'endpoint' (the unique HTTPS push service delivery URI), 'expirationTime' (optional null or DOMHighResTimeStamp), and getKey('p256dh') / getKey('auth') which expose the client's public ECDH key and 16-octet authentication secret in raw binary form. If the push service invalidates a subscription, the host fires the 'pushsubscriptionchange' event on the Service Worker, allowing the app to resubscribe and rotate keys. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app containers must enforce strict tenancy boundaries on PushManager: (1) mandatory enforcement of userVisibleOnly=true for third-party mini-apps to prohibit covert background analytics and silent battery drain; (2) automatic scoping of PushSubscription endpoints to the tuple (mini_app_id, tenant_id, device_token), ensuring one mini-app cannot invoke or receive push events destined for another; (3) handling of pushsubscriptionchange events during host app migration, OS token rotation, or super-app account switching; (4) container-side verification that incoming PushEvents trigger a corresponding notification or foreground activity within a strict execution window (e.g. 10 seconds), revoking push permissions if silent deliveries occur repeatedly.
superapp_applicability: Container: implements the native-to-web PushManager bridge, managing hardware wake locks and dispatching push events into isolated ServiceWorker scopes. Store: provides permission manifest declarations ('push_notifications') and tracks delivery health. Runtime: exposes navigator.serviceWorker.ready.pushManager and validates that getKey() outputs are cleanly serialized for backend synchronization.

title: Super-app push gateway mediation isolates mini-app endpoints, enforces frequency caps, and controls battery impact
standard_reference: Super-App Architecture Practice: RFC 8030 Gateway Mediation & MDN Web Push Architecture Guide
detail: [SPEC FACT] In enterprise super-app architectures (such as WeChat, Alipay, and Grab), native push delivery over OS channels (APNs, FCM, Huawei Push Kit, Xiaomi Cloud Push) is unified under the host application's bundle identity. Mini-apps cannot directly establish independent OS-level notification tokens with device operating systems. Instead, the super-app platform operates a centralized Push Mediation Gateway. When a mini-app calls PushManager.subscribe(), the host gateway generates a virtual endpoint URI scoped to the mini-app's unique ID. When the mini-app backend POSTs an encrypted push message to this endpoint, the host gateway authenticates the VAPID signature, performs rate limiting, checks user notification preferences, and bundles the ciphertext into the super-app's native OS push payload. Upon receipt on device, the super-app container decrypts the envelope, instantiates the target mini-app's worker context, and dispatches the PushEvent. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Platform engineering teams must implement four core gateway controls: (1) Tiered Rate Limiting: cap daily push notifications per mini-app (e.g., maximum 3 promotional pushes per day, 50 transactional pushes per active user transaction) to prevent spam; (2) Centralized User Opt-Out: allow users to silence or block notifications for specific mini-apps in the super-app settings without muting the main host app; (3) Quiet Hours & Local Timezone Awareness: hold non-urgent push messages (Urgency: low/very-low) at the gateway during user night-time hours (e.g. 22:00 to 07:00); (4) Delivery Metrics & Audit Logging: track gateway delivery latency, bounce rates, and user dismissal rates to penalize abusive mini-apps with review suspension or push revocation.
superapp_applicability: Container: routes native APNs/FCM payloads containing mini-app metadata to the respective sandboxed container. Store: provides developer portal dashboards for push quota usage, delivery analytics, and template approval. Runtime: handles wake-up events, ensures timely processing, and terminates background contexts immediately after push handling completes.

title: WHATWG Notifications API defines permission lifecycle, tag replacement, action buttons and silent delivery
standard_reference: WHATWG Notifications API Living Standard §2.2 Permissions integration, §3.1 Notification interface, §3.3 Direction and language, §3.4 Tag matching and replacement
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG Notifications API defines cross-platform standards for displaying notifications outside a web page's viewport. Notification.permission returns 'default' (no choice made, behaves as denied), 'granted' (user allowed), or 'denied' (user explicitly rejected). Requesting permission requires a secure context and should be initiated by user activation. The Notification constructor and ServiceWorkerRegistration.showNotification(title, options) support parameters including: 'tag' (an ID string for notification grouping and replacement; a newer notification with the same tag replaces an existing one, avoiding notification clutter), 'body' (text payload), 'icon' / 'badge' (visual branding assets), 'silent' (boolean suppressing sound and vibration), 'renotify' (boolean specifying whether to re-alert the user when replacing a tagged notification), 'data' (arbitrary structured clone payload), and 'actions' (an array of interactive buttons with action IDs and titles). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app platforms must adapt the Notifications API to prevent mini-app identity spoofing: (1) automatically namespace notification tags as `${mini_app_id}:${tag}` so third-party apps cannot overwrite host notifications or other mini-apps' notices; (2) inject the mini-app's verified store icon and title into the notification header to ensure clear publisher attribution; (3) restrict 'renotify' to prevent spam vibrating/buzzing of the user device; (4) sanitize notification action clicks to deep-link directly back into the originating mini-app container context.
superapp_applicability: Container: intercepts showNotification calls, validates permission state per mini-app, and maps web parameters into native OS notification builders. Store: mandates notification declaration in manifest and provides privacy disclosures regarding notification use. Runtime: exposes Notification and ServiceWorkerRegistration.showNotification APIs while stripping unapproved action types or malformed asset URIs.

title: W3C Badging API provides unread counts and status flags with anti-spoofing and platform integration
standard_reference: W3C Badging API Draft Community Group Report §4 API definition, §4.1 setAppBadge, §4.2 clearAppBadge, §6 Security and privacy considerations
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Badging API allows installed web applications to set an application badge, typically displayed alongside the application's icon on the device home screen, application dock, or in-app launcher tiles. The API exposes `navigator.setAppBadge([contents])` and `navigator.clearAppBadge()`, also available on WorkerNavigator in service workers. The optional parameter 'contents' is an integer in the range 1 to 2^53 - 1 representing an unread count, or omitted/0 to show a generic flag indicator (a simple dot). Specifying 0 or calling clearAppBadge() clears the badge. Security considerations emphasize that badges must not be used to simulate false system-level emergency alerts, and user agents should clamp excessively large numbers (e.g. displaying '99+' above threshold) to prevent visual UI corruption and user anxiety. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Within a super-app ecosystem, mini-apps do not have direct OS dock icons unless added as home screen shortcuts. The super-app host must implement a two-level Badging architecture: (1) Virtual In-App Badging: mini-app badge counts are rendered on the mini-app icon inside the super-app's store catalog, recent apps bar, and workspace dock; (2) Aggregated Host Badge: the super-app computes the sum of unread counts from all authorized mini-apps and updates the super-app's own native OS icon badge via native platform APIs; (3) Capping and Abuse Defense: clamp mini-app badge requests to a maximum value of 99, rate-limit setAppBadge calls to prevent CPU churn, and automatically clear badges when the user launches and views the corresponding mini-app.
superapp_applicability: Container: provides the JS bridge implementation for navigator.setAppBadge / clearAppBadge, routing counts to the host badge aggregation service. Store: displays unread indicator badges in mini-app store listings and launcher grids. Runtime: validates badge value types (coercing non-integers or negative numbers) and synchronizes badge state across active mini-app instances.

title: Android Notification Channels enable granular priority, user-controlled muting, and per-mini-app channel grouping
standard_reference: Android Developer Guides: Create and Manage Notification Channels (API Level 26+ / Android 8.0+), NotificationChannelGroup and Importance Levels
detail: [SPEC FACT] Since Android 8.0 (API level 26), all native notifications must be assigned to a NotificationChannel; unassigned notifications are discarded by the system. Channels define default user-visible importance: IMPORTANCE_HIGH (makes sound and displays as a heads-up banner), IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT (makes sound, appears in shade), IMPORTANCE_LOW (silent, appears in shade), and IMPORTANCE_MIN (silent, shade only, no status bar icon). Once created, the user has exclusive control over channel settings (sound, vibration, lock screen visibility, bypass Do Not Disturb). Furthermore, NotificationChannelGroup allows applications to group related channels under shared section headings in system notification settings. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] For a super-app hosting hundreds of mini-apps, putting all mini-app notifications into a single generic 'Mini App' channel is catastrophic: if an annoying mini-app spams notifications, the user might block the entire channel, silencing all other mini-apps. Super-apps must implement dynamic NotificationChannel isolation: (1) create a dedicated NotificationChannelGroup for 'Mini Apps' or per mini-app category; (2) dynamically register a dedicated NotificationChannel per mini-app ID (e.g. `miniapp_channel_${app_id}`) upon first notification request; (3) allow users to mute or customize specific mini-apps directly from the native Android system settings without impacting the super-app's core messages; (4) gracefully delete inactive mini-app channels during app uninstallation or takedown to prevent hitting the Android system channel limit (recommended under 500 active channels).
superapp_applicability: Container: native Android container code instantiates NotificationChannel and NotificationChannelGroup dynamically before dispatching NotificationCompat.Builder instances. Store: records mini-app channel declarations and allows users to manage notification permissions from the mini-app detail page. Runtime: maps web notification priorities to appropriate Android channel importance levels.

title: Apple UserNotifications framework requires UNNotificationCategory registration, action handling and foreground presentation
standard_reference: Apple Developer Documentation: UNNotificationCategory, UNNotificationAction, UNNotificationContentExtension, and UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate
detail: [SPEC FACT] Apple's iOS UserNotifications framework governs system notification presentation and interaction. Applications register UNNotificationCategory objects with UNUserNotificationCenter. Each category binds specific UNNotificationAction buttons, custom dismissal actions, and determines options such as UNNotificationCategoryOptions.customDismissAction and hiddenPreviewsBodyPlaceholder. In the delegate (UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate), `userNotificationCenter(_:willPresent:withCompletionHandler:)` governs how notifications are handled when the app is actively running in the foreground (allowing banners, sounds, badges, or silent suppression), while `userNotificationCenter(_:didReceive:withCompletionHandler:)` handles user clicks and action responses. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app iOS implementations must structure notification mediation: (1) register standardized mini-app UNNotificationCategory types (e.g. 'MINIAPP_TRANSACTION', 'MINIAPP_MESSAGE', 'MINIAPP_REMINDER') with predefined action sets (View, Dismiss, Reply); (2) implement `willPresent` logic so if the user is currently viewing the active mini-app, foreground notifications can be converted into subtle in-app snackbars rather than disruptive system banners; (3) route `didReceive` user action clicks back into the super-app router, automatically launching the target mini-app and passing the action identifier and userInfo payload to the mini-app's notificationclick event listener; (4) include threadIdentifier scoped to the mini-app ID to enable iOS system notification grouping per mini-app.
superapp_applicability: Container: iOS native wrapper configures UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate, registers dynamic or categorized UNNotificationCategory instances, and passes responses to the JavaScript bridge. Store: enforces Apple App Store Guideline compliance (e.g. no unsolicited advertising notifications) during mini-app store review. Runtime: dispatches notificationclick events into the active mini-app context upon deep-link activation.

title: Super-app notification governance enforces user consent, frequency caps, quiet hours and anti-phishing safeguards
standard_reference: Super-App Architecture Practice: Notification Governance, Anti-Phishing UI Rules & Fatigue Control
detail: [SPEC FACT] In super-app ecosystems (e.g. WeChat Service Notifications / Template Messages, Alipay Message Center, Gojek Notifications), allowing unrestricted push notifications leads to user fatigue, high uninstallation rates of the host super-app, and phishing attacks where malicious mini-apps impersonate official bank or system alerts. Commercial super-app standards enforce strict notification governance architectures combining template-based messaging, explicit transactional opt-in, and strict anti-impersonation UI rules. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The mini-app store standard establishes five mandatory notification controls: (1) Independent Per-Mini-App Permission: users grant notification access individually per mini-app; revoking one mini-app never disables host super-app notifications; (2) Frequency & Volume Caps: enforce daily limits per user tier (e.g., promotional notifications capped at 1 per week or 3 per month; transactional notifications allowed up to 10 per day subject to active transaction context); (3) Anti-Phishing Banner Branding: the native notification banner must prominently display `[Mini App: <AppName>]` in the title bar or subtext, preventing rogue mini-apps from claiming to be 'System Update' or 'Bank Alert'; (4) Silent / Quiet Hours Enforcement: non-critical notifications are automatically muted or held in a host message inbox between 22:00 and 08:00 local device time; (5) Subscription Message Templates: adopt a template-based authorization model (as proven in WeChat and Alipay) where mini-apps specify required fields (e.g., Order ID, Status, Amount), requiring explicit user consent per notification event or recurring subscription.
superapp_applicability: Container: validates message content against registered templates and enforces client-side quiet-hour suppressions. Store: reviews notification copy templates and penalizes mini-apps with high notification opt-out or report rates. Runtime: provides user-facing settings within the mini-app menu to manage notification subscriptions and view notification history.

title: W3C Web App Manifest display_override establishes developer fallback chain across modern window modes
standard_reference: W3C Web Application Manifest §1.8 display member, WICG Manifest Incubations §2 display_override member
detail: [SPEC FACT] The standard Web Application Manifest defines the 'display' member with discrete values ('fullscreen', 'standalone', 'minimal-ui', 'browser'). To support advanced windowing capabilities while maintaining graceful degradation, the WICG Manifest Incubations specification introduces the 'display_override' member. It contains an ordered list of display modes (including extensions like 'window-controls-overlay', 'tabbed', and 'unframed') or DisplayOverrideEntryObject items with URL pattern matching. The browser iterates through the display_override list in order: if the user agent supports a listed mode and any associated URL pattern matches, that mode is selected; if none are supported or match, it falls back to the standard 'display' member, and ultimately to 'browser'. This allows applications to request customized desktop or titlebar integrations while gracefully falling back to standard mobile or standalone containers. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-app store manifests must standardize on display_override semantics: (1) allow mini-apps to declare display_override preferences (e.g. ['window-controls-overlay', 'standalone', 'minimal-ui']); (2) parse and validate the fallback chain during manifest ingestion in the developer portal; (3) map unsupported or forbidden desktop modes (such as 'unframed', which removes all window controls) to 'standalone' or host-governed container views; (4) ensure uniform fallback across Android, iOS, tablet, and desktop super-app container variants.
superapp_applicability: Container: determines the viewport framing and native chrome layout according to the evaluated display mode. Store: validates manifest display_override declarations against platform capability profiles. Runtime: exposes window.matchMedia('(display-mode: ...)') to allow mini-app responsive layout adjustments.

title: WICG Window Controls Overlay enables titlebar extension with geometrychange events and CSS env() rect variables
standard_reference: WICG Window Controls Overlay Draft Community Group Report §3 WindowControlsOverlay interface, §4 CSS Environment Variables, §5 app-region property
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Window Controls Overlay (WCO) specification allows installed web applications to take control of the titlebar area typically reserved for the OS window frame. When display_override includes 'window-controls-overlay', the web viewport expands across the entire titlebar while the host/OS controls (minimize, maximize, close) remain overlaid on top. The `navigator.windowControlsOverlay` interface provides: (1) `visible` (boolean indicating if the overlay is active); (2) `getTitlebarAreaRect()` returning a DOMRect representing the available titlebar area excluding the window controls overlay; (3) `ongeometrychange` event fired when the window is resized or titlebar dimensions change. In CSS, developers access the safe titlebar geometry via four environment variables: `env(titlebar-area-x)`, `env(titlebar-area-y)`, `env(titlebar-area-width)`, and `env(titlebar-area-height)`. In addition, draggable window regions are controlled using CSS `app-region: drag` and `app-region: no-drag` (or `-webkit-app-region`). WCO is strictly restricted to top-level secure contexts and cannot be accessed inside embedded cross-origin iframes. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app desktop/tablet containers (e.g. WeChat for Mac/Windows, DingTalk, Lark desktop) must adapt WCO: (1) implement `navigator.windowControlsOverlay` to reflect the host's custom titlebar bounds; (2) inject native CSS env variables so mini-apps can place search bars, tabs, or custom branding directly in the header row without colliding with host buttons; (3) enforce `app-region: drag` handling in the container window manager, ensuring clicks on interactive elements (buttons, inputs) marked `no-drag` are properly routed to web event handlers.
superapp_applicability: Container: provides the native window frame embedding and coordinates hit-testing between native drag regions and web content. Store: inspects mini-app desktop manifests to verify titlebar usability. Runtime: exposes navigator.windowControlsOverlay and fires geometrychange events when the container frame is moved, docked, or resized.

title: WeChat mini program capsule button architecture reserves persistent host controls via wx.getMenuButtonBoundingClientRect
standard_reference: WeChat Mini Program Developer Documentation: Interface / UI / Menu / wx.getMenuButtonBoundingClientRect and window.navigationStyle
detail: [SPEC FACT] WeChat Mini Programs establish the industry benchmark for mobile super-app window and navigation governance. On mobile devices, the top right of every mini-program window contains a permanent native 'capsule button' (胶囊按钮) housing two critical host controls: the 'More / Menu' button (opening mini-app details, settings, share, rating, and complaint dialogs) and the 'Close / Exit' button (quitting the mini-app back to the super-app). When mini-program developers configure `"navigationStyle": "custom"` in app.json/page.json to render full-bleed immersive layouts, the native capsule button remains persistently overlaid on top of the web/canvas viewport. To prevent the mini-app UI from colliding with or being obscured by the capsule, the host exposes the synchronous API `wx.getMenuButtonBoundingClientRect()`, which returns a Rect object with exact physical/logical coordinates: `{ width, height, top, right, bottom, left }`. Developers use these coordinates to position their custom back buttons, title text, and navigation widgets safely to the left or below the capsule. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Every super-app standard must mandate a persistent host capsule button: (1) the capsule area is an untouchable host security zone; mini-apps cannot hide, obscure, or intercept clicks on the capsule buttons; (2) provide an equivalent synchronous API (`container.getMenuButtonBoundingClientRect()` or WCO getTitlebarAreaRect) returning exact bounding coordinates; (3) implement container layout linters that warn developers if interactive UI elements overlap the capsule bounding box; (4) ensure the capsule remains accessible and legible across light/dark themes by providing auto-adapting or developer-customizable capsule color palettes (e.g. navigationBarTextStyle: black/white).
superapp_applicability: Container: overlays the native capsule widget above the WebView hierarchy and computes its exact screen coordinates. Store: verifies that mini-apps declaring custom navigation do not break usability or obscure host controls. Runtime: implements the JSAPI bridge returning bounding rectangle dimensions taking device status bar and notch cutouts into account.

title: Super-app custom navigation enforces immutable security origins, exit guarantees and anti-spoofing overlays
standard_reference: Super-App Architecture Practice: Window Chrome Security, Phishing Defense & Unconditional Exit Guarantees
detail: [SPEC FACT] Allowing third-party mini-apps to control their window titlebars and navigation chrome introduces severe security risks: rogue mini-apps could paint fake system dialogs, forge bank authentication screens, simulate official super-app prompts, or trap the user inside an inescapable page loop (kiosk attack) by intercepting the back gesture. Commercial super-app containers (WeChat, Alipay, Douyin, Meituan) mitigate these risks through strict architectural boundaries separating host chrome from guest content. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] A robust mini-app store standard enforces four non-negotiable navigation controls: (1) Unconditional Host Exit: the close action on the capsule button executes in native host code outside the WebView JavaScript runtime, ensuring that crashing, hanging, or infinite-looping mini-apps can always be terminated immediately by the user; (2) Security Identity Indicator: when a custom titlebar is active, the container must provide an immutable security origin cue (such as displaying the verified mini-app name on cold-launch pull-down, or an icon watermark during initial render); (3) Modal & Overlay Sandboxing: host system dialogs (permission prompts, payment sheets, account pickers) must always render on a top-level native window layer above all mini-app content, preventing mini-apps from obscuring or clickjacking authorization buttons; (4) Navigation Gesture Fallback: the container provides edge-swipe back navigation by default; if a mini-app requests to intercept the back action (e.g. for unsaved form confirmation), the container enforces a maximum prompt timeout (e.g. 5 seconds), automatically popping the view if the mini-app fails to respond.
superapp_applicability: Container: implements native overlay hierarchies, priority gesture recognizers, and independent exit event handlers. Store: reviews mini-apps utilizing 'custom' navigation styles for phishing patterns or deceptive UI components. Runtime: provides page life-cycle hooks (onBackPress, onPageScroll) with strict execution time budgets.

title: Cross-platform safe area and notch integration unifies CSS env(safe-area-inset) with titlebar geometry across mobile and desktop
standard_reference: CSS Box Model / CSS Values and Units Module Level 4: env(safe-area-inset-*) & WICG Window Controls Overlay
detail: [SPEC FACT] Modern mobile and desktop operating systems exhibit diverse hardware cutouts, display notches, rounded screen corners, dynamic islands, and desktop window frames. CSS environment variables `env(safe-area-inset-top)`, `env(safe-area-inset-right)`, `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)`, and `env(safe-area-inset-left)` provide the fundamental boundaries outside of which content risks being clipped by physical display hardware. In a super-app container environment, safe areas interact directly with titlebar area geometry: on mobile devices, `safe-area-inset-top` represents the status bar height, while the capsule button sits within `safe-area-inset-top` plus the navigation bar height. On desktop environments with Window Controls Overlay enabled, `env(titlebar-area-*)` provides the horizontal bounds for titlebar widgets. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app runtime engines must provide unified layout primitives reconciling safe areas with host chrome: (1) ensure `viewport-fit=cover` is properly handled by the container web view so background colors seamlessly extend beneath status bars and navigation notches; (2) inject both standard CSS `env(safe-area-inset-*)` and super-app specific titlebar environment variables (`env(titlebar-area-*)` or JS system info metrics: `statusBarHeight`, `navBarHeight`, `capsuleRect`); (3) support automatic status bar text styling (dark-content vs light-content) when mini-apps transition between dark and light header themes; (4) provide developer tooling and emulator presets testing mini-app layouts against various screen geometries (iPhone dynamic island, Android hole-punch cameras, desktop multi-window frames).
superapp_applicability: Container: queries native window insets (iOS UIEdgeInsets safeAreaInsets, Android WindowInsetsCompat) and synchronizes them into the web view configuration. Store: tests responsive rendering across standardized device viewport profiles during automated validation. Runtime: exposes system info APIs (e.g. getSystemInfoSync().safeArea) and triggers resize/insets-change events upon orientation changes.

title: W3C FedCM establishes browser-mediated identity federation mitigating third-party cookie deprecation and link tracking
standard_reference: W3C Federated Identity Working Group: Federated Credential Management API §2 The Browser API, §2.3 IdentityCredential Interface
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Federated Credential Management (FedCM) API defines a browser-mediated mechanism allowing users to log into Relying Parties (RPs) using federated Identity Providers (IdPs) without relying on third-party cookies, tracking bounces, or hidden iframes. Initiated via `navigator.credentials.get({ identity: { providers: [{ configURL: '...', clientId: '...' }] } })`, the browser directly brokers the identity transaction. The user agent presents an unforgeable, trusted native dialog displaying user identity accounts directly to the end-user, without allowing the RP to detect whether the user has an existing account at the IdP until the user explicitly selects an account and grants consent. Upon selection, the browser fetches an identity assertion token from the IdP's assertion endpoint and resolves the Promise with an `IdentityCredential` containing `token`. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] A super-app mini-app container must leverage FedCM principles for guest identity: (1) mini-apps acting as RPs authenticate users via the super-app's native identity provider without receiving cross-site tracking cookies; (2) the super-app container intercepts FedCM requests or provides an equivalent high-trust native bottom-sheet showing verified mini-app and user profile identities; (3) unauthenticated silent probing is strictly blocked, ensuring mini-apps cannot enumerate user identity accounts without explicit user interaction.
superapp_applicability: Container: renders trusted native account-selection sheets outside mini-app WebView reach. Store: audits mini-app authentication configurations against approved IdP manifests. Runtime: polyfills or mediates navigator.credentials.get({ identity }) calls.

title: FedCM Identity Provider HTTP API enforces strict endpoint routing, /.well-known validation and account metadata isolation
standard_reference: W3C FedCM §3 Identity Provider HTTP API (§3.1 Well-Known, §3.2 Config, §3.3 Accounts, §3.5 Assertion, §3.6 Disconnect)
detail: [SPEC FACT] The FedCM specification mandates four core HTTP endpoints on the Identity Provider to govern identity mediation: (1) `/.well-known/web-identity`: hosted on the eTLD+1 domain of the IdP, listing authorized config file URLs to prevent arbitrary subdomains from masquerading as identity roots; (2) Config File (`configURL`): a JSON manifest declaring endpoints for `accounts_endpoint`, `id_assertion_endpoint`, `client_metadata_endpoint`, and optional `disconnect_endpoint`, alongside branding (icons, colors); (3) `accounts_endpoint`: returning the list of active user accounts (id, name, email, avatar) signed with the IdP's session; (4) `id_assertion_endpoint`: receiving the RP's clientId, accountId, and nonce via HTTP POST, and returning the signed authentication token; (5) `disconnect_endpoint`: allowing an RP to request disconnection and account de-linking. All requests automatically send Sec-Fetch-Dest: webidentity headers and require CORS mode without credential leakage to non-whitelisted callers. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app platforms acting as IdPs or proxying enterprise IdPs must standardize endpoint schemas: (1) host a secure internal identity configuration endpoint matching FedCM structures; (2) validate that mini-app assertion requests bind a cryptographically random client nonce to prevent replay; (3) implement the disconnect endpoint so users revoking mini-app access from the super-app Account Settings page synchronously notify the mini-app backend.
superapp_applicability: Platform Backend: hosts FedCM-compatible web-identity endpoints and signs OAuth/JWT identity assertions. Container: orchestrates account fetching and token delivery. Store: verifies IdP endpoint domain ownership and TLS compliance.

title: FedCM integrates with W3C Permissions Policy requiring identity-credentials-get delegation for embedded contexts
standard_reference: W3C FedCM §4 Permissions Policy Integration & W3C Permissions Policy 'identity-credentials-get'
detail: [SPEC FACT] The FedCM specification defines the `identity-credentials-get` policy-controlled feature under the W3C Permissions Policy framework. The default allowlist is `'self'`, meaning that only top-level documents can execute `navigator.credentials.get({ identity })` by default. If an embedded cross-origin iframe attempts to invoke FedCM without an explicit allowlist directive, the user agent immediately rejects the promise with a `NotAllowedError` DOMException. To delegate federated login to an embedded third-party widget (e.g., a shared login or payment iframe), the parent document must explicitly specify `allow="identity-credentials-get <origin>"` on the iframe element, or the server must emit the corresponding HTTP response header `Permissions-Policy: identity-credentials-get=(self "https://auth.example.com")`. Furthermore, user activation (a transient user gesture) is required for embedded contexts to prevent clickjacking or automated identity scraping. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-app store security profiles must enforce Permissions Policy gating: (1) mini-app WebViews must enforce `identity-credentials-get 'self'` by default; (2) embedded webviews or sub-frames inside mini-apps cannot invoke identity federation unless explicitly declared in the mini-app manifest's frame permission profile; (3) guest mini-apps cannot access host-level authentication tokens through un-delegated iframes.
superapp_applicability: Container: enforces Permissions Policy HTTP headers and iframe attribute allowlists. Store: scans mini-app manifests for unauthorized cross-origin iframe identity delegation. Runtime: blocks unauthorized credential requests originating from non-top-level frames.

title: W3C Credential Management API establishes a unified container for passwords, federated tokens, and public-key credentials
standard_reference: W3C Web Application Security WG: Credential Management Level 1 §2 CredentialsContainer interface, §2.1 create(), §2.2 get(), §2.3 store(), §2.4 preventSilentAccess()
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Credential Management API defines the `CredentialsContainer` interface (exposed as `navigator.credentials`), providing a unified browser surface for creating, storing, retrieving, and mediating diverse credential types: (1) `PasswordCredential`: legacy username/password pairs stored in the user agent credential manager; (2) `FederatedCredential` / `IdentityCredential`: federated identity tokens (FedCM, OpenID Connect); (3) `PublicKeyCredential`: asymmetric FIDO2 / WebAuthn passkeys; (4) `OTPCredential`: SMS / WebOTP verification codes. The container enforces critical lifecycle controls: `navigator.credentials.store(credential)` stores newly created or updated credentials, while `navigator.credentials.preventSilentAccess()` disables automatic/silent credential return after user sign-out, requiring explicit user mediation on subsequent logins to prevent account session hijack. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-app platforms must adopt the Credential Management container abstraction: (1) provide standard `navigator.credentials` polyfills or native delegates in mini-app WebViews; (2) ensure that mini-apps calling `preventSilentAccess()` on logout notify the container to clear cached guest credentials; (3) isolate credential storage compartments per mini-app appId so mini-apps cannot read or overwrite credentials owned by peer mini-apps or the host super-app.
superapp_applicability: Container: implements CredentialsContainer bridge coordinating with OS and secure enclave storage. Store: verifies mini-app authentication lifecycle compliance (handling logout, session expiry). Runtime: ensures origin-partitioned credential vaults.

title: Super-app guest identity mediation isolates host master credentials and enforces scoped pseudonymous identifiers
standard_reference: Super-App Identity Architecture: Privacy-Preserving Single Sign-On, Pseudonymous Pairwise Identifiers & Zero-Trust Token Boundaries
detail: [SPEC FACT] In commercial super-app ecosystems (e.g. WeChat, Alipay, Grab, Gojek), mini-apps run as semi-trusted third-party guest applications. If guest mini-apps were granted direct access to super-app user master identifiers (such as national ID, phone number, or global user UUID), malicious developers could track user behavior across multiple independent mini-apps without consent. Following FedCM and OAuth 2.0 OpenID Connect pairwise pseudonymous identifier (PPID) standards, super-apps decouple master user identity from guest identity. The host generates an app-scoped openid (hash of master UID + mini-app appId + salt) and an optional developer-scoped unionid (for verified developers owning multiple mini-apps under the same enterprise entity). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The mini-app store standard mandates three privacy-preserving identity rules: (1) Pairwise Pseudonymous Scoping: mini-apps only receive an app-scoped OpenID; global phone numbers or real names require explicit step-up authorization with user consent; (2) Ephemeral Auth Code Exchange: login tokens delivered to the mini-app frontend are short-lived authorization codes (TTL <= 5 minutes, single-use), exchanged on the mini-app backend using the developer appSecret via server-to-server TLS; (3) Host Master Token Isolation: super-app host session tokens, cookies, and payment authorization keys are strictly unreachable from mini-app JS execution contexts.
superapp_applicability: Platform Backend: issues pairwise openids and brokers authorization code exchanges. Container: presents host-branded authorization bottom sheets displaying requested scopes (avatar, nickname). Store: enforces justification reviews for sensitive scopes (phone number, location, national ID).

title: WICG WebUSB API mandates protected interface class exclusions and device landing page validation
standard_reference: WICG WebUSB API §4 Security and Privacy, §4.3 Protected Interface Classes & Device Landing Page descriptor
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WebUSB API provides direct script access to USB devices connected to the host system via `navigator.usb`. Because unrestricted raw USB communication poses catastrophic security risks to the host OS, the specification normatively blocks a mandatory set of 'Protected Interface Classes' from being claimed or opened by web content: Audio (0x01), Communications and CDC Control (0x02), HID (0x03), Mass Storage (0x08), Smart Card (0x0B), Video (0x0E), Audio/Video (0x10), and Wireless Controller (0xE0). These classes are restricted because higher-level, sandboxed OS APIs manage them; exposing raw bulk/isochronous endpoints to web script would allow rogue sites to exfiltrate storage disk data, eavesdrop on microphones/webcams, or inject keyboard events. Additionally, WebUSB defines a WebUSB descriptor allowing manufacturers to declare a specific 'landing page' URL on device firmware, providing cryptographically bound device-to-origin pairing. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-app store security profiles must strictly control WebUSB: (1) disable WebUSB by default across all mini-apps via `Permissions-Policy: usb=()`; (2) require enterprise-tier mini-apps requiring hardware accessories (e.g. mobile POS thermal printers, barcode scanners) to submit formal hardware capability declarations; (3) enforce runtime checks ensuring the container bridge intercepts `navigator.usb.requestDevice()` and enforces a strict vendorId/productId allowlist, completely blocking access to storage, network, or communication class dongles.
superapp_applicability: Container: implements USB permission prompts and filters accessible USB devices by vendorId/productId. Store: validates hardware vendor certificates and POS accessory declarations. Runtime: enforces protected interface class blocks and blocks background USB execution.

title: WICG WebHID API enforces top-level user gesture gating and protects top-level keyboard and mouse report collections
standard_reference: WICG WebHID API §3 Security and Privacy Considerations & §4 HIDDevice interface
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WebHID API (`navigator.hid`) enables web applications to interact with Human Interface Devices using HID report descriptors (input, output, and feature reports). Because HID devices include keyboards, mice, telephony controls, and gaming accessories, unconstrained access would enable web-based keylogging and keystroke injection attacks. To prevent malicious capture or injection, the specification mandates: (1) `navigator.hid.requestDevice()` must be triggered by transient user activation in a secure, top-level context; (2) user agents must normatively filter out top-level collections for Generic Desktop Page Keyboard (Usage Page 0x01, Usage 0x06), Keypad (Usage 0x07), and Mouse/Pointer (Usage 0x01/0x02) unless implemented as vendor-specific feature reports; (3) user agents must display an unambiguous native device picker identifying the physical device name, vendorId, and productId. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-app containers must harden WebHID interfaces: (1) apply `Permissions-Policy: hid=()` by default; (2) prohibit guest mini-apps from opening dual-mode composite devices (e.g., a barcode scanner that also registers as a USB HID keyboard), preventing invisible keystroke injection into the host OS or super-app shell; (3) log all HID feature report write payloads to container audit telemetry to detect attempted firmware reconfiguration or macro tampering on connected enterprise peripherals.
superapp_applicability: Container: displays native device pairing sheets and inspects HID collection usage pages before granting access. Store: inspects mini-app manifests for legitimate hardware business requirements. Runtime: suppresses access to standard keyboard/mouse input report collections.

title: WICG Web Serial API restricts serial communication, mitigating AT-command modem hijack and baud rate saturation
standard_reference: WICG Web Serial API §7 Security Considerations & §4 SerialPort interface
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Web Serial API (`navigator.serial`) connects web applications to serial devices, including microcontroller boards (Arduino, ESP32), USB-to-UART bridges (FTDI, CH340), legacy RS-232 hardware, and cellular modems. Serial interfaces communicate through raw byte streams via ReadableStream and WritableStream. Security risks outlined in the specification include: (1) Modem AT-command attacks: cellular modems exposed over USB serial ports could be commandeered by malicious scripts to send unauthorized SMS messages, place premium phone calls, intercept two-factor SMS codes, or issue AT+CPIN commands locking the SIM card; (2) Firmware reprogramming: unauthenticated serial ports can be used to reflash attached microcontroller chips into malicious physical implants; (3) Host port exhaustion. The specification mandates transient user gestures for `requestDevice()`, secure contexts, and Permissions Policy integration (`serial`). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app platforms must govern serial communication: (1) enforce `Permissions-Policy: serial=()` by default; (2) blacklist serial ports associated with onboard cellular modems, GNSS/GPS receivers, and baseband interfaces in the native container layer; (3) restrict serial access strictly to whitelisted USB vendor/product IDs (e.g., enterprise industrial scales, RFID readers); (4) enforce container-level input sanitization blocking modem command patterns (`AT+...`) on outbound serial streams.
superapp_applicability: Container: enumerates and filters available serial ports, blacklisting baseband and system diagnostic ports. Store: evaluates security justifications for serial communication in industrial/IoT mini-apps. Runtime: wraps SerialPort streams with byte-rate throttling and AT command detection filters.

title: Hardware sandbox escape mitigations counter firmware reprogramming, macro injection and persistent peripheral grants
standard_reference: Peer-Reviewed Security Research: Trampert et al., WWW '25 ('Peripheral Instinct: How External Devices Breach Browser Sandboxes') & W3C DAS WG Charter Considerations
detail: [SPEC FACT] Peer-reviewed security research by Trampert et al. (WWW '25: 'Peripheral Instinct: How External Devices Breach Browser Sandboxes') demonstrated full exploit chains where low-level peripheral APIs (WebUSB, WebHID, Web Serial) circumvent web browser sandboxes. Key attack primitives identified include: (1) Firmware Overwrite: flashing malicious custom firmware onto connected dongles (such as wireless RF receivers) via WebHID/WebUSB vendor requests without physical user interaction beyond the initial device grant; (2) Macro / BadUSB Injection: reprogramming multi-function peripherals to emit malicious keystrokes directly into the host operating system; (3) Modem Command Exploitation: issuing raw Hayes AT commands via Web Serial to intercept 2FA codes and geolocate devices; (4) Persistent Permission Inheritance: once granted, permission persists across sessions and can be inherited by cross-site scripting (XSS) or domain takeover. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] A super-app mini-app store must implement multi-layered defenses against peripheral sandbox escapes: (1) Zero Persistent Grants: peripheral device grants must be strictly ephemeral, expiring immediately upon mini-app termination or page navigation; (2) Prohibit Low-Level DFU / Firmware Endpoints: block Device Firmware Update (DFU) class endpoints and vendor-specific firmware flashing commands in native USB/HID hooks; (3) Mandatory Physical Confirmation: require physical host button confirmation (or visual biometric verification) before any peripheral access is initiated.
superapp_applicability: Container: enforces ephemeral, single-session peripheral permission lifetimes and strips DFU/firmware interfaces. Store: subjects any mini-app requesting peripheral APIs to static and dynamic binary analysis for exploit payloads. Runtime: instruments USB/HID control transfers to detect known BadUSB/DFU command signatures.

title: Super-app container hardware policy matrix unifies device attestation, capability scoping and enterprise isolation
standard_reference: Super-App Hardware Architecture: Unified Peripheral Policy Matrix, Device Attestation & Enterprise Zero-Trust Isolation
detail: [SPEC FACT] In modern enterprise and retail super-app deployments (e.g. logistics tracking, warehouse management, mobile merchant checkout), mini-apps require integration with external hardware accessories. Exposing direct WebUSB/WebHID/Web Serial APIs without architectural mediation creates unmanageable attack surfaces. Leading enterprise platforms establish an abstracted, high-level hardware service layer rather than exposing raw byte-level bus controllers. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The mini-app store standard establishes a three-tier hardware policy matrix: (1) Tier 0 (Default - Zero Peripheral Access): WebUSB, WebHID, Web Serial, and Web Bluetooth are hard-disabled (`usb=(), hid=(), serial=()`); (2) Tier 1 (High-Level Standard JSAPIs): use standard, capability-constrained super-app JSAPIs for common accessories (e.g. `container.bluetoothPrinter.print()`, `container.barcodeScanner.scan()`), ensuring the native super-app handles device protocols, error recovery, and driver isolation; (3) Tier 2 (Certified Enterprise Hardware): for proprietary industrial hardware requiring raw communication, the mini-app must submit hardware vendor attestation (VID/PID, firmware checksum), undergo manual security audit, and operate under strict host-level cryptographic mutual authentication.
superapp_applicability: Container: provides high-level native driver abstractions (POS printer, barcode scanner) instead of exposing raw USB/HID buses. Store: enforces hardware tier classification during app submission. Runtime: monitors bus bandwidth and forcibly detaches unresponsive or rogue peripheral sessions.

title: Google Play User Choice Billing establishes dual-screen choice architecture and mandatory 24-hour transaction reporting
standard_reference: Google Play Help Center: Understanding user choice billing on Google Play & Alternative Billing APIs Integration Guide
detail: [SPEC FACT] Google Play's User Choice Billing program permits registered developers to offer an alternative in-app billing system alongside Google Play Billing for users in eligible markets (EEA, US, UK, South Korea, India, Japan, Brazil, Australia, Indonesia, South Africa). The architecture mandates: (1) Choice Presentation: the app must present a user choice screen displaying Google Play's billing option and the developer's alternative billing option with clear payment logos; (2) Service Fee Adjustment: transactions completed via the alternative billing system receive a standard service fee discount of 4% (e.g., standard 15% rate reduces to 11%, 30% reduces to 26%); (3) Mandatory Alternative Billing APIs: since the 2024 sunset of manual reporting, developers must integrate automated Alternative Billing APIs (ExternalTransactions API) to report all authorized transactions within 24 hours of authorization; (4) Top Charts Reflection: transactions reported through the APIs are incorporated into Google Play's Top Grossing charts. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] When a super app acts as an Android host distributing digital content via mini-apps: (1) if the super-app is distributed via Google Play, all digital purchases inside guest mini-apps must comply with Google Play's Payments Policy; (2) the super-app host must integrate Alternative Billing APIs at the host level, managing the user choice sheet and automated 24-hour transaction reporting; (3) the host billing gateway must reconcile the 4% fee reduction against mini-app developer payouts.
superapp_applicability: Container: renders Google Play choice bottom-sheets and handles user payment selection. Store Backend: reports alternative transactions to Google Play ExternalTransactions API within 24h. Finance/Settlement: accounts for Google Play fee deductions in publisher statements.

title: Google Play Billing Choice Program defines differentiated fee tiers for alternative billing and external web links
standard_reference: Google Play Help Center: Enrolling in the billing choice program (answer/17161464) & Fee Schedule through June 30, 2026
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Google Play Billing Choice Program (operating across the UK, EEA, and US) formalizes monetization policies allowing developers to either embed an alternative billing system in-app or guide users to external websites via web links for digital purchases. Under policy rules effective through June 30, 2026: (1) Alternative In-App Billing: applies a 4% discount against standard Google Play service fees; (2) External Web Links: Google Play charges a 10% fee for all auto-renewing subscriptions and for the first $1M USD of annual earnings (for developers on the 15% tier), while other in-app digital content purchases linked out to the web incur a 20% fee; (3) Consumer Protection Standards: developers guiding users to external websites must provide clear refund policies, order history tracking links, subscription management portals, and an explicit process for disputing unauthorized transactions; (4) Technical Integration: requires integration with Billing Choice APIs to render the one-time user information sheet and report external transactions. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-app store architectures must establish clear policy mappings: (1) define whether guest mini-apps are permitted to link out to external checkout pages or must use host in-app billing; (2) where external linking is permitted, verify that the mini-app backend reports transaction metadata to the super-app host so the host can fulfill upstream app store obligations; (3) dynamically display mandatory regulatory disclosure notices before launching external web payment sheets.
superapp_applicability: Container: intercepts external payment link navigation and displays required store disclosures. Store: audits mini-app external checkout URLs and dispute resolution mechanisms. Finance: reconciles the 10%/20% external link commission tiers against mini-app gross revenue.

title: Apple EU alternative payment framework enforces StoreKit external purchase entitlements, disclosure sheets and reporting
standard_reference: Apple Developer Support: Alternative payment options in the European Union & StoreKit External Purchase Entitlement
detail: [SPEC FACT] In compliance with the European Union Digital Markets Act (DMA), Apple established alternative payment options for apps distributed in the EU: (1) Alternative Payment Service Providers (PSPs): developers can integrate approved third-party PSPs (e.g. Stripe, Adyen) directly within their iOS app; (2) StoreKit External Purchase Link Entitlement: developers can use the StoreKit External Purchase API (`StoreKit.ExternalPurchase`) to link out to a developer-owned website for purchase; (3) Mandatory System Disclosure Sheet: before navigating to an external PSP or web checkout, the iOS system presents a standardized Apple modal sheet informing the user that Apple is not responsible for the privacy or security of the transaction, cannot offer family sharing, and cannot handle refunds; (4) Strict Reporting and Audit: developers must report all external purchase transactions to Apple on a monthly basis and provide secure server endpoints for transaction reconciliation and audit verification. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] For super-apps distributed on iOS in the EU: (1) the super-app host application must apply for and configure the StoreKit External Purchase Entitlement; (2) guest mini-apps cannot invoke proprietary private payment bridges bypassing host review; (3) all mini-app alternative checkouts must execute through host-mediated StoreKit APIs ensuring Apple system disclosure sheets are displayed; (4) the super-app platform must maintain transaction logs to support mandatory Apple monthly reporting.
superapp_applicability: Container: invokes native StoreKit external purchase sheets prior to opening third-party payment views. Store: reviews mini-app PSP integrations against Apple EU compliance rules. Platform Backend: aggregates monthly transaction reports for Apple compliance submissions.

title: Apple EU commercial terms establish reduced commissions, payment processing surcharges and the Core Technology Fee
standard_reference: Apple Developer Support: Alternative Terms for Apps in the EU & Core Technology Fee (CTF) Specification
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under Apple's Alternative Terms Addendum for EU Apps, commercial structures are unbundled into three distinct fee components: (1) Reduced App Store Commission: apps adopting the alternative terms pay a reduced base commission of 10% (for developers enrolled in the Small Business Program or subscriptions after year 1) or 17% (for standard digital goods and services); (2) Payment Processing Fee: developers choosing to use Apple's in-app purchase system pay an additional 3% payment processing fee (waived if using an alternative PSP or external web purchase); (3) Core Technology Fee (CTF): developers pay €0.50 for each first annual install per year over 1 million installs, covering Apple's ongoing developer platform investments (with exemptions for non-profits, educational institutions, and government entities). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app business models must factor in unbundled platform economics: (1) the host super-app easily exceeds 1 million annual installs, meaning every new user install incurs the €0.50 CTF; (2) mini-app commercial agreements must account for whether host commission covers the CTF overhead and Apple 10%/17% commissions; (3) when mini-apps utilize alternative PSPs, the super-app saves the 3% Apple processing fee, enabling more competitive revenue-sharing splits with mini-app merchants (e.g. 85/15 vs 70/30).
superapp_applicability: Finance/Settlement: incorporates tiered commissions (10%/17%), 3% PSP fee waivers, and CTF cost attribution into publisher ledger. Store Governance: structures developer monetization tiers aligned with regional host operating costs.

title: Super-app unified multi-provider billing abstraction layer reconciles host store compliance with mini-app monetization
standard_reference: Super-App Architecture Practice: Unified In-App Commerce Gateway, Multi-Platform Compliance & Dynamic Route Mediation
detail: [SPEC FACT] Super apps operate in heterogeneous cross-platform environments: iOS (governed by Apple App Store Guidelines and regional DMA addendums), Android (governed by Google Play Billing and User Choice Billing policies), and standalone/sideloaded APKs or web portals (unrestricted direct billing). Guest mini-apps cannot reasonably maintain separate billing codebases for every host distribution channel and regulatory jurisdiction. Furthermore, direct exposure of external payment links by unvetted mini-apps risks triggering store-wide ban or app removal from Apple and Google app stores. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] The mini-app store standard establishes a centralized Unified Billing Abstraction Layer: (1) Standard JSAPI: mini-apps invoke a unified client API (`container.requestPayment({ orderId, amount, currency, ... })`); (2) Dynamic Route Mediation: the super-app native container inspects host runtime flags, device OS, and user country code, automatically routing to the compliant channel (Apple In-App Purchase, Apple StoreKit External Purchase, Google Play Billing, Google User Choice Billing, or native telco/fintech carrier billing); (3) Unified Merchant Reconciliation: the super-app settlement engine centralizes order fulfillment, fee deduction, dispute management, and publisher ledger reporting regardless of the underlying payment rail.
superapp_applicability: Container: routes client payment requests dynamically to platform-compliant native sheets. Store: certifies mini-app pricing and catalog SKUs across multi-channel distribution. Finance: abstracts settlement, exchange rates, and store service fee deductions into a single merchant statement.

title: WebTransport over HTTP/3 establishes low-latency multiplexed transport via extended CONNECT and QUIC datagrams
summary: W3C WebTransport and IETF draft-ietf-webtrans-http3 define an ECMAScript API and HTTP/3 transport binding supporting bidirectional/unidirectional streams and unreliable datagrams over a single QUIC connection.
detail: [SPEC FACT] WebTransport over HTTP/3 (W3C Working Draft & IETF draft-ietf-webtrans-http3 / RFC 9297) enables web clients to establish multiplexed, bi-directional, and unreliable communication with remote servers over QUIC: (1) Protocol Handshake: clients initiate sessions via an HTTP/3 extended CONNECT request containing `:protocol = webtransport-h3` and an `Origin` header; servers must signal support via `SETTINGS_WT_ENABLED = 1` and `SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM = 1` in HTTP/3 SETTINGS frames; (2) Multiplexed Channels: a single WebTransport session supports multiple concurrent unidirectional streams, bidirectional streams, and unreliable datagrams without head-of-line blocking across streams; (3) Unreliable Datagrams: uses HTTP Datagrams (RFC 9297) mapped directly to QUIC DATAGRAM frames (RFC 9221), providing packet-level low-latency transport without retransmission overhead. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] For high-performance mini-apps (multiplayer gaming, live financial orderbooks, interactive live streaming): (1) the native container provides a managed WebTransport interface (`container.createWebTransport(url, options)`); (2) the host container enforces connection limits (maximum concurrent WebTransport sessions per mini-app, default max 3); (3) upon mini-app backgrounding or suspension, the host triggers immediate graceful session termination via `transport.close({ closeCode, reason })` to prevent lingering network sockets and radio power consumption.
standard_reference: W3C WebTransport (Working Draft) & IETF draft-ietf-webtrans-http3 / RFC 9297
relevance: Provides low-latency alternative to WebSockets and WebRTC for high-frequency financial and gaming mini-apps inside super-apps.
operational_recommendation: Expose WebTransport within container runtime; gate behind network capability permissions; auto-close sessions upon container suspension.

title: WebTransport datagram streams enforce MTU size boundaries, send order arbitration and stream backpressure
summary: W3C WebTransport exposes WebTransportDatagramDuplexStream with explicit maxDatagramSize constraints and WritableStream backpressure controls.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C WebTransport Section 4: (1) Datagram Size Limits: `transport.datagrams.maxDatagramSize` reflects the estimated Path MTU minus protocol overhead; writes exceeding `maxDatagramSize` reject immediately or are discarded by the underlying QUIC layer; (2) Asynchronous Flow Control: datagram sending is mediated by `transport.datagrams.writable`, a standard WritableStream that applies backpressure via `writer.ready` when the network congestion window or QUIC flow-control limit is reached; (3) Stream Prioritization: developers can configure `sendOrder` integers on outgoing streams to determine transport priority during bandwidth contention; (4) Unreliable Drop Semantics: datagrams that cannot be sent immediately due to buffer exhaustion are dropped without blocking subsequent data. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container network governance: (1) super-app containers monitor outbound datagram traffic rates per mini-app (e.g. max 500 KB/s in cellular data mode); (2) enforce adaptive throttling or packet dropping if a mini-app saturates the device radio buffer; (3) provide telemetry metrics on dropped datagram ratios to developers via the mini-app analytics portal.
standard_reference: W3C WebTransport Section 4 (WebTransportDatagramDuplexStream & WebTransportDatagramsWritable)
relevance: Prevents bandwidth exhaustion and radio bufferbloat from misbehaved real-time mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Enforce per-mini-app bandwidth ceilings and log datagram loss rates in container performance monitors.

title: WebTransport enforces strict TLS 1.3 encryption, Origin checks and 14-day pinned certificate hash authentication
summary: WebTransport prohibits cleartext transmission, mandates TLS 1.3/QUIC encryption, validates Origin headers, and supports serverCertificateHashes for scoped local development.
detail: [SPEC FACT] WebTransport security specification requires: (1) TLS 1.3 Mandatory: all WebTransport sessions require QUIC transport security (TLS 1.3); no unencrypted or plaintext transport mode exists; (2) Origin Header Verification: the user agent MUST send the `Origin` header during session negotiation, allowing servers to reject unauthorized cross-origin requests; (3) serverCertificateHashes: for development and private network environments without public CA infrastructure, the API allows passing SHA-256 certificate fingerprints in `WebTransportOptions.serverCertificateHashes`; (4) Strict Validity Ceiling: user agents MUST reject certificate hashes if the certificate validity duration exceeds 14 days, preventing long-lived rogue self-signed certificates from bypassing public Web PKI. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app network security policy: (1) production mini-apps are strictly prohibited from using `serverCertificateHashes`—all external WebTransport endpoints must possess trusted public Web PKI certificates; (2) `serverCertificateHashes` is only permitted when running in the Super-App DevTools / Sandbox IDE during local testing; (3) the super-app host validates target endpoints against the mini-app's manifest network domain allowlist (egress CSP).
standard_reference: W3C WebTransport Security Considerations & serverCertificateHashes algorithm
relevance: Ensures mini-app network traffic is strictly authenticated, encrypted, and isolated against eavesdropping and MITM attacks.
operational_recommendation: Block serverCertificateHashes in production mini-app builds; enforce strict domain allowlists during submission review.

title: Super-app container session pooling optimizes HTTP/3 connection re-use while isolating mini-app contexts
summary: WebTransport over HTTP/3 supports connection pooling across multiple sessions over a single QUIC connection while maintaining separate security contexts.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The IETF draft-ietf-webtrans-http3 specification supports pooling multiple WebTransport sessions onto an existing HTTP/3 connection to the same origin: (1) Session Isolation: each WebTransport session is assigned a unique 62-bit Session ID corresponding to its CONNECT stream; stream frame payloads and datagrams are tagged with this ID, preventing cross-session data leakage; (2) Connection Reuse: multiple sessions can coexist without incurring repeated QUIC TLS 1.3 handshakes, reducing initial connection latency from 1-RTT/2-RTT to 0-RTT; (3) Failure Containment: closing or resetting an individual WebTransport session (via `CLOSE_WEBTRANSPORT_SESSION` capsule) does not terminate the underlying HTTP/3 connection or disrupt other pooled sessions. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container architecture: (1) the super-app native networking stack pools connections for mini-apps connecting to the same platform backend API host; (2) strict origin partitioning prevents third-party mini-apps from sharing QUIC connections with the host super-app's core banking/payment gateways; (3) independent congestion windows prevent heavy mini-app telemetry from starving host super-app transactions.
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-webtrans-http3 Section 3 (Session Establishment & Connection Reuse)
relevance: Minimizes connection establishment overhead for mini-apps while preventing cross-tenant interference.
operational_recommendation: Implement isolated connection pools for guest mini-apps separate from core super-app banking tunnels.

title: WebTransport dedicated worker execution isolates real-time network processing from UI rendering threads
summary: WebTransport is exposed in DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope, enabling asynchronous packet decoding and ingestion outside the main UI event loop.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C WebTransport is explicitly exposed to `Window` and `DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope` contexts: (1) Thread Offloading: high-frequency datagram ingestion and binary stream parsing can run entirely within a Web Worker, ensuring that 60fps/120fps UI rendering and touch input responsiveness on the main thread are never blocked by network I/O; (2) Transferable Streams: `ReadableStream` and `WritableStream` instances produced by WebTransport can be transferred across threads via `postMessage()`, allowing zero-copy pipelining to WebAssembly compute or WebCodecs decoders; (3) Worker Lifecycle Binding: if the worker thread crashes or is terminated by the host, all associated WebTransport sessions are automatically aborted and socket resources reclaimed.
