[SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app best practice: (1) mini-app SDKs encourage moving real-time data handling (e.g. stock tickers, multiplayer sync) to Dedicated Workers; (2) container monitors enforce CPU usage caps on background workers (max 25% CPU core usage over 10s); (3) workers exceeding resource caps receive graceful termination signals.
standard_reference: W3C WebTransport Section 3 (WebTransport Interface & DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope Exposure)
relevance: Ensures fluid UI performance and stable frame rates during heavy real-time data streaming inside mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Encourage worker-based WebTransport ingestion in developer guidelines and provide SDK starter templates.

title: W3C WebGPU establishes hardware-abstracted GPUAdapter and GPUDevice architectures with explicit limit contracts
summary: W3C WebGPU Candidate Recommendation defines GPUAdapter and GPUDevice interfaces with enforceable hardware limits on buffer, texture, and compute storage.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C WebGPU Candidate Recommendation provides direct, safe access to modern graphics and compute hardware (Vulkan, Metal, Direct3D 12): (1) Adapter and Device Split: `navigator.gpu.requestAdapter()` discovers available physical GPUs, while `adapter.requestDevice(descriptor)` creates an isolated logical device; (2) Hardware Limits Contract: the `GPUDevice.limits` interface exposes strict operational ceilings, including `maxBufferSize` (minimum default 256MB), `maxComputeWorkgroupStorageSize` (minimum default 16KB), and `maxTextureDimension2D` (minimum default 8192); (3) Sandboxed Execution: unlike legacy WebGL, WebGPU does not expose global state machines; all state is encapsulated in immutable pipeline and bind group objects; (4) Memory Isolation: GPU memory allocations are bound to the specific GPUDevice and cannot be accessed or inspected by cross-origin contexts. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app container controls: (1) WebGPU access is gated by the mini-app manifest capability declaration (`"capabilities": ["gpu"]`); (2) the host container clamps `requiredLimits` to prevent rogue mini-apps from requesting excessive VRAM allocations on resource-constrained mobile devices; (3) low-tier devices (<3GB RAM) reject device creation or fall back to lightweight Canvas2D.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU (Candidate Recommendation Draft) Sections 3-5
relevance: Enables next-generation 3D graphics and on-device AI/ML acceleration in super-app mini-apps under strict memory bounds.
operational_recommendation: Enforce container-level memory limit clamps during GPUDevice initialization based on device RAM tiers.

title: WebGPU Shading Language enforces compile-time memory safety, bounds checking and deterministic execution
summary: W3C WGSL eliminates arbitrary pointer arithmetic and mandates strict array/buffer out-of-bounds safety rules.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C WebGPU Shading Language (WGSL) Candidate Recommendation is designed specifically for web security and multi-platform compilation: (1) Memory Safety: WGSL prohibits raw pointer arithmetic and unchecked memory access; pointers only exist within specific address spaces (function, private, workgroup, storage, uniform); (2) Mandatory Bounds Checking: any out-of-bounds buffer or array read returns 0 or a clamped valid value; out-of-bounds writes are discarded without corrupting adjacent memory; (3) Deterministic Shader Validation: shader modules created via `device.createShaderModule()` undergo rigorous semantic and syntactic validation before compilation to native SPIR-V, MSL, or DXIL; (4) Driver Bug Mitigation: WebGPU implementations sanitize WGSL code to neutralize known GPU driver vulnerabilities and infinite execution hangs. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Security review and store policy: (1) static analysis during mini-app store submission parses WGSL shaders to detect abusive compute loops or cryptographic mining signatures; (2) host containers enforce maximum execution time limits on compute shaders; (3) non-compliant or unvalidated shader constructs trigger immediate build rejection.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU Shading Language (WGSL) Candidate Recommendation Draft
relevance: Guarantees that mini-app shader code cannot crash native GPU drivers or execute out-of-bounds memory exploits.
operational_recommendation: Incorporate WGSL AST validation into automated store pipeline to flag crypto-mining and driver stress exploits.

title: WebGPU device.lost lifecycle arbitration enables resilient error recovery and background VRAM reclamation
summary: GPUDevice.lost Promise notifies applications of GPU context invalidation (OOM, driver reset, or deliberate host eviction) with reason tagging.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C WebGPU Section 5.3: (1) `device.lost` Promise: resolves with a `GPUDeviceLostInfo` object when the device is lost, carrying a `reason` property (`'destroyed'` for deliberate user/host disposal, or `'unknown'` for OS GPU driver reset, thermal throttling, or out-of-memory crash); (2) Non-Recoverable State: once a GPUDevice is lost, all associated buffers, textures, bind groups, and pipelines become invalid; subsequent commands result in silent no-ops or rejected promises; (3) Explicit Destruction: calling `device.destroy()` immediately releases GPU memory without waiting for garbage collection. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Host container lifecycle management: (1) when a mini-app enters background state, the super-app container issues `device.destroy()` to immediately reclaim VRAM for foreground tasks; (2) when the mini-app resumes, the container signals the guest runtime to re-initialize an adapter and rebuild GPU state; (3) mini-app SDK guidelines mandate listening to `device.lost` to ensure seamless user state restoration without crashing the super-app.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU Section 5.3 (Device Loss & GPUDeviceLostInfo)
relevance: Prevents super-app out-of-memory crashes on mobile devices by systematically releasing GPU resources when mini-apps are backgrounded.
operational_recommendation: Call device.destroy() on backgrounded mini-apps; require mini-app developers to implement device.lost recovery handlers.

title: WebGPU timestamp queries enforce Cross-Origin Isolation gating and microsecond clock coarsening
summary: WebGPU restricts high-resolution timestamp queries behind Cross-Origin Isolation and applies clock coarsening to neutralize GPU cache timing attacks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] GPU execution timing can expose side-channel signals revealing cross-origin memory layouts or cryptographic keys: (1) Feature Gating: the `timestamp-query` feature in `requestDevice({ requiredFeatures: ['timestamp-query'] })` is restricted by browsers and user agents to secure contexts possessing Cross-Origin Isolation (`crossOriginIsolated = true`); (2) Clock Coarsening: even when permitted, timestamp query results are coarsened (e.g. rounded to 100 microseconds) to defeat microarchitectural cache-probing and side-channel timing attacks; (3) Disallowed Cross-Origin Textures: WebGPU canvas contexts cannot import tainted or cross-origin images without explicit CORS approval, preventing cross-origin pixel leakage through shader timing differentials. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app security configuration: (1) mini-app containers disable `timestamp-query` by default; (2) only enterprise/certified partner mini-apps with strict COOP/COEP isolation can request performance profiling flags; (3) all external media assets imported into WebGPU textures must undergo strict origin verification.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU Security Considerations (Timing Attacks & Timestamp Queries)
relevance: Protects against sophisticated GPU microarchitectural side-channel attacks across co-hosted mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Disable timestamp-query feature flags in production mini-app containers; mandate CORS on all GPU texture assets.

title: Super-app container GPU governance establishes capability tiers, VRAM quotas and graceful WebGL 2 fallback
summary: Super-app multi-tier container governance audits WebGPU hardware availability, bounds VRAM usage per tenant, and arbitrates fallback to WebGL 2 or 2D rendering.
detail: [SPEC FACT] WebGPU support across mobile ecosystems remains heterogeneous (older Android devices and budget chipsets may lack Vulkan 1.1+ or stable drivers): (1) Capability Discovery: host containers evaluate `navigator.gpu` availability and driver stability profiles before exposing the API to mini-app WebViews; (2) Multi-Tier Fallback: standard mini-app rendering frameworks (Three.js, Babylon.js, PixiJS) support dual backends (WebGPU with WebGL 2 fallback); (3) Per-Tenant VRAM Quotas: host OS memory observers track aggregate GPU memory consumption per mini-app WebView process (alert at 150MB, hard kill at 300MB on mid-range devices); (4) Blacklisted GPU Drivers: super-app runtime maintains an up-to-date driver blocklist to disable WebGPU on devices known to suffer kernel panics or visual corruption. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Operating model: (1) include GPU capability tier in mini-app store discovery filters (hide WebGPU-only games from incompatible devices); (2) capture GPU crash telemetry via the host crash reporter; (3) automatically downgrade crashing mini-apps to WebGL 2 mode upon next launch.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU Implementation Guidance & Chrome WebGPU Deployment Best Practices
relevance: Ensures wide compatibility, stability, and crash prevention across diverse smartphone hardware tiers in super-app deployments.
operational_recommendation: Implement client-side driver blocklists, device capability filtering in store search, and automatic WebGL 2 fallback.

title: W3C WebCodecs defines low-overhead hardware-accelerated video/audio encoding and decoding interfaces
summary: W3C WebCodecs Working Draft standardizes VideoEncoder, VideoDecoder, AudioEncoder, and AudioDecoder interfaces for raw frame manipulation without WebAssembly overhead.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C WebCodecs (Working Draft) exposes low-level access to the browser's built-in platform codecs (H.264, VP8, VP9, AV1, AAC, Opus): (1) Core Interfaces: provides `VideoDecoder`, `VideoEncoder`, `AudioDecoder`, and `AudioEncoder` operating on `VideoFrame`, `AudioData`, `EncodedVideoChunk`, and `EncodedAudioChunk` objects; (2) Hardware Acceleration: leverages native OS hardware decoders (Apple VideoToolbox, Android MediaCodec) without requiring bundled third-party WebAssembly codec binaries (saving 5-15MB bundle size and reducing battery consumption by 60-80%); (3) Real-Time Configuration: codecs support dynamic reconfiguration via `.configure()` (e.g. changing bitrate, latencyMode: 'realtime', or keyframe generation) without destroying the decoding session. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container architecture: (1) super-app containers expose WebCodecs to approved mini-apps (video editors, security camera monitors, live-stream shopping); (2) enforce concurrent hardware decoder limits (maximum 2 simultaneous hardware decoders per mini-app) to avoid starving the host super-app; (3) automatically suspend decoder pipelines when mini-apps are minimized.
standard_reference: W3C WebCodecs (Working Draft) Sections 3-6
relevance: Enables ultra-fast, power-efficient multimedia editing and live video streams in mini-apps without bloating bundle size.
operational_recommendation: Expose WebCodecs for media-tier mini-apps; throttle concurrent hardware decoder allocations to prevent OS resource exhaustion.

title: WebCodecs VideoFrame lifecycle mandates explicit disposal to prevent GPU texture and memory leaks
summary: VideoFrame and AudioData objects hold underlying GPU memory and require explicit .close() invocations to avoid catastrophic memory leaks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] VideoFrame objects wrap native GPU surfaces (e.g. Android GraphicBuffer, Apple CVPixelBuffer, DirectX textures) or CPU shared memory: (1) Explicit Resource Disposal: because JavaScript garbage collection is non-deterministic and uncoupled from GPU memory pressure, VideoFrame instances MUST be explicitly released via `videoFrame.close()`; (2) Memory Leak Hazard: retaining unclosed VideoFrames in JavaScript arrays quickly exhausts GPU VRAM, leading to browser tab crashes within seconds during 60fps video processing (60 frames/sec * 8MB/frame = ~480MB/sec uncollected memory); (3) Transferable Semantics: VideoFrames can be cloned via `videoFrame.clone()` or transferred to Web Workers via `postMessage([frame], [frame])`, passing memory ownership and invalidating the source frame. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-app container watchdog: (1) the container injects a proxy wrapper around `VideoDecoder` to monitor outstanding unclosed VideoFrame counts; (2) if unclosed frames exceed 30 frames, the container logs a memory warning and forces garbage collection; (3) store automated linter scans mini-app source code for missing `.close()` calls in decoder output callbacks.
standard_reference: W3C WebCodecs Section 7 (VideoFrame Interface & Resource Reclamation)
relevance: Eliminates the primary cause of out-of-memory crashes in video-processing mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Enforce automated code inspection for VideoFrame.close() calls and track active frame counts in container telemetry.

title: W3C WebXR Device API standardizes spatial computing sessions, reference spaces and immersive rendering loops
summary: W3C WebXR Device API Recommendation defines XRSession modes ('inline', 'immersive-vr', 'immersive-ar') and XRReferenceSpace coordinates for spatial applications.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C WebXR Device API Recommendation provides standardized hardware access to AR/VR headsets, smart glasses, and mobile AR camera tracking: (1) Session Modes: `navigator.xr.requestSession(mode)` supports `'inline'` (embedded canvas), `'immersive-vr'` (exclusive headset display), and `'immersive-ar'` (camera passthrough with virtual overlay); (2) Reference Spaces: applications request coordinate reference spaces (`'viewer'`, `'local'`, `'local-floor'`, `'bounded-floor'`, `'unbounded'`) to track user head position and movement relative to the physical room; (3) Render Loop: immersive sessions use `session.requestAnimationFrame(callback)` synchronized with the XR hardware refresh rate (72Hz, 90Hz, or 120Hz); (4) Input Sources: `session.inputSources` exposes controllers, optical hand-tracking joints, and screen-touch hit testing. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container spatial governance: (1) mini-app AR experiences must declare `"capabilities": ["xr"]` in the mini-app manifest; (2) host container requires explicit user activation (transient user gesture) before invoking `requestSession()`; (3) super-app renders a permanent native close button / exit HUD over the immersive viewport to prevent rogue mini-apps from trapping users in VR/AR mode.
standard_reference: W3C WebXR Device API (Recommendation) Sections 3-7
relevance: Enables immersive AR product try-ons, 3D showroom mini-apps, and metaverse interactions within super-apps.
operational_recommendation: Mandate native overlay exit controls during immersive AR sessions and restrict session initialization to user gestures.

title: WebXR xr-spatial-tracking Permissions Policy restricts physical room scanning and biometric tracking telemetry
summary: The xr-spatial-tracking Permissions-Policy directive gates access to real-world coordinate tracking, protecting user physical environments and gaze data.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Spatial computing introduces severe privacy hazards (room dimension fingerprinting, biometric eye gaze tracking, facial expression inference): (1) Permissions Policy Directive: access to spatial tracking requires the `Permissions-Policy: xr-spatial-tracking=(self)` HTTP header or iframe `allow="xr-spatial-tracking"` attribute; without this directive, `navigator.xr.requestSession()` rejects with a `SecurityError`; (2) Raw Sensor Isolation: WebXR intentionally denies raw camera image access and raw depth sensor arrays to standard sessions; only derived pose matrices and hit-test results are exposed; (3) Gaze Privacy: eye tracking for foveated rendering is handled internally by the platform compositor and never exposed as raw gaze coordinates to script without specialized biometric permissions. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Privacy enforcement: (1) the super-app host controls the `xr-spatial-tracking` policy on mini-app container frames; (2) before granting AR/VR access, the host displays a native consent sheet explaining physical space access; (3) guest mini-apps are prohibited from transmitting spatial mesh data to third-party servers without explicit user disclosure and DPIA compliance.
standard_reference: W3C WebXR Device API Privacy & Security Considerations & Permissions Policy Directive
relevance: Protects user physical privacy and complies with EU GDPR and global privacy standards during AR/VR mini-app usage.
operational_recommendation: Enforce Permissions-Policy: xr-spatial-tracking gating and display clear host consent modals explaining spatial data handling.

title: Super-app container multimodal governance enforces camera, GPU and audio concurrency arbitration
summary: Unified host arbitration coordinates camera hardware, hardware media decoders, and audio focus between concurrent mini-apps and host features.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Multimodal mini-apps combine WebCodecs, WebXR, WebGPU, and camera capture simultaneously, placing extreme strain on mobile OS subsystems: (1) Hardware Mutex: mobile camera sensors (Camera2 on Android, AVCapture on iOS) cannot be shared simultaneously across multiple apps or disjoint WebViews; (2) Audio Session Arbitration: background music, voice chat, and audio decoders must adhere to OS audio focus protocols (e.g. ducking, pausing when incoming phone calls arrive); (3) Thermal Throttling: running WebGPU rendering alongside 4K WebCodecs decoding rapidly elevates device temperature, triggering OS-level CPU/GPU throttling down to 15-30fps. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Operating model: (1) the super-app native container acts as a central hardware arbiter, releasing camera and microphone locks immediately when a mini-app loses user focus; (2) host thermal observers monitor device battery temperature—if temperature exceeds 42°C, the container notifies the mini-app via a lifecycle event to reduce rendering resolution or frame rate; (3) mini-app review audits hardware utilization profiles to certify energy efficiency.
standard_reference: Super-App Container Practice: Multimodal Hardware Arbitration, Thermal Monitoring & Focus Lifecycle
relevance: Prevents device overheating, battery drain, and hardware lock contention in graphics- and media-heavy super-apps.
operational_recommendation: Implement container-level hardware mutexes for camera/mic and emit thermal warning events to throttling-capable mini-apps.
